67.x: APGENCO / APPDCL – State power generation

67.x: APSECM – Energy conservation

67.x: PM Surya Ghar in AP – 20.5 lakh SC/ST households (~2 kW)

67.x: Virtual Net Metering – For ~16 lakh SC/ST households without their own rooftops

68.s: Which of these man-made units can also be studied as an ecosystem?
68.x: Ecosystem – A community of organisms together with the non-living environment in which they live, interacting as one functional unit (pond, ocean, forest, even an aquarium)

68.s: Who coined the term "ecosystem" in 1935?
68.x: Term coined by – British botanist Sir Arthur G. Tansley in 1935

68.s: Besides biotic, what is the other component of an ecosystem?
68.x: Two components – Biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic (energy, water, air, soil, nutrients, climate); evolution is a process, not a component

68.s: What kind of system is an ecosystem, with energy and matter entering and leaving?
68.x: Nature – A natural, open system – energy and matter enter and leave; it has its own productivity; it has no fixed, closed boundaries

68.s: Where do the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere meet to form a narrow zone of life?
68.x: Biosphere – Narrow zone where the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere meet; treated as an open system – energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat; strictly, the Earth is open for energy but nearly closed for matter

68.s: How are all components of an ecosystem related, so that a change in one affects the rest?
68.x: Interdependence – All components are interdependent – a change in one population affects the rest; human activities affect the environment

68.s: Which ecosystem function is also called homeostasis?
68.x: Functions – Energy flow (one-way), nutrient cycling, production, self-regulation (homeostasis)

68.s: Which part of an ecosystem is its dynamic part, as against producers, consumers and decomposers?
68.x: Structure vs dynamics – Producers, consumers and decomposers form the structure; the food chain is the dynamic part

68.s: Which of these does NOT cycle in an ecosystem?
68.x: Biogeochemical (nutrient) cycle – Movement of chemical elements (C, N, P) through biotic and abiotic components – energy does not cycle; photosynthesis removes CO₂; the phosphorus cycle begins with rock weathering

68.s: What is the primary source and driving force of energy in an ecosystem?
68.x: Energy – Sunlight – primary source and driving force

68.s: Which of these is a climatic abiotic factor?
68.x: Climatic – Light, temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind

68.s: To what do edaphic factors relate?
68.x: Edaphic – Soil – texture, pH, minerals, drainage

68.s: Which factors do altitude, slope and aspect make up?
68.x: Topographic – Altitude, slope, aspect

68.s: Which of these is an abiotic material of an ecosystem?
68.x: Materials – CO₂, water, nitrates, phosphates; humus and other organic compounds

68.s: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
68.x: Abiotic factor – Any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment – air, water, light (plants, bacteria and animals are biotic)

68.s: Which of these is an abiotic stressor of forests?
68.x: Frost – An abiotic stressor of forests (freezes soil moisture, injures tissue); oomycetes, parasites and pathogens are biotic

68.s: Which law says growth is limited by the nutrient in shortest supply?
68.x: Liebig's Law of the Minimum – Growth is limited by the nutrient in shortest supply

68.s: Which law says both too little and too much of a factor limit growth?
68.x: Shelford's Law of Tolerance – Both too little and too much limit

68.s: What is an organism that tolerates only a narrow temperature range called?
68.x: Stenothermal – Tolerates only a narrow temperature range; eurythermal a wide range (likewise stenohaline / euryhaline for salinity)

68.s: Which of these animals is cold-blooded (poikilothermic)?
68.x: Cold-blooded (poikilothermic) – Frogs, snakes, lizards, fish, crocodiles – take the temperature of their surroundings

68.s: Why does terrestrial life need fresh water?
68.x: Water balance – Organisms must maintain body water; terrestrial life needs fresh water because it cannot tolerate the high salt of saline water

68.s: What do autotrophs take in to make carbohydrates with sunlight and chlorophyll?
68.x: Autotrophs – Make their own food; their carbon and energy needs are met by photosynthesis – they take in CO₂ and water and, with sunlight and chlorophyll, make carbohydrates

68.s: Which process turns light energy into chemical energy?
68.x: Photosynthesis – Turns light energy into chemical energy; needs light – normally daytime sunlight, but it also runs under moonlight or artificial light

68.s: Which organisms are the major producers in water?
68.x: Major producers – On land herbaceous and woody plants; in water phytoplankton / microscopic algae and seaweeds

68.s: Which compound do chemoautotrophic bacteria of deep-sea vents oxidise?
68.x: Chemoautotrophs – Bacteria of deep-sea vents / active volcanoes oxidise hydrogen sulphide; many archaea (methanogens) use energy from chemical compounds – also producers

68.s: Which light do green sulphur bacteria use for photosynthesis?
68.x: Infrared photosynthesis – Some bacteria (green sulphur bacteria) use invisible infrared light

68.s: Which organisms act as intermediaries between the biotic and abiotic components?
68.x: Link between biotic and abiotic – Producers act as intermediaries; decomposers are also called the link, as they return nutrients to the abiotic pool

68.s: Which green alga has the highest efficiency of converting solar energy into chemical energy?
68.x: Chlorella – Green alga with the highest efficiency of converting solar energy into chemical energy

68.s: From where does most of the world's oxygen come?
68.x: Oxygen – Most comes from algae / marine phytoplankton – ocean phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria give about 50% of the world's oxygen, more than rainforests; surface water holds far less oxygen than air

68.s: In which part does a cactus carry out photosynthesis?
68.x: Cactus – Photosynthesises in its green stem (leaves reduced to spines)

68.s: Which of these is a primary consumer?
68.x: Primary consumers (herbivores) – Cow, deer, goat, rabbit, caterpillar, zooplankton

68.s: Which of these is a secondary consumer?
68.x: Secondary consumers – Wolves, frog, fox

68.s: Which of these is a top carnivore?
68.x: Tertiary / top carnivores – Lion, tiger, hawk, eagle

68.s: Which of these is an omnivore?
68.x: Omnivores – Man (primary and secondary consumer; top-order heterotroph), bear

68.s: Which organisms are decomposers (saprotrophs)?
68.x: Decomposers (saprotrophs) – Bacteria and fungi (viruses are not decomposers); recycle nutrients

68.s: Which of these is a detritivore?
68.x: Detritivores – Earthworms, millipedes, woodlice, nematodes

68.s: What mode of nutrition do fungi mostly have?
68.x: Fungi – Heterotrophs – mostly saprotrophs absorbing food from dead matter; some parasitic or symbiotic

68.s: What is getting food from another living organism without killing it called?
68.x: Parasitic nutrition – Food from another living organism without killing it

68.s: What is the breakdown of dead organic matter by microbes into simple nutrients called?
68.x: Decomposition – Breakdown of dead organic matter by microorganisms (bacteria, fungi) into simple inorganic nutrients; bacteria turn biodegradable waste into compost

68.s: What is fully decomposed litter called?
68.x: Steps – Fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralisation; fully decomposed litter = humus

68.s: What kind of detritus decomposes fast?
68.x: Speed – Fast when detritus is rich in nitrogen and sugars and the climate warm and moist; slow with lignin, chitin, cold or anaerobic conditions

68.s: What is blocked if decomposers are absent from an ecosystem?
68.x: Without decomposers – Mineral (nutrient) movement is blocked – energy flow continues for a while, but nutrients are not recycled

68.s: What are microconsumers (osmotrophs) also called?
68.x: Consumer types – Macroconsumers = phagotrophs; microconsumers = saprotrophs (osmotrophs)

68.s: What kind of organism is Azotobacter?
68.x: Azotobacter – Free-living nitrogen fixer

68.s: What are protists?
68.x: Protists – Unicellular eukaryotes; cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes

68.s: How does the camel adapt to dry conditions?
68.x: Other adaptations – Reptiles – stenothermal; camel – passes little urine

68.s: Which of these is a natural terrestrial ecosystem?
68.x: Natural terrestrial – Forest, grassland, desert, tundra, mountain

68.s: Which of these is a natural aquatic ecosystem?
68.x: Natural aquatic – Pond, lake, river, wetland, estuary, ocean

68.s: Which of these is an artificial (man-modified) ecosystem?
68.x: Artificial (man-modified) – Crop field, aquarium, park, village; city = extreme example

68.s: Which is the classic self-sufficient natural ecosystem?
68.x: A lake / pond is the classic self-sufficient (complete, self-regulating) natural ecosystem; an aquarium, farmland or polyhouse depends on human inputs.

68.s: Which organisms are also called the link because they return nutrients to the abiotic pool?
68.x: Link role – Producers act as intermediaries between the biotic and abiotic components (many books also call decomposers the link – they return nutrients to the abiotic pool)

68.s: Under which conditions is decomposition slow?
68.x: Rate – Fast with nitrogen- and sugar-rich detritus in warm, moist climate; slow with lignin, chitin, cold or anaerobic conditions

68.s: What are macroconsumers also called?
68.x: Consumer terms – Macroconsumers = phagotrophs; microconsumers = saprotrophs (osmotrophs)

68.s: What is the order in which organisms feed on each other, from producer to carnivore, called?
68.x: Food chain: the order in which organisms feed upon each other – producer → herbivore → carnivore; energy passes along it. It runs across species (not within one species' population) and does not show the numbers eaten – that is shown by a pyramid or food web.

68.s: What does a grazing food chain start with?
68.x: Grazing – Living green plants (autotrophs capture energy and pass it to herbivores) – Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake (→ eagle); grass → goat → human

68.s: Which of these is a grazing food chain?
68.x: Grazing – Living green plants (autotrophs capture energy and pass it to herbivores) – Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake (→ eagle); grass → goat → human

68.s: What does a detritus food chain start with?
68.x: Detritus (DFC) – Dead organic matter (dead leaves) – Leaf litter → earthworm → chicken → hawk

68.s: Which of these is a detritus food chain?
68.x: Detritus (DFC) – Dead organic matter (dead leaves) – Leaf litter → earthworm → chicken → hawk

68.s: With which organisms does a pond food chain start?
68.x: Pond / aquatic – Phytoplankton – → zooplankton → small fish → large fish

68.s: What comes after phytoplankton in a pond food chain?
68.x: Pond / aquatic – Phytoplankton – → zooplankton → small fish → large fish

68.s: With which organisms does the marine food chain ending in herrings start?
68.x: Marine – Diatoms – → Crustaceans → herrings

68.s: Which animals eat diatoms and are eaten by herrings in a marine food chain?
68.x: Marine – Diatoms – → Crustaceans → herrings

68.s: Which animals eat the grasshopper or rabbit in a grassland food chain?
68.x: Grassland – Grass – → grasshopper or rabbit → snake or hawk

68.s: Through which food chain does more energy flow on land?
68.x: In water the grazing chain is the main energy conduit; on land more energy flows through the detritus chain.

68.s: What is the feeding step an organism occupies in a food chain called?
68.x: Trophic level – The functional position (feeding step) an organism occupies in a food chain

68.s: Which of these is a producer at trophic level I?
68.x: I – Producers – green plants, phytoplankton, seaweeds, chemosynthetic bacteria (vents, active volcanoes), algae

68.s: Which of these aquatic organisms is a primary consumer (trophic level II)?
68.x: II – Primary consumers / herbivores – deer, ants, caterpillar, goat, zooplankton

68.s: Which of these is a secondary consumer at trophic level III?
68.x: III – Secondary consumers – frog, fox; a man eating goat flesh

68.s: At which trophic level is the snake in grass → grasshopper → frog → snake?
68.x: IV – Tertiary / top carnivores – snake (in grass → grasshopper → frog → snake), hawk, lion

68.s: To which trophic level do decomposers and detritivores belong?
o: No single level – they recycle all levels
68.x: No single level – Decomposers and detritivores recycle all levels

68.s: Which organisms occupy the highest trophic level?
68.x: Highest trophic level – Carnivores (top carnivores)

68.s: When man eats goat flesh, he acts as a?
68.x: Man – Omnivore – primary as well as secondary consumer; eating goat flesh makes him a secondary consumer

68.s: Which organisms are the most numerous in a typical food chain?
68.x: Numbers – Producers outnumber primary consumers (energy and numbers fall at each level)

68.s: How many levels do food chains rarely exceed?
68.x: Chain length – A species can occupy more than one level; chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels

68.s: Which level is missing from the chain "tiger, grass, snake, frog"?
68.x: Missing level – "Tiger, grass, snake, frog" has no herbivore – the second level is missing

68.s: How does a more complex food web affect an ecosystem?
68.x: Food web: a network of interlinked food chains; more complex → more stable (alternative feeding paths).

68.s: What is an ecosystem's ability to withstand a disturbance called?
68.x: Resistance – Withstand a disturbance

68.s: What is an ecosystem's ability to recover after a disturbance called?
68.x: Resilience – Recover after a disturbance

68.s: What is self-regulation of an ecosystem up to a limit through feedback called?
68.x: Homeostasis – Self-regulation up to a limit through feedback

68.s: Which is the most stable ecosystem?
68.x: Diverse systems (rainforest, coral reef) are more stable than tundra, desert or monoculture; the ocean (marine ecosystem) is the most stable ecosystem – it stays unchanged over long periods. Warming and ocean acidification weaken calcifying plankton and corals, disrupting marine food webs.

68.s: What is bioaccumulation?
o: Build-up of a pollutant inside one organism over its life
68.x: Build-up of a pollutant inside one organism over its life – Rising concentration of toxicants at each higher trophic level – maximum in the topmost level

68.s: Which kind of pollutants biomagnify along food chains?
68.x: What biomagnifies – Only persistent, fat-soluble, non-biodegradable pollutants (DDT, mercury, PCBs) – an increase in toxicants

68.s: What effect of DDT caused seabird population crashes?
68.x: DDT (a chlorinated hydrocarbon) – Food crop → rat → snake → hawk – highest in the hawk; grasshopper → toad → snake – highest in the snake; causes eggshell thinning and seabird crashes

68.s: Which disease was caused by methylmercury poisoning in Japan?
68.x: Methylmercury – Minamata disease (Japan)

68.s: Which of these is a secondary pollutant?
68.x: Pollutant types – Biodegradable = sewage; non-biodegradable = DDT, plastic, asbestos; primary = CO, SO₂, NOx; secondary = O₃, PAN, smog

68.s: What is dead, decaying animal flesh eaten by vultures and hyenas called?
68.x: Carrion – Dead, often decaying, animal flesh – food of scavengers (vultures, hyenas)

68.s: Which of these is an example of mutualism?
68.x: Mutualism – +/+ – Lichen, fig–fig wasp, mycorrhiza; bees and flowers

68.s: What happens to the two partners in commensalism?
68.x: Commensalism – +/0 – Epiphytic orchid on a tree; cattle egret near cattle; suckerfish on shark

68.s: Which of these is an example of parasitism?
68.x: Parasitism – +/− – Cuscuta, ticks, lice, tapeworm

68.s: Which of these is an example of predation?
68.x: Predation – +/− – Tiger–deer; Pisaster eating mussels

68.s: Which principle applies to competition for the same limited resource?
68.x: Competition – −/− – Same limited resource; Gause's exclusion principle

68.s: What happens to the two partners in amensalism?
68.x: Amensalism – −/0 – Large tree shading a small plant; Penicillium (antibiosis)

68.s: Which of these is an example of amensalism?
68.x: Amensalism – −/0 – Large tree shading a small plant; Penicillium (antibiosis)

68.s: How are the two species affected in neutralism?
68.x: Neutralism – 0/0 – Neither affected

68.s: What is mycorrhiza?
o: Fungi and plant roots in mutualism
68.x: Mycorrhiza – Fungi + roots (mutualism)

68.s: Which dye is extracted from lichens such as Roccella?
68.x: Lichen – Fungus + alga; litmus is a dye extracted from lichens (e.g. Roccella)

68.s: Which pair is a coevolved plant–pollinator?
68.x: Coevolved pollinators – Fig–fig wasp, yucca–yucca moth, Ophrys orchid–bee (sexual deceit)

68.s: What kind of relationship do bees and flowers share?
68.x: Bees and flowers – Symbiotic (mutualistic) – bees get nectar and pollen, flowers get pollinated

68.s: For what do epiphytes use their host plant?
68.x: Epiphytes – Use the host only for mechanical support; take moisture and nutrients from air and rain

68.s: What kind of parasite is mistletoe?
68.x: Mistletoe – Partial (hemi-) parasite – green and photosynthetic, but draws water and minerals from the host (green plants are autotrophs)

68.s: What is a species whose effect is far larger than its numbers called?
68.x: Keystone – Effect far larger than its numbers – Pisaster sea star (controls mussels), sea otter

68.s: Which of these is a keystone species?
68.x: Keystone – Effect far larger than its numbers – Pisaster sea star (controls mussels), sea otter

68.s: What does a foundation species do?
68.x: Foundation – Creates or shapes habitat – Corals, kelp

68.s: Which of these is a foundation species?
68.x: Foundation – Creates or shapes habitat – Corals, kelp

68.s: What is a charismatic species that draws support for conservation called?
68.x: Flagship – Charismatic, draws support – Tiger, giant panda

68.s: Which of these is a flagship species?
68.x: Flagship – Charismatic, draws support – Tiger, giant panda

68.s: What does an indicator species do?
68.x: Indicator – Signals environmental health – Lichens (SO₂)

68.s: Which organisms are indicators of SO₂ pollution?
68.x: Indicator – Signals environmental health – Lichens (SO₂)

68.s: What is a wide-ranging species whose protection protects many others called?
68.x: Umbrella – Wide-ranging; protecting it protects many – Tiger, snow leopard

68.s: Which of these is an umbrella species?
68.x: Umbrella – Wide-ranging; protecting it protects many – Tiger, snow leopard

68.s: What is the predictable appearance of species after a disturbance called?
68.x: Community structure is shaped by foundation and keystone species; succession = the predictable appearance of species after a disturbance.

68.s: Which statement about the environment is true?
68.x: Environment – Sum total of living and non-living components, influences and events surrounding an organism; biotic and abiotic factors interact; never static

68.s: Which element of the environment includes land, water, air and nutrients?
68.x: Composite – Physical (land, water, air, nutrients), biological (organisms) and cultural elements

68.s: Who first used the term "environment" in English (1828)?
68.x: Term first used in English – Thomas Carlyle (1828)

68.s: Which spheres make up the physical environment?
68.x: Physical – Lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere; nutrients, water, air

68.s: What does the biotic environment include?
68.x: Biotic – Plants, animals, microbes

68.s: What does the cultural environment include?
68.x: Cultural – Man-made – social, economic, political institutions

68.s: From which parts of the environment do renewable resources come?
68.x: Renewable resources – Come from both biotic and abiotic parts (sunlight, wind, water)

68.s: Which is a primary function of the environment?
68.x: Primary functions – Provide resources, assimilate wastes, habitat for biodiversity

68.s: Which statement on habitat and environment is correct?
o: Every habitat is an environment, but an environment may exist without life
A habitat can exist without life
68.x: Habitat and environment – Every habitat is an environment, but an environment may exist without life

68.s: Which of these is NOT a natural resource?
68.x: Natural resources – Coal, petrol (from crude oil), cow dung; concrete is man-made

68.s: Which science is named from Greek oikos (home) and logos (study)?
68.x: Ecology – Greek *oikos* = home + *logos* = study – the relationship between organisms (plants, animals) and their environment

68.s: Who coined the term "ecology" in 1866?
68.x: Coined by – Ernst Haeckel in 1866 ("Ökologie")

68.s: Which other name is ecology known by?
68.x: Also called – Bionomics – stresses natural systems that influence human systems

68.s: What is the ecology of a single species in relation to its environment called?
68.x: Autecology – Ecology of a single species in relation to its environment

68.s: What is the ecology of communities called?
68.x: Synecology – Ecology of communities

68.s: Who coined the term "deep ecology" in 1973?
68.x: Deep ecology – Term of the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess (1973)

68.s: Whose concept is "The Ecological Transition" (1976)?
68.x: Ecological transition – Concept of John W. Bennett (*The Ecological Transition*, 1976)

68.s: What is an ecad?
o: A plant modified by its environment without genetic change
68.x: Ecad – An organism (plant) modified by its environment – a habitat form without genetic change

68.s: What are differences among individuals of the same species called?
68.x: Variation – Differences among individuals of the same species

68.s: Which level of organisation lies between community and biome?
68.x: Smallest to largest: organism → population → community → ecosystem → (landscape) → biome → biosphere.

68.s: What are individuals of one species in an area called?
68.x: Population – Individuals of one species in an area

68.s: What are all the populations of different species in an area called?
68.x: Community – All populations of different species in an area

68.s: What is a community plus its non-living environment called?
68.x: Ecosystem – Community + its non-living environment; basic functional unit of ecology

68.s: What is a large region defined by climate and dominant vegetation called?
68.x: Biome – Large region defined by climate + dominant vegetation (rainforest, tundra, desert)

68.s: What do all the ecosystems of the Earth together form?
68.x: Biosphere – Narrow zone of contact of lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere where life exists; all ecosystems together

68.s: Who coined the term "biological diversity"?
68.x: Biodiversity – Measured as alpha, beta, gamma; "biological diversity" coined by Raymond F. Dasmann

68.s: Who proposed the biodiversity hotspot concept?
68.x: Hotspot concept – Norman Myers (≥1,500 endemic vascular plants, ≥70% habitat lost)

68.s: What is the whole sequence of communities in a succession called?
68.x: Sere – Whole sequence of communities in succession

68.s: What is a continuous habitat broken into isolated patches called?
68.x: Habitat fragmentation – Continuous habitat broken into isolated patches

68.s: What is a human-altered terrestrial biome called?
68.x: Anthrome – Human-altered terrestrial biome

68.s: Who coined the term "biosphere" in 1875?
68.x: Eduard Suess – Coined "biosphere" (1875)

68.s: Who gave the ecological (habitat) niche concept in 1917?
68.x: Joseph Grinnell – Ecological niche concept (habitat niche, 1917)

68.s: Who wrote *Animal Ecology* (1927) and introduced the pyramid of numbers?
68.x: Charles Elton – *Animal Ecology* (1927); food chains; pyramid of numbers

68.s: Who proposed the n-dimensional niche (1957)?
68.x: G.E. Hutchinson – n-dimensional niche (1957)

68.s: Who gave the ten percent law of energy transfer (1942)?
68.x: Raymond Lindeman – Ten percent law (1942)

68.s: Who wrote *Fundamentals of Ecology* (1953)?
68.x: E.P. Odum – *Fundamentals of Ecology* (1953)

68.s: Who studied ecological succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes?
68.x: H.C. Cowles – Ecological succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes

68.s: Who described the phases of succession in 1916?
68.x: F.E. Clements – Phases of succession (1916)

68.s: Who is called the father of Indian ecology?
68.x: Ramdeo Misra – Father of Indian ecology

68.s: Who discovered the cell nucleus?
68.x: Robert Brown – Discovered the cell nucleus

68.s: Who is called the father of microbiology?
68.x: Leeuwenhoek – Father of microbiology

68.s: Who gave the universal law of gravitation?
68.x: Newton – Universal law of gravitation

68.s: What is a transition zone where two communities meet called?
68.x: Ecotone – Transition zone where two communities meet – mangroves (marine–terrestrial), estuary, grassland (forest–desert), river bank; a uniform forest stand has none

68.s: What is the occurrence of more species and higher density in an ecotone called?
68.x: Edge effect – More species and higher density of some species in the ecotone; they are edge species

68.s: Which ecogeographic rule says animals in colder climates are larger?

68.x: Allen – Colder = shorter ears and limbs

68.x: Jordan – Fish vertebrae – colder = more

68.s: Which rule says animals in warm-humid regions are darker?
68.x: Gloger – Colouration – warm-humid = darker

68.s: Which rule says sexual size dimorphism increases with body size?
68.x: Rensch's rule – Sexual size dimorphism increases with body size (tested in shorebirds)

68.s: In which habitat do xerophytes grow?

68.s: Which plant is a typical xerophyte with a green photosynthetic stem?
68.x: Xerophytes – Dry – Thick cuticle, sunken stomata, spines, CAM, green photosynthetic stem – Opuntia (cactus); generally succulent; long, deep roots to search for water; no broad thin leaves

68.s: What water supply do mesophytes need?
68.x: Mesophytes – Moderate water supply – Neither very dry nor very wet

68.s: What kind of conditions suit mesophytes?
o: Neither very dry nor very wet
68.x: Mesophytes – Moderate water supply – Neither very dry nor very wet

68.s: In which habitat do hydrophytes grow?

68.s: Which of these is a hydrophyte?
68.x: Hydrophytes – Water – Aerenchyma, reduced roots – Hydrilla, lotus

68.s: In which habitat do halophytes grow?
68.x: Halophytes – Saline – Pneumatophores, vivipary – Rhizophora; salt filtered out at the roots (ultrafiltration), salt glands, succulence

68.s: Which mangrove halophyte shows pneumatophores and vivipary?
68.x: Halophytes – Saline – Pneumatophores, vivipary – Rhizophora; salt filtered out at the roots (ultrafiltration), salt glands, succulence

68.s: From where do phreatophytes draw water?
68.x: Phreatophytes – Groundwater – Deep roots

68.s: What adaptation do phreatophytes have?
68.x: Phreatophytes – Groundwater – Deep roots

68.s: What do lithophytes grow on?
68.x: Lithophytes – Rocks

68.s: In which habitat do cryophytes grow?
68.x: Cryophytes – Snow and ice – Mostly algae, mosses, lichens – e.g. red snow (Chlamydomonas nivalis)

68.s: Which alga causes "red snow" as a cryophyte?
68.x: Cryophytes – Snow and ice – Mostly algae, mosses, lichens – e.g. red snow (Chlamydomonas nivalis)

68.s: Which Raunkiaer life form has buds below ground or water?
68.x: Cryptophytes are Raunkiaer's life form with buds below ground or water. Hot desert soil does not promote root growth.

68.s: Which plants have pneumatophores (breathing roots)?
68.x: Aerial roots: mangroves have pneumatophores (breathing roots) and stilt roots; epiphytic orchids have aerial (velamen) roots.

68.s: What kind of plant is Cuscuta (dodder)?
68.x: Cuscuta (dodder) – Parasitic angiosperm, stem parasite: leafless, without chlorophyll; haustoria tap the host's stem (xylem and phloem)

68.s: Which insectivorous plant is called the pitcher plant?
68.x: Nepenthes – Pitcher plant

68.s: Which insectivorous plant is the aquatic bladderwort?
68.x: Utricularia (bladderwort) – Aquatic insectivorous plant

68.s: What is the common name of Drosera?
68.x: Drosera – Sundew

68.s: What does Aldrovanda have on its leaf midrib to trap insects?
68.x: Aldrovanda – Free-floating, rootless aquatic insectivorous plant; the only species in India in the salt marshes of the Sunderbans, also in fresh-water ponds and lakes; sensitive trigger hairs on the leaf midrib

68.s: Where in India is Pinguicula (butterwort) found?
68.x: Pinguicula (Butterwort) – Alpine Himalayas, Kashmir to Sikkim; stream-sides in cool boggy places

68.s: What is Nostoc?
68.x: Sequoia / Nostoc – Giant conifer / a cyanobacterium

68.s: For which nutrient do insectivorous plants trap insects?
68.x: Insectivorous plants trap insects for nitrogen.

68.s: What is a short-term, individual-level adjustment to environmental change called?
68.x: Acclimation – Short-term, individual-level physiological, anatomical or morphological adjustment to environmental change

68.s: What is a genetic, multi-generation change in a population called?
68.x: Adaptation – Genetic, multi-generation change in a population

68.s: In what conditions does acclimatization take place?
68.x: Acclimatization – Compensatory adjustment in natural (outdoor) conditions, e.g. to seasonal temperature; plants acclimatize to rising CO₂, so the CO₂-fertilization effect diminishes over time

68.s: In which direction does energy flow in an ecosystem?
68.x: Direction – Unidirectional: sunlight → producers → herbivores → carnivores; energy is not cycled

68.s: What is the primary source and driving force of an ecosystem?
68.x: Solar energy – Primary source and driving force of an ecosystem

68.s: Which law says energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only transformed?
68.x: Law of conservation of energy (first law of thermodynamics) – Energy can be neither created nor destroyed but can be transformed – light → chemical energy in photosynthesis

68.s: What form is energy lost in at each transfer, by the second law of thermodynamics?
68.x: Second law – Each transfer loses energy as heat

68.s: What share of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) do plants fix?
68.x: PAR – Under 50% of sunlight; plants fix about 2–10% of PAR

68.s: What share of the sunlight falling on leaves do green plants capture?
68.x: Capture by leaves – Green plants capture only about 1% of the sunlight falling on their leaves

68.s: What is the total primary production efficiency of incoming solar energy?
68.x: Total primary production efficiency – Share of incoming solar energy captured and used in photosynthesis – about 1–2%

68.s: What is the total rate of organic matter fixed by producers in photosynthesis called?
68.x: GPP (Gross Primary Production) – Total rate of organic matter (solar energy) fixed by producers in photosynthesis

68.s: What is GPP minus producer respiration called?
68.x: NPP – GPP − producer respiration; available to consumers

68.s: At which level is primary productivity measured?
68.x: Primary productivity – Rate at which solar energy is stored in green plants as food (autotroph level)

68.s: At which level is secondary productivity measured?
68.x: Secondary productivity – Rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers (heterotroph level)

68.s: Which organisms are the producers in aquatic primary production?
68.x: Aquatic primary production – Depends on light penetration, nutrients and temperature; phytoplankton are the producers

68.s: Which ecosystem has the highest NPP per unit area?
68.x: Highest NPP per unit area – Tropical rainforest; estuaries, coral reefs, swamps, mangroves also high

68.s: Which ecosystems have the lowest productivity?
68.x: Lowest – Deserts and open ocean (ocean total still large by area)

68.s: Which of these has the highest productivity?
68.x: Decreasing productivity – Mangroves > grasslands > lakes > oceans; ecotones (mangroves, estuaries) beat their surroundings

68.s: What does upwelling bring to the ocean surface?
68.x: Upwelling – Brings nutrient-rich deep water to the surface – high phytoplankton productivity

68.s: Which ecosystem had the highest NPP (~2,500 g/m²/yr) in Whittaker & Likens (1975)?
68.x: NPP (Whittaker & Likens 1975, g/m²/yr) – Algal beds and reefs ~2,500, tropical rainforest ~2,200, swamps and marshes ~2,000, estuaries ~1,500; tropical forests are usually given as highest

68.s: What is the salinity of freshwater?
68.x: Freshwater – < 5 ppt – Lotic: rivers; Lentic: ponds, lakes, swamps

68.s: What are flowing freshwater bodies like rivers called?
68.x: Freshwater – < 5 ppt – Lotic: rivers; Lentic: ponds, lakes, swamps

68.s: What is the salinity range of brackish water?
68.x: Brackish – 5–35 ppt – Estuaries (≈35 ppt at the mouth), mangroves

68.s: Which of these is a brackish water ecosystem?
68.x: Brackish – 5–35 ppt – Estuaries (≈35 ppt at the mouth), mangroves

68.s: What is the salinity of marine water?
68.x: Marine – ≥ 35 ppt – Open ocean, coral reefs, hydrothermal vents

68.s: Which of these is a marine ecosystem?
68.x: Marine – ≥ 35 ppt – Open ocean, coral reefs, hydrothermal vents

68.s: Which lake zone is shallow, with light reaching the bottom and rooted plants?
68.x: Littoral (lake) – Shallow; light reaches the bottom; rooted plants

68.s: Which lake zone is the open, sunlit surface water where phytoplankton abound?
68.x: Limnetic zone (lake) – Open, sunlit surface water away from the shore – phytoplankton abound

68.s: Which lake zone is deep and dark, with decomposers?
68.x: Profundal (lake) – Deep, dark; decomposers

68.s: What is the ocean's open water column called?
68.x: Pelagic / Benthic (ocean) – Open water column / sea floor

68.s: Which ocean zone lies below ~1,000 m in darkness?
68.x: Aphotic (ocean) – Below ~1,000 m, dark

68.s: What is a lake with low nutrients and clear water called?
68.x: Lakes – Oligotrophic = low nutrients, clear; eutrophic = nutrient-rich, algal blooms

68.s: Which is the largest ecosystem, covering ~71% of the surface?
68.x: Ocean – Largest ecosystem (~71% of the surface)

68.s: How many million years ago (Ordovician) do the oldest coral reefs date from?
68.x: Coral reefs – "Rainforests of the sea"; also break storm waves; usually named the oldest ecosystem (reefs from ~485 million years ago, Ordovician)

68.s: In which year's Indian Ocean tsunami did mangroves prove a bio-shield?
68.x: Mangroves – Specialised tropical/subtropical coastal forests that stabilise the shoreline; buffer cyclones; a bio-shield against tsunamis and storm surges (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami)

68.s: Which rivers form estuaries on India's west coast?
68.x: West-coast estuaries – Narmada, Tapi

68.s: When was the Ramsar Convention on wetlands signed?
68.x: Ramsar Convention – 2 Feb 1971, Ramsar, Iran; not punitive; no duty to protect every wetland; Montreux Record

68.s: Since when has India been a party to the Ramsar Convention?
68.x: India – Party since 1982; 103 Ramsar sites (Oct 2026)

68.s: Which rules replaced India's Wetlands Rules 2010?
68.x: Indian law – Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 (replaced India's own Wetlands Rules 2010, which covered the wetland's drainage / catchment area)

68.s: Which State has India's largest wetland area?
68.x: Largest wetland area – Gujarat

68.s: What share of India's wetland area is coastal (National Wetland Atlas 2011)?
68.x: Wetland types in India – Inland ≈ 69%, coastal ≈ 27% of wetland area (SAC National Wetland Atlas 2011)

68.s: Which of these is a coastal wetland?
68.x: Wetland functions – Flood moderation, purification, biodiversity, carbon storage; lagoons are coastal wetlands

68.s: Why are wetlands called the "kidneys" of the landscape?
o: Aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and nutrients
68.x: Wetlands as kidneys – Aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and excess nutrients

68.s: Which freshwater lake lies between the Godavari and Krishna deltas?
68.x: Kolleru – Freshwater lake between the Godavari and Krishna deltas

68.s: Which brackish lagoon lies on the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu border?
68.x: Pulicat – Brackish lagoon, AP–TN border

68.s: Which mangrove estuary lies in the Godavari delta?
68.x: Coringa – Mangrove estuary, Godavari delta

68.s: To which forest range do Nallamala and Seshachalam belong?
68.x: Nallamala, Seshachalam – Eastern Ghats forests

68.s: What is the length of Andhra Pradesh's coastline (revised, PIB Dec 2025)?
68.x: AP coastline – 1,053.07 km – 3rd in India after Gujarat and Tamil Nadu (revised figures, PIB Dec 2025)

68.s: Which mangrove swamp fringes Andhra Pradesh's coastal plain in the Godavari delta?
68.x: Coastal plain – Fringed by mangrove swamps (Coringa, Krishna delta) and palm trees

68.s: Which body plans Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs) in AP?
68.x: OECMs – The AP State Biodiversity Board plans Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures – conserved areas outside protected areas

68.s: What is an organism's ecological niche, as against its habitat ("address")?
68.x: Physical place where an organism lives – its "address" – Functional role of a species in its habitat – its "profession"

68.s: How many species can share an identical niche?
68.x: One habitat holds many species – Unique to each species – no two species have identical niches

68.s: Whose concept is the ecological niche (1917)?
68.x: Ecological niche – Physical space plus the functional role in the community – range of conditions tolerated, resources used, role played; concept of Grinnell

68.s: What is the full range of conditions a species could use without other species' interference called?
68.x: Fundamental niche – Full range of biotic and abiotic conditions and resources a species could use free from interference of other species

68.s: What is the actual range of conditions a species uses under competition called?
68.x: Realised niche – Actual range used under competition

68.s: Which animal is a classic niche specialist, eating only eucalyptus?
68.x: Niche breadth – Specialists (koala – only eucalyptus) vs generalists

68.s: What is coexistence of competing species by using different parts of a resource called?
68.x: Resource partitioning – Competing species coexist by using different parts of a shared resource

68.s: What are hydrophytes?
68.x: Terrestrial vs hydrophytes – Terrestrial organisms live on land; hydrophytes are aquatic plants (not necessarily rootless)

68.s: What is the birth rate of a population called?
68.x: Natality – Birth of individuals; rate per unit population per unit time, or individuals produced per female per unit time

68.s: What is the number of deaths in a population per unit time called?
68.x: Mortality – Deaths per unit time

68.s: What is the number of individuals per unit area called?
68.x: Density – Individuals per unit area (or volume)

68.s: Which is a community trait rather than a population attribute?
68.x: Others – Age structure, sex ratio, dispersal (dominant vegetation is a community trait)

68.s: Which growth curve shows exponential growth with unlimited resources?
68.x: J-curve – Exponential growth, unlimited resources

68.s: Which growth curve shows logistic growth levelling at carrying capacity K?
68.x: S-curve – Logistic growth levelling at carrying capacity K

68.s: Which shape of age pyramid shows a declining population?
68.x: Age pyramids – Triangular = expanding; bell = stable; urn = declining

68.s: What is the maximum population an environment can sustain without being degraded called?
68.x: Carrying capacity – The maximum population an environment can sustain for ever without being degraded; dynamic – changes with resources, climate and technology

68.s: How must resource extraction compare with regeneration for sustainability?
68.x: Conditions – Resource extraction stays below regeneration; waste within the absorption capacity

68.s: Why do birds mainly migrate as seasons change?
68.x: Bird migration – Mainly in search of food and suitable breeding grounds as seasons change

68.s: Which strategy do elephants and humans (few large offspring, much care) follow?
68.x: Many small offspring, little care, short life, unstable habitats – insects, weeds – Few large offspring, much care, long life, near K – elephants, humans

68.s: How many types of ecological pyramids are there?
68.x: Structure – Show trophic levels; base = producers, apex = top consumers; three types – numbers, biomass, energy

68.s: Who first put forward the pyramid of numbers (1927)?
68.x: First put forward by – Charles Elton (1927) (pyramid of numbers)

68.s: In which ecosystem is the pyramid of numbers upright?
68.x: Numbers – Grassland, pond – Tree ecosystem; parasitic chain

68.s: In which ecosystem is the pyramid of numbers inverted?
68.x: Numbers – Grassland, pond – Tree ecosystem; parasitic chain

68.s: In which ecosystem is the pyramid of biomass upright?
68.x: Biomass – Forest, grassland – Pond, marine (small, fast-turning phytoplankton crop)

68.s: In which ecosystem is the pyramid of biomass inverted?
68.x: Biomass – Forest, grassland – Pond, marine (small, fast-turning phytoplankton crop)

68.s: How often is the pyramid of energy upright?
68.x: Energy – Always – Never

68.s: How often is the pyramid of energy inverted?
68.x: Energy – Always – Never

68.s: What is the total dry weight of organisms per unit area called?
68.x: Biomass – Total (dry) weight of organisms per unit area

68.s: What is the living biomass in a trophic level per unit area at a given time called?
68.x: Standing crop – Living biomass in a trophic level per unit area at a given time – a quantity, not a rate

68.s: How is energy mainly lost going up an ecological pyramid?
68.x: Energy loss upward – Mainly through heat loss

68.s: Which organisms get no place in ecological pyramids?
68.x: Limitations – Assume a simple chain and ignore food webs; a species cannot be shown at two levels; saprophytes and decomposers get no place

68.s: Which of these is a natural ecosystem?
68.x: Natural – Forests, grasslands, oceans, lakes, deserts

68.s: Which is an extreme example of an artificial ecosystem?
68.x: Artificial – Crop fields, parks; city = extreme example

68.s: Which of these is an aquatic, not terrestrial, ecosystem?
68.x: Aquatic (not terrestrial) – Estuary, marine, wetlands

68.s: Which land ecosystem has the highest species richness but poor soil?
68.x: Rainforest – Highest land species richness; fast decay → poor soil

68.s: Which biome has slow decay, thick litter and acidic soil?
68.x: Taiga – Slow decay, thick litter, acidic soil

68.s: Why do mature forests give little net oxygen?
68.x: Mature forests – Little net oxygen (respiration balances photosynthesis)

68.s: Which of these is a hot desert?
68.x: Hot desert – Thar, Sahara

68.s: Which of these is a cold desert?
68.x: Cold desert – Ladakh, Gobi

68.s: What is the defining feature of grasslands?
68.x: Grassland – Rainfall too low for forest – low water availability is its defining feature

68.s: Where are the Prairies grasslands?
68.x: Prairie – North America

68.s: In which country are the Pampas grasslands?
68.x: Pampas – Argentina

68.s: Where are the Steppe grasslands?
68.x: Steppe – Eurasia

68.s: In which country is the Veld grassland?
68.x: Veld – South Africa

68.s: In which country are the Downs grasslands?
68.x: Downs – Australia

68.s: In which mountain range are Shola grasslands found?
68.x: Shola – Western Ghats – Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu

68.s: Which invasive plant threatens the Banni grassland of Kutch?
68.x: Banni – Kutch – threat Prosopis juliflora

68.s: At which UNCCD COP was India's first guide to Open Natural Ecosystems launched (Aug 2026)?
68.x: India's first guide to Open Natural Ecosystems was launched at UNCCD COP17, Ulaanbaatar (Aug 2026): they cover over 10% of India, under 5% protected.

68.s: What is a large terrestrial community shaped by temperature and rainfall called?
68.x: Biome: a large terrestrial community shaped mainly by temperature and rainfall; its dominant vegetation gives it its name.

68.s: How much rain does a tropical rainforest get a year?
68.x: Tropical rainforest – Near the equator; rain above 200 cm, hot all year; multi-layered canopy, epiphytes, lianas

68.s: Which trees are typical of tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests?
68.x: Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forest – Trees shed leaves in the dry season; teak, sal

68.s: What kind of biome are prairies, steppes, pampas, veld and downs?
68.x: Temperate deciduous and temperate grassland – Four distinct seasons; grasslands = prairies, steppes, pampas, veld and downs – deep fertile soils (chernozem), "granaries of the world"

68.s: Which biome: Tropical grassland with scattered trees and a long dry season; Africa (Serengeti); India's terai grasslands are…?
68.x: Savanna – Tropical grassland with scattered trees and a long dry season; Africa (Serengeti); India's terai grasslands are savanna-like

68.s: Between which latitudes does the taiga lie?
68.x: Taiga (boreal coniferous forest) – About 50°–70° N; conifers (spruce, fir, pine) with needle leaves; long cold winters; acidic podzol soils with thick litter; the largest land biome by area

68.s: What is the frozen subsoil of the tundra called?
68.x: Tundra – Beyond the treeline (Arctic) or high on mountains (alpine); permafrost, very short growing season, mosses, lichens and sedges, no trees; reindeer, musk ox; lowest productivity of the land biomes

68.s: How much rain does a desert get a year?
68.x: Desert – Rain below 25 cm; hot – Thar and Sahara; cold – Ladakh, Spiti and Gobi

68.s: Which mosaic of vegetation is found in the Nilgiris and Anamalai?
68.x: Mountain (montane) – Vegetation zones change with altitude; Shola–grassland mosaic in the Nilgiris and Anamalai

68.s: What do man-made ecosystems like croplands need?
68.x: Man-made – Croplands, plantations, gardens, aquaria, cities – low diversity, need energy subsidies

68.s: What share of India's area is forest cover as per ISFR 2023?
68.x: ISFR 2023 (released Dec 2024) – Forest cover 7,15,343 sq km = 21.76% of area; with tree cover 25.17%

68.s: Who classified India's forests into 16 type groups (1968)?
68.x: Classification – Champion and Seth (1968) – 16 type groups

69.s: What is the main reservoir of nitrogen?
69.x: Main reservoir – Atmosphere (N₂ about 78% of air)

69.s: In which form do plants mainly take up nitrogen?
69.x: Plant uptake – As nitrate; atmospheric N₂ is not directly usable

69.s: From where can plants never take nitrogen directly?
69.x: Uptake forms – Inorganic nitrates/nitrites (also ammonium) and some organic compounds – never directly from the air

69.s: What does lightning fix nitrogen into, which rain carries down?
69.x: Rain – Raises soil nitrogen – lightning fixes N₂ into nitrogen oxides that rain carries down as nitrates

69.s: Which enzyme carries out nitrogen fixation?
69.x: Fixation – N₂ → ammonia/nitrate (enzyme nitrogenase) – Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc), lightning, industrial Haber process

69.s: Which industrial process fixes nitrogen?
69.x: Fixation – N₂ → ammonia/nitrate (enzyme nitrogenase) – Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc), lightning, industrial Haber process

69.s: What is the conversion of organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia called?
69.x: Ammonification – Organic N in dead matter → ammonia – Decomposer bacteria and fungi

69.s: Which organisms carry out ammonification?
69.x: Ammonification – Organic N in dead matter → ammonia – Decomposer bacteria and fungi

69.s: What is the conversion of ammonia into nitrite and nitrate called?
69.x: Nitrification – Ammonia → nitrite → nitrate – Nitrosomonas (to nitrite), Nitrobacter (to nitrate)

69.s: Which bacterium converts ammonia to nitrite?
69.x: Nitrification – Ammonia → nitrite → nitrate – Nitrosomonas (to nitrite), Nitrobacter (to nitrate)

69.s: What is the conversion of nitrate into N₂ gas called?
69.x: Denitrification – Nitrate → N₂ gas, returned to air – Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus

69.s: Which bacterium carries out denitrification?
69.x: Denitrification – Nitrate → N₂ gas, returned to air – Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus

69.s: Which process removes usable nitrogen from the soil?
69.x: Fixation, ammonification and nitrification add usable nitrogen to the soil; denitrification removes it.

69.s: Which Rhizobium species fixes nitrogen in soybean?
69.x: Rhizobium – Symbiotic, in legume root nodules (pulses, pea); Rhizobium japonicum – soybean

69.s: Which pink pigment in root nodules keeps oxygen low for nitrogenase?
69.x: Leghaemoglobin – Pink/red pigment in nodules (alfalfa, soybean); binds oxygen to keep it low, since nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen

69.s: Which micronutrient is necessary for root nodule formation?
69.x: Boron – Necessary for nodule formation

69.s: To which plant family do groundnut, horse-gram and soybean belong?
69.x: Pea family (Fabaceae/Leguminosae) – Groundnut, horse-gram, soybean; nitrogen-fixing plants: alfalfa, chickpea, clover

69.s: Which nutrient is deficient in the soils where insectivorous plants grow?
69.x: Insectivorous plants – Grow in nitrogen-deficient (often waterlogged) soils and trap insects for nitrogen

69.s: What kind of nitrogen fixer is Rhizobium?
69.x: Rhizobium – Symbiotic, legume nodules – Pulses, pea

69.s: For which crops is Rhizobium used as a biofertiliser?
69.x: Rhizobium – Symbiotic, legume nodules – Pulses, pea

69.s: What kind of nitrogen fixers are Azotobacter and Azospirillum?
69.x: Azotobacter, Azospirillum – Free-living nitrogen fixers – Cereals, millets, non-leguminous upland crops

69.s: For which crops are Azotobacter and Azospirillum used?
69.x: Azotobacter, Azospirillum – Free-living nitrogen fixers – Cereals, millets, non-leguminous upland crops

69.s: In which special cells do blue-green algae fix nitrogen?
69.x: Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) – Photosynthetic nitrogen fixers; heterocysts – Rice / paddy

69.s: For which crop are blue-green algae used as biofertiliser?
69.x: Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) – Photosynthetic nitrogen fixers; heterocysts – Rice / paddy

69.s: Which cyanobacterium lives in the leaves of the water fern Azolla?
69.x: Azolla–Anabaena – Water fern Azolla + Anabaena in its leaves – Water-logged rice fields (Azolla pinnata)

69.s: What kind of organism is the nitrogen fixer Frankia?
69.x: Frankia – Actinomycete, non-legumes – Alnus, Casuarina

69.s: With which plants does Frankia fix nitrogen?
69.x: Frankia – Actinomycete, non-legumes – Alnus, Casuarina

69.s: What does VAM (mycorrhiza) help plants take up?
69.x: VAM (mycorrhiza) – Fungus–root association – Phosphorus and water uptake

69.s: Which bacterium is a phosphate-solubilising biofertiliser?
69.x: PSB – Bacillus megaterium, Pseudomonas striata – Solubilise phosphate

69.s: What do phosphate-solubilising bacteria (PSB) do?
69.x: PSB – Bacillus megaterium, Pseudomonas striata – Solubilise phosphate

69.s: Which raw materials does the environment supply as its first function?
69.x: Supplies resources – Both renewable AND non-renewable raw materials – the first function

69.s: What is the environment's waste-assimilation function, done by microbes, called?
69.x: Assimilates waste – Biodegradation – microorganisms break organic waste into nutrients for reuse

69.s: Which of these is part of the environment's life-sustaining function?
69.x: Sustains life – Genetic diversity, biodiversity, ozone layer UV protection

69.s: Which environmental function covers scenery and recreation?
69.x: Aesthetic services – Scenery, recreation

69.s: What is organic waste broken down into by waste decomposition?
69.x: Waste decomposition – Breakdown of organic waste into simpler compounds

69.s: Which ecosystem function is a source of traditional practices, knowledge and identity?
69.x: Cultural heritage – Source of traditional practices, knowledge and identity

69.s: Which ecosystem function gives scenic and leisure value?
69.x: Recreation and aesthetics – Scenic and leisure value

69.s: Which ecosystem function supplies drugs and herbal remedies?
69.x: Medicinal resources – Supply of drugs and herbal remedies

69.s: Which ecosystem function maintains ecological balance?
69.x: Ecosystem functions – Ecological succession, nutrient cycling, energy flow through food chains, homeostasis (maintenance of ecological balance)

69.s: Which statement about energy in an ecosystem is true?
o: It flows through and is not recycled
69.x: Nutrients and energy – Nutrients are recycled; energy flows through and is not recycled

69.s: Which is NOT one of the four functions of the environment?
69.x: Not a function – "Recycling" is not one of the four listed functions

69.s: Which is the first function of the environment?
69.x: Order – The first function is production / supply of raw materials (resources); waste recycling by microbes = biodegradation function

69.s: Which process removes CO₂ from the air?
69.x: Respiration, decomposition, fossil-fuel combustion, volcanic activity, deforestation – Photosynthesis (plants, algae, some bacteria), dissolving in oceans, carbonate sedimentation, silicate weathering

69.s: Which are the long-term carbon reservoirs?
69.x: Reservoirs and sinks – Atmosphere, oceans, forests, soils; long-term – carbonate rocks and fossil fuels; forests = vital carbon sinks

69.s: Where does most of the extra CO₂ from human activity go?
69.x: Where the extra CO₂ goes – Much is removed by ocean uptake and photosynthesis by phytoplankton (it does not escape to the outer stratosphere; polar ice only archives old air)

69.s: During which period did the Deep Carbon Observatory run?
69.x: Deep Carbon Observatory (DCO, 2009-2019) – Global research programme on the role of carbon in Earth, including field studies of deep microbial life

69.s: What is the movement of nutrient elements through biotic and abiotic components called?
69.x: Biogeochemical (nutritional) cycle – Movement of nutrient elements through the biotic and abiotic components

69.s: To which cycle are all nutrient cycles linked?
69.x: Nature – Nutrients recycle indefinitely between organisms, air and the Earth's crust; driven by energy flow; all cycles are linked to the water cycle

69.s: How many elements, at the least, do organisms need?
69.x: Elements needed – At least 27 elements (15 metals)

69.s: Which of these is a macronutrient?
69.x: Macronutrients – Potassium, sodium, magnesium, calcium, sulphur, phosphorus, chlorine

69.s: Which three are the major soil nutrients?
69.x: Soil's major nutrients – Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium (NPK)

69.s: Which of these is a gaseous biogeochemical cycle?
69.x: Gaseous – Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, water – Atmosphere / ocean

69.s: What is the main reservoir of the gaseous cycles?
69.x: Gaseous – Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, water – Atmosphere / ocean

69.s: Which of these is a sedimentary cycle?
69.x: Sedimentary – Phosphorus, sulphur, calcium, potassium, iron – Earth's crust – soil and rocks

They are different things; a theory does not become a law
A theory becomes a law when proven

An in-depth study of one individual

112.x: ANRF / RDI Scheme: funds projects at TRL 4 and above; strategic technologies; Deep-Tech Fund of Funds.

112.x: Nature – Know-why – Know-how

112.s: Which feature is a characteristic of science?
