112.s: What is pseudoscience?
o: Something claiming scientific status that cannot be tested
112.x: Pseudoscience – Claims scientific status but cannot be tested

112.s: Which subject did J.V. Narlikar say is not a science?
112.x: J.V. Narlikar – Astrology is not a science; astronomy (celestial bodies), cosmology and nanotechnology (1-100 nm) are

113.s: Which device in a microwave oven produces ~2.45 GHz waves that rotate water molecules?
113.x: Microwave oven – Magnetron; ~2.45 GHz rotates water molecules

113.s: How does a refrigerant cool the inside of a refrigerator?
o: It absorbs heat while evaporating inside
113.x: Refrigerator – Vapour compression: refrigerant absorbs heat while evaporating inside, releases it at the condenser outside; needs external work (second law)

113.s: Why does a freezer need defrosting?
113.x: Freezer – Ice build-up insulates the coils (ice is a poor conductor) – hence defrosting

113.s: On which principle does an induction cooktop work?
113.x: Induction cooktop – Electromagnetic induction, eddy currents

113.s: On which side is pressure applied in a reverse osmosis (RO) purifier?
113.x: RO purifier – Pressure on the concentrated side, against osmosis; desalination; reverse osmosis removes ions and bacteria

113.s: What does a UV water purifier do?
113.x: UV water purifier – Only kills/inactivates microorganisms; does not remove odour, dissolved salts or turbidity

113.s: What temperature does a pressure cooker raise the boiling point of water to?
113.x: Pressure cooker – Higher pressure raises the boiling point (~120 °C)

113.s: Which alloy is a fuse wire made of?
113.x: Fuse – Heating effect; tin-lead; in series; low melting point, high resistivity

113.s: What between the double glass walls of a thermos flask stops conduction and convection?
113.x: Thermos flask – Vacuum between double glass walls stops conduction and convection; silvered walls reduce radiation; cork supports are poor conductors

113.s: On which principle does a desert cooler work?
113.x: Desert cooler – Evaporative cooling (works best in dry air)

113.s: How does a fan make us feel cool?
o: It speeds up evaporation of sweat
113.x: Fan – Speeds up evaporation of sweat, which takes latent heat from the skin; it does not cool the air

113.s: On which principle do a spin drier and a cream separator work?
113.x: Washing machine (spin drier), cream separator – Centrifugation; in churning milk the lighter fat moves to the centre (centrifugal force)

113.s: What should a vacuum cleaner not be used to pick up?
113.x: Vacuum cleaner – Dust from floors, upholstery, cars – not for picking up glass pieces

113.s: What is a transformer breather filled with?
113.x: Transformer breather – Filled with silica gel (absorbs moisture; blue → pink when wet)

113.s: What is the choke of a tube light?
113.x: Choke of a tube light – An inductor – starting voltage surge, then limits current

113.s: Where is the bulb placed in a car headlight's concave reflector to get a parallel beam?
113.x: Car headlight, torch, searchlight – Concave reflector, bulb at the focus → parallel beam

113.s: Which type of mirror is used as a vehicle's rear-view mirror?
113.x: Rear-view mirror = convex – Convex – virtual, erect, diminished image (magnification < 1), wide field of view; "Objects in mirror are closer than they appear" (diminished image looks farther)

113.s: Which mirror do dentists use to get an erect, magnified image of teeth?
113.x: Dentist's mirror, shaving mirror – Concave – teeth within focus give an erect, magnified image

113.s: What is the specific heat of water, which makes it good for hot water bags?
113.x: Hot water bag – Water has a high specific heat (4.2 J/g °C) – holds and gives out heat slowly

113.s: Why does ice packed in sawdust melt slowly?
113.x: Ice in sawdust – Sawdust is a poor conductor – ice melts slowly

113.s: On which principle do a stethoscope and a megaphone work?
113.x: Stethoscope, megaphone, ear trumpet, sound boards – Multiple reflection of sound

113.s: On which principle does a kaleidoscope work?
o: Multiple reflections in inclined plane mirrors
113.x: Kaleidoscope – Multiple reflections in inclined plane mirrors

113.s: At what angle to the tube is each plane mirror of a simple periscope fixed?
113.x: Simple periscope – Two plane mirrors parallel to each other, each at 45° to the tube (reflection); prism periscope and optical fibre – total internal reflection

113.s: How much LPG does a domestic cylinder hold in India?
113.x: LPG cylinders – Domestic 14.2 kg, commercial (non-domestic) 19 kg; LPG = propane + butane; CNG/PNG = mainly methane

113.s: What forms the negative terminal of a dry cell?
113.x: Dry cell – Metal cap = positive terminal; zinc case = negative

113.s: How are appliances connected in house wiring?
o: In a ring of series loops
113.x: House wiring – Parallel; copper, aluminium – good conductors (free electrons)

113.s: Which material is used for the core of an electromagnet?
113.x: Electromagnet core = soft iron – Soft iron (magnetises and loses it easily); permanent magnets – steel, alnico

113.s: What do magnetic keepers (soft-iron pieces across the poles) protect magnets from?
113.x: Magnetic keepers – Soft-iron pieces across the poles – protect magnets from self-demagnetisation

113.s: Why is ebonite (hard vulcanised rubber) used for cooker handles?
o: It is a heat and electric insulator
113.x: Ebonite (hard vulcanised rubber) – Heat and electric insulator – cooker handles

113.s: How does wool keep us warm?
o: By air trapped between its fibres
113.x: Wool – Keeps us warm mainly by air trapped between its fibres; the fibre (keratin) is also a poor conductor

113.s: Why are white or light-coloured clothes preferred in summer?
113.x: Light/white clothes – Reflect heat (poor absorbers) – summer; dark colours absorb heat – winter; umbrella white on top, black underneath

113.s: Which material of cup lets tea cool fastest?
113.x: Metal cup – Tea cools fastest – metals conduct heat best; clay, glass, porcelain are insulators

113.s: What is an invar tape (nickel-steel) used for?
113.x: Invar tape (nickel-steel, tiny expansion) – Precise linear measurement in surveying

113.s: What does a lactometer test?
113.x: Lactometer – Milk (Archimedes' principle; also hydrometer)

113.s: What does a hygrometer measure?
113.x: Hygrometer – Humidity

113.s: Which clock gives the most exact time?
113.x: Caesium atomic clock – Most exact time

113.s: What does an ammeter measure, connected in series?
113.x: Ammeter – Current – in series (with fuse and galvanometer)

113.s: What does a voltmeter measure, connected in parallel?
113.x: Voltmeter – Potential difference – in parallel

113.s: How is a high resistance connected to a galvanometer to make a voltmeter?
113.x: Galvanometer – Detects the presence (and direction) of current; → voltmeter with high resistance in series; → ammeter with a low resistance (shunt) in parallel

113.s: What does a rheostat do in a circuit?
113.x: Rheostat – Varies resistance

113.s: What does a Bragg spectrometer measure?
113.x: Bragg spectrometer – X-ray wavelength (nλ = 2d sin θ); GM counter detects radiation; cyclotron accelerates particles

113.s: What does an atomic force microscope (and STM) do?
113.x: Atomic force microscope (and STM) – Images individual atoms

113.s: What does a planimeter measure?
113.x: Planimeter – Area of plotted maps; pyrometer – very high temperatures

113.s: What does a fathometer (echo sounder) measure?
113.x: Fathometer (echo sounder), SONAR – Depth of the sea (reflection of sound)

113.s: What does a thermopile (many thermocouples) detect?
113.x: Thermopile (many thermocouples) – Radiant heat; liquid and Six's thermometers measure temperature

113.s: On which property does a mercury thermometer work?
113.x: Thermometer – Temperature; calorimeter – heat; mercury thermometer works on thermal expansion

113.s: At what temperature does alcohol freeze, making alcohol thermometers good for very low temperatures?
113.x: Alcohol (spirit) thermometer – Very low temperatures (alcohol freezes at ~−114 °C, mercury at −39 °C)

113.s: Which instrument is used to view tiny nearby objects?
113.x: Telescope – Distant objects; microscope – tiny near objects; spectroscope – spectra; chronometer – time at sea

113.s: What is a sextant used for?
o: Angular measurement in astronomy and navigation
113.x: Sextant – Angular measurement in astronomy and navigation

113.s: What do a refractometer and a viscometer measure?
113.x: Refractometer, viscometer – Refractive index; viscosity

113.s: What does a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) display?
113.x: Oscilloscope (CRO) – Displays waveforms – to see sound waves (via a microphone)

113.s: Which waves does RADAR reflect off aircraft to detect them?
113.x: RADAR = Radio Detection And Ranging – Detects aircraft with radio waves (microwave band) – reflection of radio waves

113.s: What is the SI unit of force and weight?
113.x: Force, weight – Newton (kg m/s²); weight is a force – not pascal; dyne – CGS force

113.s: Which of these is a unit of pressure?
113.x: Pressure, stress – Pascal = N/m² (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²); bar = 10⁵ Pa; atm, torr/mm Hg, kg/cm² (kgf/cm²); kg/cm and kg/mm are not pressure units

113.s: How many joules make one calorie?
113.x: Energy, work – Joule = N m = W s; calorie (1 cal = 4.18 J; 4.186 J, so 1 J ≈ 0.24 cal); kWh, eV, erg

113.s: How many watts equal one British horsepower?
113.x: Power – Watt; 1 horsepower (British) = 746 W; metric hp = 735.5 W ≈ 736 W

113.s: What is the SI unit of momentum and impulse?
113.x: Momentum, impulse – kg m s⁻¹ = newton second (N s) (kg m s⁻² is force)

113.s: What is the SI unit of torque?
113.x: Torque – N m – same dimension as work, but not joule

113.s: Which of these is not a unit of speed?
113.x: Velocity, acceleration – m/s; m s⁻²; speed = distance/time (m/s, km/h, cm/s); m²/h is not a speed unit

113.s: What is the SI unit of the spring constant?
113.x: Spring constant – N/m (k = F/x)

113.s: What is the SI unit of temperature?
113.x: Temperature – Kelvin; centigrade is a scale

113.s: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
113.x: Resistance; resistivity – Ohm (Ω); ohm-metre

113.s: What is the SI unit of electrical conductance?
113.x: Conductance; conductivity – Siemens (older mho); S/m

113.s: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
113.x: Charge; current; p.d. – Coulomb; ampere; volt (1 V = 1 J/C)

113.s: What is the SI unit of inductance?
113.x: Inductance – Henry (H) (farad – capacitance)

113.s: What is the SI unit of magnetic field?
113.x: Magnetic field; flux – Tesla; weber; Maxwell (Mx) = CGS unit of flux (1 Mx = 10⁻⁸ Wb)

113.s: What is the SI unit of frequency?
113.x: Frequency – Hertz (1 cycle per second)

113.s: In what unit is the power of a lens measured?
113.x: Lens power – Dioptre (P = 1/f in m)

113.s: What is the SI unit of luminous intensity?
113.x: Light – Candela – luminous intensity (not sound); lumen – flux; lux – illuminance / luminous emittance (lm/m²)

113.s: In which unit is sound level measured?
113.x: Sound terms – Hertz, decibel (sound level), Mach

113.s: What does a light year measure?
113.x: Light year – Distance

113.s: How long is one nautical mile?
113.x: Knot – Speed of ships – 1 nautical mile/hour; nautical mile (1.852 km) – navigation distance; fathom = depth (6 ft)

113.s: How much is one angstrom (Å)?
113.x: Angstrom (Å) – 10⁻¹⁰ m – length; wavelengths, atomic sizes

113.s: How much is one fermi (femtometre), the scale of nuclear radius?
113.x: Fermi (femtometre) – 10⁻¹⁵ m – nuclear radius; micron – cells

113.s: How many metres make one kilometre?
113.x: Metric prefixes – kilo 10³ (1 km = 1000 m), centi 10⁻², milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹ (1 nm = 10⁻⁷ cm), pico 10⁻¹²

113.s: What is the charge of an electron?
113.x: Electron charge – e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C

113.s: Which of these is NOT an SI base quantity?
113.x: SI base quantities – Length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount, luminous intensity; weight is derived

113.s: Which quantity is the pascal, named after a scientist, a unit of?
113.x: Named after scientists – Pascal – pressure; joule – energy; watt – power; newton – force

113.s: Which of these quantities is dimensionless?
113.x: Dimensionless – Strain, refractive index, relative density (no unit); gas constant, viscosity, Planck's constant have dimensions

113.s: What are the dimensions of work and energy?
113.x: Dimensions – Work and energy ML²T⁻²; power ML²T⁻³; A·m/s² = [I L T⁻²]

113.s: What kind of motion is free fall?
113.x: Free fall – Uniformly accelerated (g); speed keeps increasing; in vacuum all bodies fall together – coin, feather and mango land at the same time

113.s: What is non-uniform motion?
113.x: Non-uniform motion – Unequal distances in equal times

113.s: What is the acceleration of a body moving with constant velocity?
113.x: Constant velocity – Straight-line motion, constant speed, zero acceleration; change of velocity in any interval zero

113.s: What shape does the distance–time graph of a body at rest have?
113.x: Distance–time graph – At rest – horizontal; straight line = uniform speed; curve = non-uniform; slope = speed

113.s: What does the slope of a velocity–time graph give?
113.x: Velocity–time graph – Slope = acceleration; area under it = distance

113.s: What is velocity the rate of change of?
113.x: Velocity – Rate of change of displacement; acceleration – rate of change of velocity; retardation = negative acceleration (velocity decreases)

113.s: What are v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as called?
113.x: Equations of motion – v = u + at (velocity–time); s = ut + ½at² (position–time; distance depends on initial velocity u); v² = u² + 2as (position–velocity); u = initial velocity, v = final

113.s: What is the average velocity of a uniformly accelerated body?
113.x: Uniform acceleration – Average velocity = (u + v)/2, so v = 2 × average velocity − u

113.s: What is the average speed of a 100 km round trip done in 2 hours?
113.x: Round trip – Displacement zero → average velocity zero (average speed 100 km / 2 h = 50 km/h)

113.s: At what angle of projection is a projectile's range maximum?
113.x: Projectile – Maximum range at 45°

113.s: What stays constant in uniform circular motion?
113.x: Uniform circular motion – Speed and magnitude of acceleration constant; velocity and acceleration directions change (centripetal – non-zero, not constant)

113.s: In which direction does a whirled stone fly off when the string snaps?
113.x: String snaps – Stone flies off along the tangent

113.s: Which of these are scalar quantities?
113.x: Scalars – Speed, distance, mass, energy, work, electrostatic potential, pressure

113.s: Which of these are vector quantities?
113.x: Vectors – Velocity, displacement, force, torque, momentum, angular momentum

113.s: What is Newton's first law also called the law of?
113.x: Newton's first law = law of inertia – Body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a net force acts; mass measures inertia

113.s: What causes a passenger to lurch forward when a bus brakes?
113.x: Inertia – Body lurches forward when a bus brakes, backward when it starts; dust leaves a beaten carpet (inertia of rest)

113.s: How does acceleration vary with mass for a given force?
113.x: Second law F = ma – Force = rate of change of momentum, in its direction; for a given force acceleration ∝ 1/mass

113.s: What is impulse equal to?
113.x: Impulse – F × t = change in momentum (unit N·s)

113.s: What do the action and reaction of Newton's third law act on?
113.x: Third law – Action and reaction are equal and opposite and act on different bodies

113.s: Which is an example of Newton's third law?
113.x: Third-law examples – Horse pulling a cart, walking, swimming (swimmer pushes water back), bird flight, cannon/gun recoil, rocket and jet propulsion (also momentum conservation)

113.s: How can a man move on frictionless ground?
o: Only by throwing something or sneezing
113.x: Frictionless ground – A man moves only by throwing something or sneezing (momentum conservation); friction is a non-conservative, non-central force

113.s: When no external force acts, what stays constant?
o: Velocity of the centre of mass
113.x: No external force – Velocity of the centre of mass stays constant; momentum conserved only then

113.s: What kind of equilibrium does a ball balanced on a vertical rod have?
113.x: Equilibrium – No net force or moment; ball on a vertical rod – unstable; in a bowl – stable; on a flat floor – neutral

113.s: When does a body not topple?
o: While the vertical through its centre of gravity falls within its base
113.x: Stability – Body does not topple while the vertical through its centre of gravity falls within its base (Leaning Tower of Pisa)

113.s: What do two unequal opposite forces not in one line produce?
113.x: Unequal opposite forces not in one line – Net force + torque → rotation and translation; equal ones = a couple (rotation only)

113.s: Where should a door handle be fixed so the least force opens the door?
113.x: Torque – Force × perpendicular distance; door handle far from the hinges needs least force

113.s: Why does an ice-skater spin faster when pulling the arms in?
113.x: Angular momentum – Ice-skater spins faster when arms are pulled in

113.s: Which of these does the moment of inertia not depend on?
113.x: Moment of inertia – Depends on mass, its distribution and the axis – not on angular velocity; same M, R: disc ½MR² > solid sphere 2/5 MR²

113.s: What is power?
113.x: Power – Rate of doing work (work ÷ time), unit watt

113.s: What does positive net work do to a body's kinetic energy (work–energy theorem)?
113.x: Work–energy theorem – Positive net work increases KE (W = ΔKE)

113.s: How much does kinetic energy rise when momentum is doubled?
113.x: Doubling momentum – KE rises by +300%

113.s: How much work does a centripetal force do?
113.x: Centripetal force – Does zero work

113.s: What does the law of conservation of energy state?
o: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
113.x: Conservation of energy – Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; mass-energy too (E = mc²) – 'something from nothing' is impossible

113.s: What energy conversion takes place in hydroelectricity?
113.x: Hydroelectricity – Potential → kinetic → electrical energy

113.s: Which machines are classified as class I, II and III, like scissors, wheelbarrow and tongs?
113.x: Levers – Class I – scissors, seesaw; class II – wheelbarrow, nutcracker (load in the middle); class III – tongs, forearm

113.s: Which factors does the spring constant of a spring depend on?
113.x: Spring balance – Hooke's law – extension ∝ force within the elastic limit; spring constant depends on material, wire thickness, coil diameter (and length); in orbit, T = 2π√(m/k) still gives mass

113.s: Why is steel more elastic than rubber?
o: It needs a larger deforming force for the same strain
It melts at a lower temperature
113.x: Steel more elastic than rubber – Needs a larger deforming force for the same strain (higher Young's modulus)

113.s: Where is the acceleration zero in simple harmonic motion?
113.x: SHM – a = −ω²x – acceleration maximum at the extremes (amplitude), zero at the mean (speed maximum there)

113.s: For which device is T = 2π√(L/g), independent of bob mass?
113.x: Simple pendulum – T = 2π√(L/g) – depends on length and g, not on bob mass or small amplitude; 4 × length doubles the period

113.s: What kind of force is gravity?
113.x: Gravity – Only attractive, weakest fundamental force, long range; universal, dominant between celestial bodies, negligible for atoms; not the same for all pairs (F = Gm1m2/r²)

113.s: What happens to gravitational force when the distance between two bodies is doubled?
113.x: F ∝ 1/r² – Doubling the distance makes the force one-fourth

113.s: What happens to g if Earth's radius shrinks by 1% with mass unchanged?
113.x: g = GM/R² – More mass or smaller radius raises g; radius shrinks 1% → g rises ~2%

113.s: Where on Earth is g maximum?
113.x: g varies – g = 0 at Earth's centre (weight zero); maximum at the poles, minimum at the equator; decreases with height and depth

113.s: How does a body's mass vary from place to place?
o: It is greatest at the poles
It is zero on the Moon
113.x: Mass vs weight – Mass is the same everywhere; weight = force with which the Earth attracts a body towards its centre (W = mg, unit newton) – varies with place

113.s: On which body is surface gravity about 1/6 of Earth's?
113.x: Moon – Surface gravity ≈ 1/6 of Earth's – weight 1/6, mass unchanged; a floating body floats as before (weight and buoyancy both scale with g)

113.s: In what situation does a person's apparent weight become zero?
o: A lift whose cable breaks (free fall)
113.x: Lift – Cable breaks (free fall) → apparent weight zero; accelerating down → weight less (apparent weight < real); up → more; uniform speed → equal

113.s: What is Earth's escape velocity?
113.x: Escape velocity – 11.2 km/s; launched below it a body stays bound – total energy (KE + PE) negative; zero at escape velocity

113.s: Why does a sharp needle exert more pressure than a nail for the same force?
113.x: Pressure = force/area (pascal: 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²) – Pressure is scalar (normal component of force per unit area, no direction); a sharp needle exerts more than a nail

113.s: Which factors does liquid pressure depend on?
o: Height and density of the liquid
113.x: Liquid pressure p = hρg – Depends on height and density, not on base area; p = p₀ + ρgh – rises with depth (dams thicker at the base)

113.s: What danger does high water pressure pose in deep-sea diving?
o: It removes oxygen from air tanks
113.x: Deep-sea diving – High water pressure can rupture the eardrum

113.s: Which device works on Pascal's law?
113.x: Pascal's law – Pressure on a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions – hydraulic lift, brakes

113.s: What is the upward force on a body in a fluid equal to, by Archimedes' principle?
113.x: Archimedes' principle – Upward force = weight of fluid displaced; uses – purity of metals (king's crown), lactometer, hydrometer, ships, submarines

113.s: Which of two bodies that weigh equal in water weighs more in air?
113.x: Archimedes – apparent weight – W(1 − ρ_water/ρ); of two bodies equal in water, the less dense one weighs more in air

113.s: Where does an object weigh the most, since buoyancy exists only because of gravity?
113.x: Buoyancy (upthrust) – Exists only because of gravity; an object weighs most in vacuum

113.s: What decides whether a body floats or sinks in a liquid?
113.x: Floating or sinking – Depends on the difference in densities (floats if lower); iron (sp. gr. ~7.8) floats on mercury (13.6), sinks in water (1)

113.s: Why does a helium balloon rise?
o: Helium is less dense than air
113.x: Helium balloon rises – Helium less dense than air (buoyant force > weight)

113.s: What happens to the water level when floating ice melts in a glass?
113.x: Floating ice melts – Water level stays the same (floating body displaces its own weight)

113.s: What happens to the lake level when iron nails are removed from a floating boat into the shore?
113.x: Floating boat – Removing iron nails makes it rise and the lake level falls

113.s: At which temperature of water is specific gravity measured against?
113.x: Specific gravity (relative density) – Density ÷ density of water at 4 °C; ratio, no unit; hydrometer

113.s: What does faster-moving air produce, by Bernoulli's principle?
113.x: Bernoulli's principle – Faster air → lower pressure – passing cars pushed together, person near a fast train pushed towards it, roofs blown off, aeroplane wing lift (convex top)

113.s: How does the velocity at a point behave in steady (streamline) flow?
113.x: Steady (streamline) flow – Velocity at a point constant in time, particles follow the same path, streamlines never intersect

113.s: What happens to the viscosity of liquids like honey on heating?
113.x: Viscosity – Internal friction – a stirred liquid comes to rest; liquids – decreases with temperature (glycerin, honey); gases – increases

113.s: Which of these is an effect of surface tension?
113.x: Surface tension – Meniscus, capillary rise, spherical drops and soap bubbles (least surface) – not evaporation; ordinary flow of a liquid is not a surface-tension effect

113.s: What do detergent and soap do to the surface tension of water?
113.x: Detergent, oil, soap – Lower the surface tension of water (better wetting and cleaning)

113.s: What makes a drinking straw work, unlike a lamp wick?
113.x: Capillarity – Lamp wick, blotting paper, water rise in plants; a straw works by air pressure

113.s: How does the pressure inside a soap bubble compare with atmospheric pressure?
113.x: Soap bubble – Pressure inside > atmospheric (excess 4T/r)

113.s: Which temperature scale has no negative values?
113.x: Temperature scales – K = °C + 273(.15); C = K − 273; absolute zero = 0 K = −273.15 °C (molecular motion would cease); kelvin has no negative values; °F = 9/5 °C + 32; −40° reads the same on Celsius and Fahrenheit

113.s: What is the boiling point of water at 1 atm on the Kelvin scale?
113.x: Boiling point of water – 100 °C = 373 K = 212 °F at 1 atm; falls with altitude (lower air pressure; cooking slower); rises with dissolved solute and pressure (cooker)

113.s: What are the bubbles rising in boiling water mostly made of?
113.x: Bubbles in boiling water – Mostly water vapour (steam)

113.s: At what temperature is water densest?
113.x: Water densest at 4 °C (1 g/cc) – Anomalous expansion – contracts from 0 to 4 °C, then expands; a freezing lake stays at 4 °C at the bottom

113.s: What is the density of ice, which lets it float on water?
113.x: Water expands on freezing – ~9%; ice ~0.92 g/cc floats; sealed glass vessel in a freezer breaks; pipes burst

113.s: What does pressure do in regelation of ice?
113.x: Regelation – Pressure lowers the melting point of ice – pressed blocks refreeze into one; ice skating

113.s: What is the heat absorbed during melting or boiling at constant temperature called?
113.x: Latent heat – Melting/boiling at constant temperature; fixed at a given temperature but varies with temperature (→ 0 at the critical point); independent of volume

113.s: What property makes ice cool a drink so well?
113.x: Ice cools a drink – Latent heat of fusion (336 J/g)

113.s: What is mass × specific heat called?
113.x: Specific heat – Property of the material, independent of mass and shape; thermal capacity = mass × specific heat

113.s: What does the principle of calorimetry state?
113.x: Principle of calorimetry – Heat lost = heat gained

113.s: Which mode of heat transfer occurs mainly in solids?
113.x: Heat transfer – Conduction (mainly solids), convection (only fluids), radiation (also through vacuum); evaporation is a phase change

113.s: What decides the direction of heat flow between two bodies?
113.x: Heat flow – Depends only on temperature – hotter to colder

113.s: What is the thermal conductivity of copper (W/m·K)?
113.x: Thermal conductivity – Copper ~400 > zinc ~116 > lead ~35 > mercury ~8 W/m·K; stainless steel < aluminium < copper < silver

113.s: Why does a metal feel colder than wood at the same temperature?
113.x: Metal feels colder; copper feels hotter than glass – Metals conduct heat faster (not because they are denser)

113.s: Which surface process is a cooling process that rises with surface area, wind and lower humidity?
113.x: Evaporation – Surface, cooling process; rises with surface area, temperature, wind, lower humidity

113.s: What is sublimation?
113.x: Sublimation – Solid → vapour (camphor, naphthalene, dry ice, iodine)

113.s: What is the change of a liquid into a gas below its boiling point called?
113.x: Changes of state – Evaporation – liquid → gas; freezing – liquid → solid; melting – solid → liquid

113.s: How does the rate of cooling vary, by Newton's law of cooling?
113.x: Newton's law of cooling – Rate ∝ temperature difference (doubles when it doubles) – equal drops take longer as the body cools

113.s: Why is the apparent expansion of a liquid less than its real expansion?
113.x: Liquid expansion – Container also expands – apparent < real expansion

113.s: What happens to a hole in a metal plate when the plate is heated?
113.x: Heating a plate with a hole – The hole expands too

113.s: Which law does the first law of thermodynamics express?
113.x: First law of thermodynamics – Conservation of energy (ΔQ = ΔU + W; ΔU = Q − W; if W = 0, ΔU = Q); zeroth law – thermal equilibrium

113.s: What does the second law of thermodynamics (Clausius) state?
o: Heat cannot flow by itself from colder to hotter
113.x: Second law (Clausius) – Heat cannot flow by itself from colder to hotter

113.s: Which of these is an adiabatic process?
113.x: Isobaric; adiabatic – Constant pressure (open pan, open pipe); no heat exchange (tyre burst); isothermal – constant temperature

113.s: To what is the average kinetic energy of gas molecules proportional?
113.x: Kinetic theory – Average KE = (3/2)kT – ∝ absolute temperature

113.s: What does a graph of V against 1/p give under Boyle's law?
113.x: Gas laws – Boyle (PV const; V vs 1/p = straight line), Charles (V ∝ T), Avogadro, Gay-Lussac's combining volumes; Joule's law = heating by current

113.s: What type of wave is sound?
113.x: Nature – Longitudinal mechanical wave (compressions + rarefactions), a form of energy; needs a medium – no sound in vacuum (none from the Moon); cannot be polarised; not electromagnetic

113.s: About how fast does sound travel in steel?
113.x: Speed of sound – Solids > liquids > gases: steel ~5,000 m/s (metals 5000–6400; aluminium > glass), water ~1,500 m/s (1500 m/s in water), air ~330–343 m/s (331 at 0 °C, 343 at 20 °C); rises with temperature and humidity (moist air less dense); independent of pressure; zero in vacuum

113.s: With which property of sound is pitch linked?
113.x: Pitch – ↔ frequency (one octave higher = double frequency, 500 → 1000 Hz)

113.s: With which property of a sound wave is loudness linked?
113.x: Loudness – ↔ amplitude

113.s: What does the quality (timbre) of a sound depend on?
113.x: Quality (timbre) – ↔ harmonics / waveform; tone of a stringed instrument set by the wave form

113.s: What is the audible range of human hearing?
113.x: Audible range = 20 Hz – 20,000 Hz – 20 Hz–20 kHz

113.s: Which of these produce infrasound (below 20 Hz)?
113.x: Infrasound (< 20 Hz) – Earthquakes (before the main shock), elephants, whales

113.s: Which crystals under AC produce ultrasonic waves?
113.x: Ultrasonic waves – ultrasound > 20 kHz (e.g. 30,000 Hz) – Bats (echolocation), dolphins; made by piezoelectric crystals (quartz) under AC; hypersonic = speeds above Mach 5

113.s: What minimum time gap is needed to hear a distinct echo?
113.x: Echo – Reflection of sound; needs ≥ 0.1 s gap → reflector at least ~17 m away (~344 m/s)

113.s: What is reverberation?
o: Persistence of sound by multiple reflections in large halls
113.x: Reverberation – Persistence of sound by multiple reflections in large halls

113.s: How long does the impression of a sound persist in the ear?
113.x: Persistence of hearing – ~0.1 s; denser compressions = higher pressure

113.s: In which frequency band is the human ear most sensitive?
113.x: Ear – Roughly logarithmic response (decibel scale); sensitivity varies with frequency (best ~1–4 kHz)

113.s: What waves does plucking a sitar string set up?
113.x: Sitar / stretched string – Plucking sets up stationary transverse waves

113.s: Which media can carry only longitudinal waves?
113.x: Liquids and gases – Carry only longitudinal waves – an undersea explosion sends longitudinal waves

113.s: What are phonons?
113.x: Phonons – Quanta of vibration – 'sound particles'

113.s: What is a speed above Mach 5 called?
113.x: Mach number – Speed ÷ speed of sound; > 1 supersonic, < 1 subsonic, > 5 hypersonic

113.s: Which kind of waves alone can cross a vacuum?
113.x: Waves – Carry energy only, not matter; all waves reflect, carry energy, exert pressure; only EM waves cross vacuum

113.s: What does the distance from a crest to the next trough equal?
113.x: Wavelength – Crest to next trough = half a wavelength; crest to crest = one

113.s: Which of these is a mechanical wave?
113.x: Mechanical waves – Sound, water, seismic waves; radio, light, X-rays = electromagnetic

113.s: Which angle equals the angle of incidence, by the law of reflection?
113.x: Law of reflection – Angle of incidence = angle of reflection; incident ray, reflected ray and normal in one plane

113.s: What kind of image does a plane mirror form?
113.x: Plane mirror – Image virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted (AMBULANCE), as far behind as the object in front; R and focal length infinite; never a real image

113.s: Of which phenomenon is lateral inversion an effect?
113.x: Lateral inversion – A reflection effect; twinkling and mirage are refraction

113.s: For which mirror is R = 2f, with pole and centre of curvature defined?
113.x: Spherical mirror – Pole = centre of the reflecting surface; centre of curvature = centre of the sphere; R = 2f

113.s: Which is the only mirror that gives enlarged and inverted (real) images?
113.x: Concave mirror – Surface curved inwards; only mirror giving enlarged and inverted (real) images

113.s: Where must an object be placed for a concave mirror to give a virtual, erect, enlarged image?
113.x: Concave – object positions – Between P and F → behind the mirror, virtual, erect, enlarged; at F → image at infinity; between F and C → beyond C, real, magnified; at C → at C, same size

113.s: Where is the centre of curvature of a concave mirror with f = 16 cm?
113.x: Example – f = 16 cm → C at 32 cm; object at 24 cm → real, magnified, beyond C

113.s: Which of these uses a concave mirror?
113.x: Concave mirror uses – Solar cooker and furnaces, headlights, torches, searchlights, shaving/make-up and dentist's mirrors; not a rear-view mirror

113.s: What kind of image does a convex mirror always form?
113.x: Convex mirror – Surface bulging outwards; image always virtual, erect, diminished between pole and focus (point-sized for a far object); rear-view mirror; a mirror that always shows you smaller

113.s: How many images are formed between two parallel mirrors?
113.x: Images in two mirrors – n = 360°/θ − 1; parallel mirrors → infinite

113.s: What is the minimum object–image distance for a real image by a convex lens?
113.x: Convex lens – Object within F → magnifying glass; real images in camera, compound microscope, telescope; burning glass converges sun rays; real image – minimum object–image distance 4f

113.s: What is the focal length of a lens of +2 dioptres?
113.x: Lens power – P = 1/f (m), dioptre; + = convex, – = concave; +2 D → f = 0.5 m

113.s: What do a convex and a concave lens of equal focal length together act as?
113.x: Convex + concave of equal focal length – Plane glass (zero power)

113.s: What happens to the image if part of a lens is covered?
o: The complete image forms, only less bright
113.x: Covering part of a lens – Still the complete image, only less bright

113.s: How does an air bubble in water behave optically?
113.x: Air bubble in water / glass – Acts as a concave (diverging) lens

113.s: What is the approximate focal length of the human eye lens?
113.x: Human eye – Lens (just behind the pupil) forms a real, inverted image on the retina (the film of a camera); focal length ~2.5 cm

113.s: What does the Eustachian tube of the ear do?
o: Equalises pressure on both sides of the eardrum
113.x: Eustachian tube (ear) – Equalises pressure on both sides of the eardrum

113.s: Which muscles change the eye lens thickness in accommodation?
113.x: Accommodation – Ciliary muscles relax → lens thinner, focal length increases (distant); contract → thicker (near)

113.s: What is the least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye?
113.x: Least distance of distinct vision – 25 cm; far point = infinity

113.s: About how long is the persistence of vision, which lets films run at 24 frames/s?
113.x: Persistence of vision – ~1/16 s (often quoted 0.1 s) – films at 24 frames/s

113.s: Which lens corrects myopia?
113.x: Myopia – Image in front of the retina; near objects clear; concave lens (negative power)

113.s: What distance can a person with hypermetropia not read closer than?
113.x: Hypermetropia (long sight) – Near objects blurred, image behind the retina, near point beyond 25 cm (cannot read closer than 1 m) – convex lens (reading glasses)

113.s: Which lens corrects presbyopia when both near and far vision fail?
113.x: Presbyopia – Age, weak ciliary muscles, cannot read near print; often near and far vision fail → bifocal lens (upper concave, lower convex)

113.s: Which lens corrects astigmatism?
113.x: Astigmatism – Cylindrical lens

113.s: What is cataract?
113.x: Glaucoma; cataract – Progressive optic-nerve damage; lens clouding

113.s: Which colours are most commonly confused in colour blindness?
113.x: Colour blindness – Mostly red–green (red looks greenish)

113.s: What kind of final image does an astronomical telescope form?
113.x: Astronomical telescope – Final image virtual, inverted, magnified; larger objective diameter → higher resolving power

113.s: How does the eyepiece focal length of a compound microscope compare with the objective's?
113.x: Compound microscope – Eyepiece f larger than objective f; final image virtual, magnified, inverted; shorter focal lengths give more magnification (≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e))

113.s: What is resolving power?
o: Ability to show two close objects as separate
113.x: Resolving power – Ability to show two close objects as separate

113.s: Which property of light never changes on refraction?
113.x: Refraction – Denser → rarer: light speeds up, bends away from the normal; frequency never changes (speed, wavelength do)

113.s: How do objects such as a lemon look in water due to refraction?
113.x: Refraction effects – Bent pencil, objects in water look bigger (lemon), early sunrise, twinkling, mirage

113.s: How much earlier is the Sun seen before sunrise due to atmospheric refraction?
113.x: Atmospheric refraction – Sun seen ~2 min before sunrise and after sunset

113.s: What is the refractive index of air?
113.x: Refractive index n = c/v – Always greater than 1; air 1.0003, water 1.33, glass ~1.5, diamond 2.42; lower n → faster (quartz 1.46 faster than sapphire 1.77)

113.s: Which colour travels slowest in glass?
113.x: In glass – Violet is slowest (highest n), red fastest and bends least

113.s: Which colour deviates the most in dispersion by a prism?
113.x: Dispersion – White light → VIBGYOR by a prism – violet deviates most, red least

113.s: Which phenomena together form a rainbow?
o: Refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection
113.x: Rainbow – A shower of raindrops: refraction + dispersion + total internal reflection

113.s: Which colour of the visible spectrum has the shortest wavelength?
113.x: Visible spectrum – Violet shortest wavelength, highest energy; red longest, lowest energy

113.s: What makes the sky blue?
113.x: Blue sky – Rayleigh scattering; no atmosphere → black sky (Moon, space)

113.s: What is the Tyndall effect?
113.x: Tyndall effect – Scattering of light by colloids

113.s: What causes the colours of soap bubbles and oil films?
113.x: Soap-bubble / oil-film colours – Thin-film interference

113.s: What are the primary colours of light?
113.x: Primary colours of light – Red, green, blue (screens, photography); pigments – red, yellow, blue; yellow, cyan, magenta – secondary (printing inks); black is not a colour of light

113.s: What colour results from mixing red, green and blue light?
113.x: Additive mixing – R + G + B = white; red + green = yellow; green + blue = cyan; red + blue = magenta; paints mix subtractively

113.s: How do a red and a green object look through red glass?
113.x: Through red glass – Red and white objects look red; others black

113.s: Why does a black surface look black?
o: It absorbs all colours and reflects none
113.x: Black surface – Absorbs all colours, reflects none (blackboard)

113.s: Which of these is not a luminous object?
113.x: Luminous objects – Emit their own light (Sun, lamp, candle); the Moon only reflects

113.s: At what speed does light travel in vacuum?
113.x: Light – Electromagnetic wave (transverse, no medium, 3 × 10⁸ m/s); photons – energy packets (Planck, Einstein)

113.s: Which phenomenon shows the wave nature of light?
113.x: Particle vs wave nature – Photoelectric effect – particle; interference, diffraction, polarisation – wave

113.s: What is the speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum?
113.x: EM waves – Transverse, E ⟂ B, no medium, travel in vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m/s (3 lakh km/s); carry energy and momentum; polarisable; carry no charge – not deflected by fields

113.s: Which electromagnetic radiation has the highest frequency?
113.x: Frequency order (wavelength order the reverse) – Cosmic/gamma > X-rays > UV > visible > infrared > microwaves > radio waves (wavelength the reverse)

113.s: By which relation is photon energy given, making X-rays more energetic than radio waves?
113.x: Photon energy E = hf = hc/λ – X-rays > light > microwaves > radio; UV > visible > infrared; E = pc (p = 10 MeV/c → E = 10 MeV)

113.s: At what speed do all photons travel in vacuum?
113.x: All photons – Travel at c in vacuum; X-ray photon – shorter wavelength, higher frequency than visible

113.s: What is the wavelength range of microwaves?
113.x: Microwaves – ~300 MHz–300 GHz (1 mm–1 m) – radar, ovens (2.45 GHz), satellite links; infrared above (300 GHz–400 THz)

113.s: Which of these uses infrared radiation?
113.x: Infrared – TV remote, night vision, reading faded documents, heat lamps and physiotherapy

113.s: What is ultraviolet radiation used for?
113.x: UV – Detecting forgery, sterilisation, vitamin D

113.s: How do electric and magnetic fields affect X-rays?
113.x: X-rays – Penetrate soft tissue and light metals (Al); not deflected by fields; detected with photographic plates

113.s: What happens to most of the electron energy in an X-ray tube?
o: It becomes heat at the target
113.x: X-ray tube – Only ~1% of electron energy → X-rays; the rest is heat at the target (tungsten anode, cooled); cut-off wavelength λmin = hc/eV – doubling the voltage halves it

113.s: What are cosmic rays mostly made of?
113.x: Cosmic rays – High-energy charged particles (mostly protons) – not EM waves

113.s: How does potential difference vary with current in a nichrome wire at constant temperature?
113.x: Ohm's law – V = IR – p.d. ∝ current at constant temperature (rises linearly in nichrome); Ohm's law is not universal – semiconductors, diodes, strong fields deviate

113.s: What are metals like silver and copper that obey Ohm's law called?
113.x: Ohmic conductors – Metals – silver, copper; semiconductors (Ge, Si) and carbon are non-ohmic

113.s: On which of these does the resistance of a wire not depend?
113.x: Resistance R = ρl/A – Depends on length, area, material and temperature – not on the current; same size: aluminium (lower conductivity) has higher resistance than copper

113.s: What does resistivity depend on?
113.x: Resistivity – Depends on material and temperature, not on length or area; conductivity = 1/resistivity (product 1)

113.s: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
113.x: Best conductor – Silver (lowest resistivity), then copper, aluminium

113.s: Why are manganin and constantan used for standard resistors?
o: Their resistivity is almost unchanged with temperature
113.x: Manganin, constantan – Resistivity almost unchanged with temperature → standard resistors; nichrome – high resistivity, heater coils

113.s: What is the resistivity range of insulators like ebonite and mica?
113.x: Insulators – Ebonite, rubber, glass, mica, dry wood – ~10¹²–10¹⁷ Ω m; electrons tightly bound; a conductor with appreciable resistance = resistor

113.s: Which of these liquids is an insulator?
113.x: Liquids – Electrolytes (salt solution), mercury conduct; pure water, oils, kerosene insulate

113.s: What happens to the resistance of a semiconductor on heating?
113.x: Semiconductor resistance – Decreases on heating; a metal's increases

113.s: What is common to resistors in series?
113.x: Series resistors – Rs = R1 + R2 + … – increases; same current

113.s: How does the total resistance of resistors in parallel compare with the smallest one?
113.x: Parallel resistors (resistances in parallel) – 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 – less than the smallest (2, 4, 8 Ω → 8/7 Ω); same potential difference

113.s: What is potential difference?
o: Work done to move a unit charge
113.x: Potential difference – Work to move a unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C)

113.s: In which direction does conventional current flow?
113.x: Conventional current – Positive to negative

113.s: Which laws express conservation of charge (junction rule) and energy (loop rule) in circuits?
113.x: Kirchhoff's laws – Junction rule (current in = out) – conservation of charge; loop rule – conservation of energy

113.s: What does the heat produced by a current depend on (Joule's law)?
113.x: Electrical energy – VIt; Joule's law H = I²Rt = V²t/R – depends on voltage, current and time

113.s: Which of two bulbs in parallel has the higher resistance?
113.x: Bulbs in parallel – P = V²/R – dimmer bulb has higher resistance (series: reverse)

113.s: What is the frequency of AC supply in India?
113.x: DC frequency = zero – Flows one way; AC in India = 50 Hz (USA 60 Hz)

113.s: What does a rectifier (diode) do?
113.x: Rectifier (diode) – AC → DC; inverter DC → AC

113.s: Which materials are charged by friction, as in static electricity?
113.x: Static electricity – Insulators charged by friction (comb, glass rod); negative = gaining electrons, positive = losing (protons never move); door-handle shock – charge transfers

113.s: What is transferring charge from a charged object to the Earth called?
113.x: Earthing – Transfer of charge from a charged object to the Earth

113.s: What happens to the electrostatic force between two charges when the distance doubles?
113.x: Coulomb's law – ∝ 1/r² – doubling the distance makes it one quarter

113.s: In which year did Hertz observe the photoelectric effect?
113.x: Electron emission – By light – photoelectric (Hertz 1887, Einstein); by heat – thermionic; by strong field – field emission

113.s: What is the minimum energy needed to eject photoelectrons called?
113.x: Threshold frequency – Minimum frequency ejecting photoelectrons; minimum energy = work function

113.s: Of which process is the photoelectric effect the reverse?
113.x: Photoelectric effect – Reverse of X-ray production; light ejects electrons

113.s: What do an electron and a proton accelerated through the same p.d. gain equally?
113.x: Electron vs proton through the same p.d. – Equal KE (qV); the electron moves faster

113.s: What is the critical temperature below which lead becomes a superconductor?
113.x: Superconductors – Zero resistance below a critical temperature (BCS: Bardeen, Cooper, Schrieffer); lead ~7.2 K; mercury 4.2 K (first, Onnes 1911)

113.s: Which technology is based on the Meissner effect?
113.x: Meissner Effect – Perfect diamagnetism – fields expelled; basis of Maglev trains, MRI magnets

113.s: In which year did Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley invent the transistor?
113.x: Transistor – Semiconductor amplifier and switch (Bardeen, Brattain, Shockley 1947) – hearing aids, radios; diode – rectifier; capacitor stores charge

113.s: Which region of a bipolar junction transistor is most heavily doped?
113.x: BJT doping – Emitter heavily, base lightly doped and thin, collector moderately

113.s: Which type of semiconductor does doping silicon with trivalent boron give?
113.x: Doping – Trivalent (B, Al, Ga) → p-type; pentavalent (P, As) → n-type; raises conductivity

113.s: What are silicon wafers mainly used to make?
113.x: Semiconductors – Silicon, germanium (metalloids), gallium arsenide – chips, integrated circuits on silicon wafers; quartz (SiO2) is an insulator but piezoelectric (quartz clocks)

113.s: Which low-work-function metals are used in photoelectric cells?
113.x: Photoelectric cells – Low-work-function alkali metals – rubidium, caesium, potassium; photocell, solar cell, automatic doors

113.s: Which of these converts chemical energy, not electrical energy, into light?
113.x: Electrical → light – LED, laser, TV, bulb; a candle – chemical energy → light and heat

113.s: What does LASER stand for?
o: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Low Amplitude Spectral Emission of Rays
Light Absorption by Simple Electron Resonance
Linear Amplified Source of Emitted Radiation
113.x: LASER – Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation

113.s: Who found that an electric current deflects a compass needle?
113.x: Magnetic field – Region around a magnet where its force can be detected; current makes one (Oersted – compass deflects)

113.s: What kind of curves are magnetic field lines?
113.x: Magnetic field lines – Closed curves, never cross; outside N → S, inside S → N; none begin at a point (no monopole); lines near pole ends curve

113.s: What happens to pole strength when a bar magnet is cut into two?
113.x: Cutting a bar magnet – Two complete magnets; pole strength stays the same, magnetic moment halves; poles cannot be isolated

113.s: How does unmagnetised iron respond to a magnet's poles?
113.x: Unmagnetised iron – Attracted by either pole

113.s: What acts on a bar magnet placed in a uniform magnetic field?
o: Net force zero, only a torque
113.x: Bar magnet in a uniform field – Net force zero, only a torque

113.s: What is the magnetic meridian?
o: The vertical plane through a freely suspended magnet's axis
113.x: Magnetic meridian – Vertical plane through a freely suspended magnet's axis

113.s: What is the angle of dip at the magnetic poles?
113.x: Angle of dip – 90° at the magnetic poles, 0° at the magnetic equator

113.s: What is the Curie point of iron, above which it loses its magnetism?
113.x: Curie point – Above it a ferromagnet loses its magnetism (iron ~770 °C)

113.s: What is the magnetic field like inside a solenoid?
113.x: Solenoid – Field inside is uniform – electromagnets

113.s: What happens to two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction?
113.x: Parallel wires – Currents in the same direction attract, opposite repel

113.s: What happens to a charge's speed when it moves in a magnetic field?
113.x: Charge in a magnetic field – Force ⟂ velocity, no work – speed constant, direction changes

113.s: Which way is the magnetic field if a positive charge moving west is deflected north?
113.x: Lorentz force F = q(v × B) – Positive charge moving west, deflected north → field upward

113.s: Which rule gives the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, as in a motor?
113.x: Fleming's left-hand rule – Force on a current in a magnetic field (motor): middle finger = current, forefinger = field, thumb = force

113.s: Which rule gives the direction of induced current in a generator?
113.x: Fleming's right-hand rule – Induced current (generator); wire falling along East–West → current West → East

113.s: What does faster relative motion of a magnet and coil produce?
113.x: EM induction (Faraday's law) – Current induced by relative motion of magnet and coil (changing flux); faster motion → larger induced current; maximum when moving perpendicular to the field; in a rotating coil it reverses every half revolution (AC)

113.s: On which kind of supply do transformers work?
113.x: Uses of induction – Generators, transformers (AC only), induction cooktops, wireless charging, dynamic microphone

113.s: What does an AC generator use to collect current?
113.x: AC generator – Slip rings; DC generator – split-ring commutator

113.s: What does a step-down transformer do to current?
113.x: Transformer (works only on AC) – Step-down transformer: lowers voltage, raises current (power nearly constant); step-up the reverse; low-voltage winding – larger cross-section, fewer turns

113.s: Which of these is a transformer loss?
113.x: Transformer losses – Copper (I²R), hysteresis, eddy currents, flux leakage

113.s: Which motor is started with full external rotor resistance to raise starting torque?
113.x: Slip-ring induction motor – Started with full external rotor resistance – adding rotor resistance raises starting torque, lowers starting current

113.s: Who showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field?
113.x: Electromagnetism – Changing magnetic field induces current (Faraday); current produces a field (Oersted)

113.s: Which is the fourth state of matter?
113.x: States of matter – Solid, liquid, gas, plasma (4th), Bose–Einstein condensate (5th) – near absolute zero; predicted by S.N. Bose & Einstein, made in 1995

113.s: Which state of matter has negligible compressibility?
113.x: Solids – Definite shape, high density, rigidity, negligible compressibility; compressibility: solid < liquid < gas

113.s: Which state lies between solid and liquid and is used in LCD displays?
113.x: Liquid crystals – Between solid and liquid (flow + order) – LCD displays

113.s: What share of oxygen does inhaled air contain?
113.x: Inhaled air – ~21% O2

113.s: Which gas did Cavendish (1766) identify as "inflammable air"?
113.x: Cavendish (1766) – Hydrogen – "inflammable air"

113.s: Which element is the second most abundant in the Earth's crust?
113.x: Silicon – 2nd most abundant crustal element

113.s: What is oxidation in terms of electrons?
113.x: Oxidation – Loss of electrons; alkaloids contain nitrogen

113.s: Which of these has the largest rest mass?
113.x: Rest mass – Electron < proton < neutron < alpha particle (He nucleus)

113.s: What is the mass of an electron compared with a proton?
113.x: Electron – In cathode rays; negative; mass ≈ 1/1836 of a proton; deflected by electric and magnetic fields

113.s: Who discovered the positron, the antiparticle of the electron (1932)?
113.x: Positron – Antiparticle of the electron (Carl Anderson, 1932)

113.s: Which particle carries the electromagnetic force?
113.x: Force carriers – Photon – electromagnetic; gluon – strong; W/Z – weak; graviton (hypothetical) – gravity

113.s: Which particle has (near-)zero mass and no charge, emitted in beta decay?
113.x: Particles – Photon – zero mass, spin 1 (boson); neutrino – (near-)zero mass; quark – fractional charge; electron/positron – spin ½

113.s: What is the ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom?
113.x: Hydrogen atom – Ground state −13.6 eV → ionisation energy 13.6 eV

113.s: In which region of the spectrum does the Lyman series of hydrogen lie?
113.x: Hydrogen series (spectrum) – Larger gap → shorter wavelength; n=2 → n=1 shortest among 2→1, 3→2, 4→3, 5→4; Lyman – ultraviolet (to n=1), Balmer – visible (n=2), Paschen, Brackett, Pfund – infrared

113.s: Who discovered radioactivity in 1896?
113.x: Radioactive elements – Emit α, β and γ (Becquerel, 1896)

113.s: Who called atomic power "moonshine" in 1933?
113.x: Rutherford (1933) – Called atomic power 'moonshine' – energy input exceeded output

113.s: Which theory, used in GPS corrections, does the equivalence principle underlie?
113.x: Equivalence principle – General relativity, GPS corrections

113.s: Which shift of light from receding galaxies is a Doppler effect?
113.x: Doppler – Red shift; Huygens' – wavefronts, reflection, refraction

113.s: Which effect makes a fan under an AC lamp seem to turn backwards?
113.x: Stroboscopic effect – Fan under an AC lamp seems to reverse

113.s: Why is a bird sitting on one live wire safe?
o: Its feet are insulated by feathers
There is no potential difference across it
113.x: Bird on one live wire – Safe – no potential difference

113.s: What does a candle flame look like in microgravity (NASA)?
113.x: Candle in space – Microgravity flame is spherical, dim, blue (NASA)

113.s: What is the movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane from low to high solute concentration called?
113.x: Osmosis – Water molecules move through a semi-permeable (plasma) membrane from low to high solute concentration (roots absorb water)

113.s: What happens to a cell in a hypertonic medium?
113.x: Hypertonic medium (more concentrated outside) – The cell loses water (plasmolysis); hypotonic – gains water

113.s: Which of these is a non-contact force?
113.x: Non-contact forces – Gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic; push, friction and strain are contact forces

113.s: What does a substance's melting point indicate?
113.x: Melting point – Indicates the strength of intermolecular forces of attraction

113.s: What is the defect in thalassemia?
o: Reduced synthesis of a globin chain of haemoglobin
113.x: Thalassemia – Autosomal recessive; reduced rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains (α or β) of haemoglobin → anaemia

113.s: What is haemophilia?
o: An X-linked defect of a clotting factor
113.x: Haemophilia – X-linked recessive defect of a clotting factor – a cut keeps bleeding

113.s: In which way is colour blindness inherited?
113.x: Colour blindness – X-linked recessive; colour-blind father × normal (non-carrier) mother → no colour-blind child, all daughters carriers; affected mother × normal father → all sons colour-blind, daughters normal carriers

113.s: What type of inherited disorder is phenylketonuria (PKU)?
113.x: Phenylketonuria (PKU) – Autosomal recessive metabolic disorder – lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase (converts phenylalanine into tyrosine), so phenylalanine builds up

113.s: Which feature, with short stature, is typical of Down's syndrome?
113.x: Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) – Short stature, furrowed tongue, mental retardation; confirmed by amniocentesis (chromosome test of amniotic fluid cells); ultrasound only screens

113.s: Which metal builds up in Wilson's disease?
113.x: Wilson's disease – Copper build-up – speech, movement, fluid build-up

113.s: Which list gives examples of genetic disorders?
o: X-linked recessive defect of a clotting factor – a cut keeps bleeding
Albinism, haemophilia, colour blindness, Down's syndrome
Bulimia – cannot stop eating (binges); anorexia nervosa – refuses food
Night blindness and xerophthalmia (vitamin A deficiency)
113.x: Genetic disorders – Albinism, haemophilia, colour blindness, Down's syndrome

113.s: Which are examples of non-genetic (deficiency) disorders?
o: Night blindness and xerophthalmia (vitamin A deficiency)
Albinism, haemophilia, colour blindness, Down's syndrome
X-linked recessive defect of a clotting factor – a cut keeps bleeding
Bulimia – cannot stop eating (binges); anorexia nervosa – refuses food
113.x: Non-genetic – Night blindness and xerophthalmia (vitamin A deficiency)

113.s: In which condition is the Barr body absent?
113.x: Barr body – Inactive X chromosome; absent in Turner syndrome (XO) and normal males; present in Klinefelter (XXY); two in triple-X

113.s: Which substance at high levels causes gout?
113.x: Gout – High uric acid (end product of purine breakdown from nucleic acids) → urate crystals in joints; patients limit purine-rich food (organ meat, some seafood)

113.s: Which disorder: Plaques of amyloid-beta, cut from amyloid precursor protein (APP), plus tau tangles?
113.x: Alzheimer's disease – Plaques of amyloid-beta, cut from amyloid precursor protein (APP), plus tau tangles

113.s: What does the immune system attack in multiple sclerosis?
o: Myelin in the central nervous system
113.x: Multiple sclerosis – Autoimmune – the immune system attacks myelin in the central nervous system; linked to genes (HLA-DR2), Epstein-Barr virus, low vitamin D

113.s: What is metastasis?
o: Spread of cancer cells to other organs
113.x: Metastasis – Spread of cancer cells via blood or lymph to other organs

113.s: What is fluid in the peritoneal (abdominal) cavity called?
113.x: Ascites – Fluid in the peritoneal (abdominal) cavity; hydrothorax – pleural cavity; hydroamnion – excess amniotic fluid; oedema – tissues

113.s: Which eating disorder makes a person refuse food?
113.x: Eating disorders – Bulimia – cannot stop eating (binges); anorexia nervosa – refuses food

113.s: Which gland is called the master gland?
113.x: Pituitary (master gland) – At the base of the brain; pea-sized – the smallest of the common glands; single, not paired; GH, TSH, ACTH, ADH; oxytocin released here, made in the hypothalamus

113.s: Which gland: Endocrine gland in the brain (epithalamus); melatonin – biological clock; melatonin falls in bright light?
113.x: Pineal – Endocrine gland in the brain (epithalamus); melatonin – biological clock; melatonin falls in bright light

113.s: Which hormone of the thyroid contains iodine?
113.x: Thyroid (largest endocrine) – Thyroxine (T4, T3) contains iodine; calcitonin; deficiency: cretinism, goitre

113.s: Which gland behind the sternum matures T cells?
113.x: Thymus – Behind the sternum; trains (matures) T cells

113.s: Which gland: Back of the thyroid; PTH – blood calcium; works independent of the pituitary?
113.x: Parathyroid – Back of the thyroid; PTH – blood calcium; works independent of the pituitary

113.s: Which gland above the kidneys is called the life-saving gland?
113.x: Adrenal (above the kidneys) – Adrenaline, cortisol, aldosterone; the life-saving gland; helps control blood pressure; female adrenals also secrete testosterone

113.s: Which cells of the pancreas produce insulin?
113.x: Pancreas – Endocrine (insulin from beta cells, glucagon from alpha cells) + exocrine (pancreatic juice)

113.s: Which cells of the testes secrete testosterone?
113.x: Testes – Sperm and testosterone (from Leydig cells)

113.s: Which hormone does the kidney secrete for RBC production?
113.x: Kidney – Erythropoietin (RBC production)

113.s: Which hormone is called the 'fight or flight' emergency hormone?
113.x: Adrenaline – 'Fight or flight' / emergency hormone

113.s: Which stress hormone is a steroid with no peptide chain?
113.x: Cortisol – A steroid (no peptide chain); rises with stress

113.s: What kind of substance is insulin, which lowers blood sugar?
113.x: Insulin – A hormone; lowers blood sugar; promotes glucose uptake and fat storage; slows glycogen breakdown; controls carbohydrate metabolism

113.s: What does glucagon do?
113.x: Glucagon – Raises blood sugar (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis)

113.s: What does excess growth hormone in childhood cause?
113.x: Growth hormone (pituitary) – Excess in childhood → gigantism, in adults → acromegaly; deficiency → dwarfism; rises with exercise

113.s: Why does drinking alcohol increase urine output?
113.x: Vasopressin (ADH) – Holds water in the kidney; alcohol suppresses ADH → more urine; deficiency → diabetes insipidus (much dilute urine, great thirst)

113.s: What is gastrin?
113.x: Gastrin – A hormone (not a gland)

113.s: Which is the first hormone released by the placenta?
113.x: hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) – The first hormone released by the placenta

113.s: Which of these is a plant hormone?
113.x: Plant hormone – Cytokinin (cell division); thyroxine, oestrogen and testosterone are animal hormones

113.s: What characterises Type 1 diabetes?
113.x: Type 1 – Low insulin

113.s: What characterises Type 2 diabetes?
113.x: Type 2 – Insulin resistance

113.s: Why is glucose lost in urine in diabetes mellitus?
113.x: Effect – High sugar, low insulin; extra glucose lost with water in urine

113.s: What is metformin?
113.x: Metformin – Oral anti-diabetic

113.s: Which is the first digestive enzyme, acting on starch in the mouth?
113.x: Start – Buccal cavity – salivary amylase (ptyalin/diastase), the first enzyme, digests starch

113.s: Which is the largest salivary gland?
113.x: Salivary glands – Parotid (largest), submandibular, sublingual

113.s: Which organ is the food pipe?
113.x: Oesophagus – Food pipe

113.s: Which stomach cells secrete HCl?
113.x: Stomach HCl – From parietal (oxyntic) cells; pH ~1.5–3.5; activates pepsinogen → pepsin (pepsinogen = inactive pepsin)

113.s: Which enzyme is made in the abomasum, the 'true stomach' of cattle?
113.x: Cattle – Pepsin is made in the abomasum (the 'true stomach'); rumen, reticulum and omasum make no gastric juice

113.s: How does bile help fat digestion despite having no digestive enzymes?
113.x: Bile – Made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder; no digestive enzymes – it only emulsifies fats, so the liver aids fat digestion without fat-digesting enzymes

113.s: Which part of the intestine do the bile and pancreatic ducts open into?
113.x: Duodenum – Bile and pancreatic ducts open here

113.s: Which juice makes the acidic chyme alkaline for pancreatic enzymes?
113.x: Neutralising chyme – Bile juice makes the acidic food from the stomach alkaline for pancreatic enzymes; pancreatic bicarbonate also helps

113.s: Where does most digestion and absorption of food take place?
113.x: Small intestine – Most digestion – complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats (pancreatic juice + bile + intestinal juice); maximum absorption into blood (villi); the pancreas only supplies enzymes

113.s: Which is the longest part of the small intestine?
113.x: Small intestine (longest to shortest) – Ileum (~3.5 m) > jejunum (~2.5 m) > duodenum (~25 cm)

113.s: What does the large intestine mainly absorb?
113.x: Large intestine – Mainly absorbs water (as do the renal tubules)

113.s: Why can humans not digest cellulose?
113.x: Cellulose – Not digested by humans (no cellulase), though diastase/amylase is present

113.s: What is sweat mainly made of?
113.x: Sweat – Water + salt

113.s: What does the gizzard do in earthworms and birds?
113.x: Gizzard – Grinds food in earthworms (red worms) and birds; the crop stores it

113.s: What is ingestion by Amoeba, with pseudopodia encircling prey, called?
113.x: Amoeba – Circumvallation = ingestion (pseudopodia encircle prey); digestion in a food vacuole

113.s: Which is the largest gland in the human body?
113.x: Size – Largest gland (internal organ); skin = the largest organ

113.s: What are liver cells called?
113.x: Cells – Hepatocytes (hepar = liver); neurons – brain; cardiomyocytes – heart

113.s: Which of these is a function of the liver?
113.x: Functions – Secretes bile; urea is made in the liver; metabolises drugs and toxins, breaks down alcohol; regulates blood chemicals (glucose, proteins); stores glycogen

113.s: Which property of the liver makes living-donor transplants possible?
113.x: Regeneration – Regrows after partial removal → living-donor transplants

113.s: Where is glycogen ('animal starch') stored?
113.x: Glycogen – Storage carbohydrate of animals ('animal starch') in liver and skeletal muscle; plants store starch

113.s: How much blood does an adult have?
113.x: Blood – A fluid connective tissue (plasma + formed elements); ~5–6 L in an adult; takes oxygen to all parts of the body

113.s: What is the normal pH of human blood?
113.x: Blood pH – 7.35–7.45 (~7.4, slightly basic); held by buffers – bicarbonate, phosphate and proteins – plus lungs and kidneys

113.s: Which blood cells are the most numerous?
113.x: RBC – Carry O2 (haemoglobin); most numerous, ~5 million/mm³

113.s: Which blood cells are called the 'soldiers' of the body?
113.x: WBC – Defend the body – the 'soldiers'; 4,000–11,000/mm³ (~7,000/mm³); made in bone marrow and lymph nodes

113.s: What is the normal platelet count?
113.x: Platelets – Clot blood; 1.5–4 lakh/mm³ (~2.5 lakh/mm³) – platelets outnumber WBC (RBC > platelets > WBC)

113.s: Which are the most abundant granulocytes?
113.x: Neutrophils – Most abundant granulocytes

113.s: In which tissue are RBCs, neutrophils and lymphocytes formed?
113.x: Bone marrow – RBCs, neutrophils and lymphocytes form in the bone marrow (of long bones)

113.s: Which enzyme turns fibrinogen into fibrin during clotting?
113.x: Thrombin – Turns fibrinogen into fibrin (clotting)

113.s: What does haemoglobin do in RBCs?
113.x: Haemoglobin – Red, iron-containing pigment of RBCs; binds oxygen, carries O2 and some CO2 (carbamino-Hb); gives the red colour; gives no immunity (that is WBC)

113.s: Besides haemoglobin, which muscle protein contains iron?
113.x: Iron and magnesium – Iron also in myoglobin (muscle); magnesium in chlorophyll

113.s: What share of the body's blood do veins hold?
113.x: Distribution – Veins hold ~70% of blood; cells ~45% of volume

113.s: What is normal human blood pressure?
113.x: Blood pressure – Normal 120/80 mmHg; greater than atmospheric pressure; narrower vessels → higher BP

113.s: Who discovered the ABO blood groups (1901)?
113.x: ABO groups – Landsteiner (1901)

113.s: Which blood group is the universal donor?
113.x: O negative – Universal donor – O gives to all

113.s: Which blood group is the universal recipient?
113.x: AB – Universal recipient – receives from all

113.s: Which blood groups can a patient of group A receive?
113.x: A / B – A → A, AB; B → B, AB; an A patient takes A or O

113.s: Which blood groups can a child of AB × O parents have?
113.x: ABO inheritance – A × O parents → A or O child; AB × O parents → only A or B children (an O child cannot be theirs)

113.s: Which is the natural pacemaker of the heart?
113.x: Natural pacemaker – SA node (right atrium); a pacemaker device regulates the heartbeat

113.s: What do coronary arteries do?
o: Supply blood to the heart muscle
113.x: Coronary arteries – Supply blood to the heart muscle

113.s: Which heart chamber receives oxygenated blood from the lungs?
113.x: Left auricle – Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs (pulmonary veins)

113.s: Which heart chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
113.x: Left ventricle – Pumps it into the aorta

113.s: Which vein brings blood from the gut to the liver?
113.x: Hepatic portal vein – Brings gut blood to the liver

113.s: What is the path of oxygen in the body?
113.x: O2 path – Lungs → blood → tissues

113.s: What is the normal resting heart rate of an adult?
113.x: Heart rate – 72/min; tachycardia = fast heart rate

113.s: What does an ECG record?
113.x: ECG – Graph of the electrical activity of the heart (EEG – brain, EMG – muscles)

113.s: Which of these is NOT a typical symptom of a heart attack?
113.x: Heart attack – Chest pain, heavy sweating, nausea, breathlessness (headache not typical)

113.s: What event does the "golden hour" of emergency care follow?
113.x: Golden hour – The first hour after a heart attack (or major trauma), when treatment saves most lives

113.s: What was the name of the artificial heart developed by Robert Jarvik in 1982?
113.x: Artificial heart – Jarvik-7 (Robert Jarvik, 1982); artificial muscle research targets the failing heart

113.s: Which of these animals has a three-chambered heart?
113.x: Heart chambers – Fish 2 (Scoliodon); amphibians (frog, salamander) and most reptiles 3; crocodiles, birds, mammals 4

113.s: What colour is the haemolymph of a cockroach?
113.x: Cockroach – Open circulation; colourless ('white') haemolymph (no haemoglobin); 13-chambered heart

113.s: Which nitrogenous waste does the kidney filter?
113.x: Role – Organ of excretion; filters urea (nitrogenous waste)

113.s: About how many nephrons does each kidney have?
113.x: Nephron – Structural and functional (excretory) unit of the kidney (~1 million per kidney)

113.s: Which nutrient is reabsorbed from the kidney filtrate along with much water?
113.x: Flow – Blood in by the renal artery, out by the renal vein; filtrate from Bowman's capsule passes the tubules, where glucose and much water are reabsorbed

113.s: What is the normal renal blood flow?
113.x: Renal blood flow – ≈ 1,200 mL (cc) per minute

113.s: What is the normal pH of urine?
113.x: Urine – ~1.5 L/day, pH ~6.0; yellow from urochrome; path kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra

113.s: Which kidney disease is also called nephritis?
113.x: Kidney damage – Albuminuria (albumin in urine – damaged glomeruli) and Bright's disease (nephritis); kidney failure → urea builds up in blood

113.s: What are most kidney stones made of?
113.x: Kidney stones – Mostly calcium oxalate; lithotripsy breaks them by shock waves

113.s: What can a dialysis machine not do that kidney tubules do?
113.x: Dialysis (dialyzer) – Removes wastes and excess water but cannot reabsorb nutrients (glucose, amino acids) as the tubules do; haemodialysis (machine) vs peritoneal dialysis (peritoneum as filter)

113.s: Which is the most commonly transplanted organ?
113.x: Transplants – Kidney = the most commonly transplanted organ (living or deceased donor)

113.s: Which organ is most affected by long fasting?
113.x: Long fasting – The kidney is the organ most affected

113.s: Which structures do the work of kidneys in insects?
113.x: Insects – Kidneys ≈ Malpighian tubules

113.s: What kind of urine does the desert kangaroo rat excrete?
113.x: Kangaroo rat – Desert animal; never drinks water; excretes almost solid, highly concentrated urine

113.s: Which condition gets worse if a person drinks sea water, as its salt draws water out of cells?
113.x: Dehydration – Sea water must not be drunk – its salt draws still more water out of the cells; tea, coffee and alcohol are diuretics but still supply water

113.s: Which is the largest part of the brain, controlling thinking and memory?
113.x: Cerebrum (forebrain) – Largest part of the brain – thinking, memory

113.s: What does the cerebellum control?
113.x: Cerebellum – Balance and posture

113.s: Which part of the brain controls heartbeat, breathing and vomiting?
113.x: Medulla oblongata – Heartbeat, breathing (respiratory centre), swallowing, vomiting

113.s: Which part of the brain is the body's thermostat?
113.x: Hypothalamus – Basal part of the diencephalon (forebrain); the body's thermostat – temperature, hunger/satiety, thirst; links nervous and endocrine systems

113.s: What do the hippocampus and frontal lobe handle?
113.x: Hippocampus / frontal lobe – Memory / reasoning

113.s: Which part of the nervous system controls reflex actions?
113.x: Spinal cord – Reflex action

113.s: Through which part does a reflex arc pass between sensory and motor neurons?
113.x: Reflex arc – Receptor → sensory (afferent) neuron → spinal cord → motor (efferent) neuron → effector; an automatic response = reflex

113.s: How many pairs of spinal nerves do humans have?
113.x: Nerves – 31 pairs of spinal nerves, 12 pairs of cranial nerves

113.s: Which ions carry nerve signals in neurons?
113.x: Neurons – Show excitability and conductivity; sodium ions carry nerve signals

113.s: Which technique is not used for brain scans because bone blocks it?
113.x: Brain scans – EEG, MEG, MRI, CT – ultrasound is not used (bone blocks it)

113.s: Which part of the eye is used in eye donation (keratoplasty)?
113.x: Cornea – Thin transparent membrane at the front; light enters here; does most of the focusing; used in eye donation (keratoplasty)

113.s: What is the path of light through the eye?
113.x: Path – Cornea → pupil → lens → retina

113.s: Which coloured muscular part of the eye sets the size of the pupil?
113.x: Iris – Coloured muscular diaphragm; sets the pupil's size and so controls the light entering; the pupil is the opening (NCERT: 'the pupil regulates and controls the amount of light')

113.s: What does the retina turn light into?
113.x: Retina – Light turned into nerve impulses (rods and cones); image real, inverted, diminished (formed by the lens)

113.s: What is cataract?
113.x: Cataract – Clouding of the lens

113.s: Which lens corrects myopia?
113.x: Myopia – Eye defect (concave lens)

113.s: How wide is each human eye's field of view to the side?
113.x: Field of view – Each eye ~60° nasally/upward, ~90–100° to the side

113.s: Which gland secretes tears?
113.x: Tears – Lacrimal gland; contain lysozyme, which kills bacteria (sometimes misspelt 'lysosome')

113.s: How many cervical vertebrae do humans have?
113.x: Bones – Adult 206 bones (~200 at age 20); skull 22 (28 with the 6 ear ossicles, 29 with the hyoid); 7 cervical vertebrae

113.s: Which is the smallest bone of the human body?
113.x: Smallest bone – Stapes (middle ear); ossicles malleus, incus, stapes (femur = thigh)

113.s: Which of these is a human bone?
113.x: Human bones – Humerus, carpals, talus (astragalus), atlas

113.s: What is inside the hollow of long bones?
113.x: Long bones – Hollow – marrow cavity

113.s: What are bone and tooth enamel made of?
113.x: Composition – Bone and tooth enamel = calcium phosphate

113.s: What joins bone to bone?
113.x: Tendons / ligaments – Tendons (collagen) join muscle to bone; ligaments (elastic) join bone to bone

113.s: What does synovial fluid do?
113.x: Synovial fluid – Lubricates and cushions movable joints

113.s: What is the Adam's apple?
o: Projecting thyroid cartilage of the larynx
113.x: Adam's apple – Projecting thyroid cartilage of the larynx (voice box), larger in males after puberty

113.s: Which of these is a skeletal (voluntary) muscle?
113.x: Muscles – Skeletal (striated, voluntary – biceps); smooth (involuntary – ureters, iris, bronchi, gut, stomach walls); cardiac (heart)

113.s: Which is the strongest muscle of the human body?
113.x: Strongest muscle – Masseter of the jaw

113.s: From which structure is Ca2+ released during muscle contraction?
113.x: Contraction – Actin–myosin; Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; relaxation = Ca2+ pumped back; lactic acid causes cramps

113.s: What mouth pH does tooth decay begin below?
113.x: Tooth decay – Begins when mouth pH < 5.5

113.s: What is a tissue?
o: A group of similar cells doing a common function
113.x: Tissue – Group of similar cells doing a common function; tissues → organ → organ system

113.s: What are the four kinds of animal tissue?
113.x: Animal tissues – Epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous

113.s: Which kind of tissue lines the mouth and blood vessels?
113.x: Epithelial – Covering / protective tissue – skin, lining of the mouth and blood vessels

113.s: Which of these is NOT a connective tissue?
113.x: Connective – Areolar, adipose, bone, cartilage, blood, tendon; skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and skin are not connective

113.s: Where is cartilage absent?
113.x: Cartilage – In the larynx, nose, ear; absent in the urinary bladder

113.s: What are fat cells called?
113.x: Connective-tissue cells – Adipocytes – fat; chondrocytes – cartilage; osteocytes – bone; reticulocytes – young RBCs

113.s: Who discovered the cell in 1665?
113.x: Cell – Basic structural and functional unit of life; discovered by Robert Hooke (1665); water is the largest component (~70–90%)

113.s: Which ribosomes do mitochondria have, letting them make some of their own proteins?
113.x: Mitochondria – 'Powerhouses' – aerobic respiration makes ATP; 70S ribosomes and circular DNA, so they make some of their own proteins

113.s: On which organelles are proteins synthesised?
113.x: Ribosomes – Protein synthesis – proteins are synthesised on ribosomes of the rough ER (Golgi packages them)

113.s: Why is rough ER called rough?
113.x: Rough ER – Rough because of ribosomes on its surface

113.s: What is the function of smooth ER?
113.x: Smooth ER – Lipid and steroid-hormone synthesis, detoxification, transport

113.s: Which organelles are called the 'suicidal bags'?
113.x: Lysosomes – Storehouse of digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes, budded from the Golgi; digest worn-out organelles; the 'suicidal bags' – can digest the damaged cell itself

113.s: What do peroxisomes remove using catalase?

113.s: What is a desmosome?

113.s: Which structure do both plant and animal cells have?

113.s: What is the cell wall of fungi made of?

113.s: What is the structure of DNA?

113.s: What is pleiotropy?
113.x: Pleiotropy – One gene controls several characters; polygenic = many genes, one trait
