113.x: Sublimation – Separates iodine (camphor, NH4Cl, naphthalene) from KCl or sand

113.s: What basis does sieving use to separate components?
113.x: Sieving – Components of different sizes; winnowing – wind blows away lighter parts

113.s: Which method produces ultra-pure silicon and germanium for semiconductors?
113.x: Zone refining – Ultra-pure Si, Ge for semiconductors

113.s: Which monomer is PVC made from?
113.x: PVC – Vinyl chloride; blood bags, dialysis tubes

113.s: Which polymer is PTFE, used as a non-stick coating?
113.x: Teflon – PTFE (tetrafluoroethene) – non-stick coating

113.s: Which monomer is neoprene made from?
113.x: Neoprene – Chloroprene (elastomer)

113.s: Which monomer is natural rubber made of?
113.x: Natural rubber – Isoprene (elastomer)

113.s: In which year did Charles Goodyear discover vulcanisation of rubber?
113.x: Vulcanisation – Rubber + sulphur (Charles Goodyear, 1839) – harder, elastic, less sticky; John Dunlop – pneumatic tyre

113.s: In which year did Baekeland make Bakelite?
113.x: Bakelite – Phenol + formaldehyde (Baekeland 1907) – first fully synthetic plastic, thermosetting, cross-linked, poor conductor – switches, handles

113.s: What raw materials was nylon, the first fully synthetic fibre, made from?
113.x: Nylon – Synthetic (Carothers, 1935) – first fully synthetic fibre, from coal, water and air; strong, elastic, light; bullet-proof vests (woven nylon/aramid Kevlar)

113.s: Which monomers make nylon-6,6?
113.x: Nylon-6,6 – Hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid (condensation copolymer, polyamide)

113.s: Which polymer: The monomer of nylon-6?
113.x: Caprolactam – The monomer of nylon-6

113.s: Which monomers make the biodegradable nylon-2-nylon-6?
113.x: Nylon-2-Nylon-6 – Glycine + amino caproic acid – biodegradable

113.s: Which biodegradable polymer is made of 3-hydroxybutanoic and 3-hydroxypentanoic acid?
113.x: PHBV – 3-hydroxybutanoic acid + 3-hydroxypentanoic acid – biodegradable

113.s: Which monomers make Buna-S?
113.x: Buna-S – 1,3-butadiene + styrene – addition copolymer (elastomer)

113.s: Which monomers make Buna-N?
113.x: Buna-N – 1,3-butadiene + acrylonitrile

113.s: Which monomer makes polypropene?
113.x: Polypropene (PP) – Propene/propylene (CH₃–CH=CH₂); polythene – ethene

113.s: Which polymer is made of ethylene glycol and phthalic acid?
113.x: Glyptal – Ethylene glycol + phthalic acid; terylene (PET) – ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid

113.s: Which monomer makes PMMA (perspex)?
113.x: PMMA (perspex, acrylic glass) – Methyl methacrylate – light, strong, shatter-resistant

113.s: Which tough, transparent polymer is used for bullet-proof windows, CDs and helmets?
113.x: Polycarbonate – Tough, transparent – bullet-proof windows, CDs, helmets

113.s: Which property makes polyester (terylene) popular in clothing?
113.x: Polyester (terylene, Dacron) – Resists wrinkling; blends – polycot (polyester + cotton), terrycot (terylene + cotton), polywool

113.s: Which synthetic fibre is called artificial wool?
113.x: Rayon – Regenerated cellulose from wood pulp – artificial silk; acrylic – artificial wool

113.s: What is styrene used to make?
113.x: Styrene – Solvent/monomer for polyester resins, reinforced plastics (FRP), polystyrene

113.s: Which of these are natural polymers?
113.x: Natural polymers – Wool, silk, leather (proteins), cellulose, rubber

113.s: What are polymers like Bakelite and melamine, which do not soften on heating, called?
113.x: Thermoplastics – Polythene, PVC, polystyrene, Teflon (soften on heating); thermosets – Bakelite, melamine

113.s: What kind of polymers are nylon-6,6 and terylene?
113.x: Homopolymers – Polythene, PVC, Teflon (addition); nylon-6,6 and terylene – condensation copolymers

113.s: Which fibre is preferred for summer clothing because it absorbs sweat?
113.x: Cotton – Summer clothing (absorbs sweat); cotton, flax, silk crease

113.s: Which interlayer is used in modern laminated safety glass?
113.x: Shatter-proof (safety) glass – Early interlayer cellulose acetate/nitrate, now PVB; laminated glass – bullet-resistant windows; cellulose – water-insoluble polysaccharide

113.s: What is a bullet-proof jacket made of?
o: Layered fibres such as fibrous glass and aramid
113.x: Bullet-proof jacket – Layered fibres (fibrous glass, nylon/aramid)

113.s: What is glass, physically?
113.x: Glass – Amorphous solid, a supercooled liquid (not gelatine or ice cream); no sharp melting point; not a true compound

113.s: What is soft (soda-lime) glass chemically?
113.x: Soft (soda-lime) glass – Sodium calcium silicate – windows, bottles

113.s: What is hard glass chemically?
113.x: Hard glass – Potassium calcium silicate

113.s: Which element in Pyrex glass makes it heat-resistant?
113.x: Pyrex/borosilicate – Contains boron – heat-resistant labware

113.s: What is flint (lead) glass used for?
113.x: Flint (lead) glass – Lenses, prisms, electric bulbs, optical instruments

113.s: Which oxide in Crookes glass absorbs UV for sunglasses?
113.x: Crookes glass – Cerium oxide – absorbs UV (sunglasses)

113.s: What is glass wool used for?
113.x: Glass wool – Heat and sound insulation

113.s: Which compound decolourises glass by removing iron's green tint?
113.x: Manganese dioxide – Decolourises glass (removes iron's green tint); SiO2 = glass former

113.s: Which acid is used to etch on glass?
113.x: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) – Writing/etching on glass (SiO₂ → SiF₄); stored in wax/plastic bottles

113.s: What makes photochromic lenses darken in UV light?
113.x: Photochromic lenses – Darken in UV light – silver chloride (halide) microcrystals

113.s: What is diamond used for?
113.x: Diamond – Cutting tools

113.s: What is graphite used for?
113.x: Graphite – Pencils, lubricant, electrodes

113.s: What role does coke play in iron extraction?
113.x: Coke – Fuel and reducing agent in iron extraction

113.s: What is carbon black used for?
o: Pigment in paints, inks and tyres
113.x: Carbon black – Pigment in paints, inks, tyres

113.s: Which form of carbon is used in gas masks?
113.x: Activated charcoal – Gas masks

113.s: What is animal (bone) charcoal used for?
113.x: Animal (bone) charcoal – Decolourises raw sugar

113.s: In which fields are carbon nanotubes used?
113.x: Carbon nanotubes – Electronics, nanotechnology

113.s: What is graphene used for?
113.x: Graphene – Electronics, sensors – not a fuel or reducing agent

113.s: What is the chemical formula of baking soda?
113.x: Baking soda – NaHCO3 – antacid, baking; with vinegar gives CO2; no water of crystallisation; 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 on heating (cakes rise)

113.s: Which gas does baking powder release with moisture and heat?
113.x: Baking powder – Baking soda + a dry acid (tartaric acid / cream of tartar) – moisture and heat release CO2

113.s: What is the formula of washing soda, which removes permanent hardness?
113.x: Washing soda – Na2CO3·10H2O – removes permanent hardness

113.s: Which compound, called hypo, is used as a photographic fixer?
113.x: Hypo – Na2S2O3 – photographic fixer

113.s: What is bleaching powder made from?
113.x: Bleaching powder – Calcium oxychloride (Cl2 + slaked lime) – releases chlorine; water purification and bleaching; a disinfectant

113.s: What is milk of magnesia?
113.x: Milk of magnesia – Mg(OH)2 antacid

113.s: What is the formula of gypsum, heated to make Plaster of Paris?
113.x: Plaster of Paris – CaSO4·½H2O = (CaSO4)2·H2O (calcium sulphate hemihydrate) – one water molecule per two formula units; casts (doctors), moulds and statues (artists, sculptors); from gypsum CaSO4·2H2O on heating

113.s: What is the formula of blue vitriol?
113.x: Blue vitriol – CuSO4·5H2O

113.s: What forms slaked lime when it reacts with water?
113.x: Lime – Quicklime CaO + water → slaked lime Ca(OH)2 (lime water; whitewash); limestone = CaCO3

113.s: What is acetone commonly used as?
113.x: Acetone – Nail-polish remover

113.s: What is phenyl used as at home?
113.x: Phenyl – Household germicide / floor disinfectant

113.s: What is ethylene glycol used as in car radiators?
113.x: Glycol (ethylene glycol) – Anti-freeze – lowers (depresses) the freezing point in car radiators; prevents freezing in aviation fuel

113.s: Which gas is called laughing gas?
113.x: Laughing gas – Nitrous oxide (N2O) – mild anaesthetic

113.s: Which gas is firedamp, explosive in coal mines?
113.x: Firedamp – Methane – explosive with air in coal mines

113.s: Which pH do mouth acids fall below to start tooth decay, which basic toothpaste neutralises?
113.x: Toothpaste – Basic – neutralises mouth acids (decay below pH 5.5); enamel = calcium phosphate

113.s: For which chemicals is common salt the raw material?
o: NaOH, Cl2, baking soda, washing soda
113.x: Common salt (NaCl) – Na⁺ + Cl⁻ (1 : 1), rock salt; raw material for NaOH, Cl2, baking soda, washing soda (chlor-alkali, Solvay); symbol of the Dandi March / Salt Satyagraha (1930)

113.s: Which salt is used as a laxative and a mordant in dyeing?
113.x: Magnesium sulphate (Epsom salt) – Mordant in dyeing, leather tanning; laxative

113.s: Which type of water hardness do permutit / zeolite remove?
113.x: Permutit / zeolite – Sodium aluminium silicate – exchanges Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ for Na⁺, removes permanent hardness

113.s: Which gas causes the pungent smell near urinals?
113.x: Pungent smell near urinals – Ammonia (bacterial breakdown of urea)

113.s: What causes the fishy smell of spoiled fish?
113.x: Fishy smell – Amines (trimethylamine); rotten egg – H2S

113.s: What smell do esters like ethyl acetate have?
113.x: Esters (e.g. ethyl acetate) – Sweet, fruity smell – flavours, perfumes; acid + alcohol (esterification)

113.s: In which year did Bayer make aspirin?
113.x: Aspirin – Acetylsalicylic acid (Bayer, 1897) from salicin of willow bark; analgesic, antipyretic

113.s: Which type of hardness do chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium cause?
113.x: Hard water – Ca/Mg bicarbonates = temporary (boiling, Clark's lime); chlorides/sulphates = permanent (washing soda, ion exchange, Calgon)

113.s: What are drugs that relieve pain called?
113.x: Antiseptics – Boric acid, iodoform, H2O2 – safe on living tissue, stop microbe growth; analgesics – pain; antibiotics – infections

113.s: Why are disinfectants like phenol used only on objects?
o: They are toxic to living tissue
113.x: Disinfectants – Phenol, bleaching powder – toxic to living tissue, only for objects

113.s: What is the making of soap from oil and NaOH called?
113.x: Soap – Saponification of vegetable oil/fat with NaOH (hard) or KOH (soft); mineral oils cannot be saponified; alkaline (harms silk and wool), biodegradable

113.s: What does soap lower to clean dirt?
113.x: How soap cleans – Lowers surface tension; micelles (hydrocarbon tail in oily dirt, ionic head outside) form an emulsion that is rinsed away; colloid-sized, so soap solution scatters light

113.s: What does soap form in hard water?
113.x: Soap vs detergent – Soap forms scum (white curdy precipitate) in hard water, fails in acidic water; detergents lather even in hard water; older detergents (branched chains) – non-biodegradable (river foam)

113.s: In what is soap dissolved to make transparent soap?
113.x: Transparent soap – Soap dissolved in ethanol, solvent evaporated; floating soap – air beaten in; shaving soap – glycerol + rosin

113.s: Which agent should be used on an oil or petrol fire?
113.x: Oil/petrol fires – Not water (oil floats and spreads) – CO2, foam or sand; electrical fires – no water

113.s: Why is CO2 used in fire extinguishers?
o: It is non-combustible and heavier than air
113.x: CO2 – Fire extinguishers – non-combustible, heavier than air, cuts off oxygen

113.s: Which chemicals react in a soda-acid fire extinguisher to give CO2?
113.x: Soda-acid fire extinguisher – Sulphuric acid + sodium hydrogen carbonate → CO2

113.s: What is brass made of?
113.x: Brass – Cu + Zn

113.s: What is bronze made of?
113.x: Bronze – Cu + tin

113.s: What is German silver made of?
113.x: German silver – Cu + Zn + Ni

113.s: What are fuse wire and solder made of?
113.x: Fuse wire / solder – Tin + lead

113.s: What is Dow metal made of?
113.x: Dow metal – Mg + Al

113.s: What is constantan made of?
113.x: Constantan – Copper + nickel (resistance wire); manganin – Cu + Mn + Ni

113.s: Which alloy of lead, antimony and tin is used for printing types?
113.x: Type metal – Lead + antimony + tin (printing types)

113.s: What is rose metal made of?
113.x: Rose metal – Bismuth + lead + tin (low-melting)

113.s: What is an amalgam?
o: An alloy of a metal with mercury
An alloy of iron and carbon
113.x: Amalgam – Alloy of a metal with mercury (Hg) (iron forms none)

113.s: What makes stainless steel rust-free?
113.x: Stainless steel – Iron + chromium (+ nickel) – rust-free

113.s: What is chromium-molybdenum steel used for?
113.x: Chromium-molybdenum (Cr-Mo) steel – Superheater (boiler) tubes

113.s: Which alloy is used as high-speed tool steel, staying hard at high temperatures?
113.x: Tungsten steel – High-speed tool steel – hard at high temperature

113.s: What is nichrome used for?
113.x: Nichrome – Heater coil

113.s: What is the melting point of tungsten, the highest among metals?
113.x: Tungsten – Bulb filament – very hard and ductile; highest melting point of metals (~3,420 °C); hardest among common metals (chromium – hardest pure metal by Mohs); carborundum and cast iron are hard but brittle

113.s: What percentage of gold does 22-carat gold contain?
113.x: Gold – Most ductile and malleable; 24 carat pure; 22 carat = 91.6%; 18 carat = 75%; 14 carat = 14/24 ≈ 58%; dissolved by aqua regia 3 : 1 (HCl : HNO3)

113.s: Which metal tarnishes black in air containing H2S?
113.x: Silver – Best conductor of heat and electricity; tarnishes black: Ag + H2S → Ag2S

113.s: What is the green coating on copper in moist air, as on the Statue of Liberty, called?
113.x: Copper in moist air – Green basic copper carbonate CuCO3·Cu(OH)2; Statue of Liberty – copper patina

113.s: What temperature do gallium and caesium melt near?
113.x: Mercury – Only metal liquid at room temperature (bromine – the liquid non-metal; gallium, caesium melt near 30 °C); cadmium, germanium, tin are solids

113.s: Which is the densest metal?
113.x: Osmium – Densest ("heaviest") metal, ~22.6 g/cm³

113.s: Which of these metals is the densest?
113.x: Densities – Uranium (~19 g/cm³) > silver > copper > aluminium

113.s: Which is the most malleable metal?
113.x: Malleable metals – Gold (most), silver, aluminium; potassium/sodium soft and too reactive; sodium kept in kerosene

113.s: What is ruby made of?
113.x: Ruby – Al2O3 + chromium

113.s: What coating is used on magnetic tapes?
113.x: Magnetic tapes – Iron oxide (ferric oxide / chromium dioxide)

113.s: What type of battery is a car storage battery?
113.x: Storage battery – Lead–acid (lead plates in dilute H2SO4)

113.s: Which metal is extracted from bauxite?
113.x: Bauxite – Aluminium

113.s: Which metal is extracted from haematite and magnetite?
113.x: Haematite, magnetite – Iron

113.s: Which metal is extracted from cinnabar?
113.x: Cinnabar – Mercury

113.s: Which metal is extracted from galena?
113.x: Galena – Lead

113.s: What is china clay chemically?
113.x: China clay – Kaolin (Al silicate)

113.s: What is corundum chemically?
113.x: Corundum – Al2O3

113.s: What is talc chemically?
113.x: Talc – Mg silicate

113.s: What is rust chemically?
113.x: Rust – Brown hydrated iron(III) oxide Fe2O3·xH2O, a compound; needs iron + oxygen + moisture; increases weight

113.s: Why does a zinc coating (galvanising) protect iron?
o: Zinc is more electropositive and corrodes first
113.x: Galvanising – Zinc coating – zinc is more electropositive, corrodes first (sacrificial); tin plating = tin

113.s: What is passed through a metal-salt solution in electroplating?
113.x: Electroplating – Electric current through a metal-salt solution: object = cathode, plating metal (pure Ni, Cr, Ag) = anode, electrolyte = its salt (nickel sulphate); gold on jewellery, chromium on taps

113.s: Which effect of electric current do electrolysis and electroplating show?
113.x: Chemical effect of current – Chemical reaction in a conducting liquid (electrolysis, electroplating)

113.s: What is the melting point of lead?
113.x: Melting points – Tin 232 °C < lead 327 °C < zinc 420 °C < silver 962 °C < iron ~1538 °C (~1500 °C; 1,808 K); boron > iron > silicon > aluminium

113.s: What is the melting point of sodium?
113.x: Low melting points – Radon ~ −71 °C; sodium 98 °C; radium 700 °C

113.s: Which substance has a higher melting point than tungsten (~3,900 °C)?
113.x: Highest melting points – Tantalum (hafnium) carbide ~3,900 °C > tungsten

113.s: In which year did Dalton propose the indivisible atom?
113.x: Atomic models – Dalton – indivisible atom (1808); J.J. Thomson – electron, 'plum pudding'; Rutherford – nucleus (gold foil); Bohr – orbits

113.s: How many electrons can the M shell hold (2n²)?
113.x: Shell capacity – 2n² – K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32; 5th period has 18 elements

113.s: What is one atomic mass unit (u)?
113.x: Atomic mass unit – 1 u = 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom

113.s: Which of these isotopes has the most neutrons?
113.x: Neutrons – Mass number − atomic number (Fe-59: 33 > Cu-61: 32 > Zn-61: 31 > Zn-60: 30)

113.s: Which quantum number gives the shape of an orbital?
113.x: Quantum numbers – n – size/energy; l – shape; m – orientation; s – spin

113.s: How many angular nodes does a 4d orbital have?
113.x: Orbital nodes – Angular = l, radial = n − l − 1 (4d: 2 angular, 1 radial)

113.s: Which rule says electrons occupy orbitals singly first?
113.x: Aufbau – Lowest energy first; Hund's rule – single occupancy first; Pauli exclusion – two electrons in one orbital differ only in spin (+½, −½)

113.s: To which group do elements with ns² np³ configuration belong?
113.x: ns² np³ – Group 15 (nitrogen, P); carbon 2s²2p², oxygen 2s²2p⁴, argon 3s²3p⁶

113.s: How many valence electrons do metals usually have?
113.x: Metals – 1–3 valence electrons (Ca 2,8,8,2); 7 = halogen (Cl 2,8,7); full shell = noble gas

113.s: What stays the same moving left to right across a period of the periodic table?
113.x: Period – Number of shells stays the same (protons, electrons +1); down a group shells increase

113.s: Why do elements in a group have similar chemical properties?
113.x: Group – Same valence electrons → similar chemical properties

113.s: Which of these is NOT a periodic property?
113.x: Periodic properties – Atomic size, valency, electronegativity, ionisation energy; radioactivity is not periodic

113.s: How many valence electrons does the O2− ion have?
113.x: Isoelectronic – Na+, O2−, F−, Mg2+, Al3+, Ne (10 e⁻); K+, Ca2+, Cl−, Ar (18 e⁻); O2− ion – 8 valence electrons

113.s: Why are noble gases chemically unreactive?
113.x: Noble gases (group 18) – He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn – chemically unreactive (full shells); hydrogen is not one

113.s: What share of air is argon?
113.x: Noble gases in air – Argon (~0.93%), neon, helium, krypton, xenon; radon – radioactive (radium decay)

113.s: Which of these exists as single atoms (monoatomic)?
113.x: Monoatomic – Noble gases (helium, neon, argon) and metals (Cu, Ba); diatomic – H2, N2, O2, I2; polyatomic – P4, S8

113.s: Which of these are metalloids?
113.x: Metalloids – Germanium, silicon, arsenic, antimony, boron

113.s: Which is the most electronegative element?
113.x: Fluorine – Most reactive halogen, most electronegative element

113.s: Which are the two elements liquid at room temperature?
113.x: Liquid elements at room temperature – Bromine (non-metal), mercury (metal)

113.s: What is the equivalent weight of iron as Fe²⁺ (atomic weight 56)?
113.x: Equivalent weight – Atomic weight ÷ valency; changes with valency (Fe: 28 as Fe²⁺, 18.6 as Fe³⁺)

113.s: What compound does an element X that forms Na2X make with Al³⁺?
113.x: Formula from valency – Na2X → X²⁻; with Al³⁺ → Al2X3

113.s: What is the oxidation number of Ni in K4[Ni(CN)4]?
113.x: Oxidation number – Ni in K4[Ni(CN)4] = 0 (4 × +1 + x + 4 × −1 = 0)

113.s: Which of these oxides has the metal in only one oxidation state?
113.x: Mixed oxides – Pb3O4, Fe3O4, Mn3O4 – two oxidation states; Fe2O3 has only Fe(+3)

113.s: What is a Lewis acid?
113.x: Lewis acid – Electron-pair acceptor (BF3, AlCl3, FeCl3); Lewis base – donor (NH3, H2O)

113.s: From which Greek word does "chiral" come?
113.x: Chiral – Greek *kheir* = hand; not superimposable on its mirror image

113.s: How many covalent bonds are there in a molecule of C3H7Cl?
113.x: Covalent bonds in C3H7Cl – 2 C–C + 7 C–H + 1 C–Cl = 10

113.s: Which molecule has the longest C–C bond?
113.x: C–C bond length – Ethane 154 pm > benzene 139 pm > ethene 134 pm > ethyne 120 pm

113.s: What holds water molecules to one another?
113.x: Water molecules – Held to one another by hydrogen bonds (O–H inside – covalent)

113.s: What makes ice float on water?
o: Hydrogen bonding forming an open cage lattice
113.x: Ice floats – Hydrogen bonding – open cage lattice; water densest at 4 °C

113.s: Which of these is an element?
113.x: Element (silver) – Cannot be split chemically; sugar, water – compounds; air – mixture

113.s: Which of these is a compound, not a mixture?
113.x: Compounds – Elements in a fixed ratio – pure, homogeneous; ice is a compound; ice-cream, air, honey, milk – mixtures

113.s: Who stated the law of constant (definite) proportions?
113.x: Law of constant (definite) proportions (Proust) – Same elements in the same mass ratio, whatever the source

113.s: What does Avogadro's hypothesis say about equal volumes of gases at the same T and P?
o: They have equal numbers of molecules
113.x: Avogadro's hypothesis – Equal volumes at the same T and P – equal numbers of molecules

113.s: Which law says PV is constant at constant temperature?
113.x: Gas laws – Boyle (PV const; V vs 1/p = straight line), Charles (V ∝ T), Gay-Lussac's combining volumes; Joule's law – heating by current

113.s: Under which conditions does a real gas behave like an ideal gas?
113.x: Real gas ≈ ideal – At low pressure and high temperature

113.s: Which of these is a path function rather than a state function?
113.x: State functions – U (= q + W), H, S, G (= H − TS); q and W alone are path functions

113.s: Which of these is a chemical change?
113.x: Chemical change – New substance, usually irreversible – cooking food, burning candle (exothermic), curdling of milk, ripening, rusting; evaporation, melting wax, dissolving, dispersion of light – physical

113.s: Which of these is an exothermic process?
113.x: Exothermic – Quicklime + water, diluting conc. H2SO4, burning natural gas, respiration, composting

113.s: Which of these is an endothermic process?
113.x: Endothermic – CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, photosynthesis, evaporation, sublimation

113.s: Which of these substances does not sublime?
113.x: Sublime – Dry ice (solid CO2), camphor, iodine, naphthalene; ice melts

113.s: What is gain of electrons called?
113.x: Redox – Oxidation – gain of O / loss of H / loss of electrons; reduction – loss of O / gain of H / gain of electrons

113.s: What happens to mercury in 2HgO → 2Hg + O2?
113.x: Redox examples – 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO; CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O (C −4 → +4, H stays +1, O reduced); CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O (CuO reduced); 2HgO → 2Hg + O2 (Hg +2 → 0, reduction); neutralisation and double displacement are not redox

113.s: What is corrosion?
113.x: Corrosion – Slow oxidation of a metal

113.s: Which compound, with sulphur in the +4 state, acts as both a reducing and an oxidising agent?
113.x: SO2 – S in +4 – both reducing and oxidising agent; H2, H2S, HI only reducing

113.s: Which metal gives a white light in fireworks?
113.x: Burning magnesium – White ash of MgO (basic oxide); fireworks: magnesium – white, sodium – yellow, strontium – red, barium – green, copper – blue

113.s: What is the ignition temperature of white phosphorus, which is kept under water?
113.x: White phosphorus – Low ignition temperature (~30 °C); glows by slow oxidation (chemiluminescence); stored under water

113.s: Why does nitric acid turn yellow in light?
o: It forms brown NO2 that dissolves in it
113.x: Nitric acid turns yellow – Light → brown NO2, which dissolves in it

113.s: What does zinc form with hot NaOH besides hydrogen?
113.x: Zinc + hot NaOH – Sodium zincate + hydrogen

113.s: Which gas turns lime water milky?
113.x: Lime water test – CO2 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3 (milky); CO, NH3, NO2 do not

113.s: Which gas is given off when limestone or marble reacts with HCl?
113.x: Carbonates + HCl – CO2 (limestone, chalk, marble = CaCO3); quicklime gives none

113.s: Which drying agent is used to dry ammonia?
113.x: Drying agents – Quicklime (CaO) (dries ammonia), anhydrous CaCl2, conc. H2SO4, silica gel

113.s: What share of cement's raw material is limestone?
113.x: Cement – Hardens by hydration; main raw material limestone (~75%) + clay; gypsum slows setting

113.s: What is concrete reinforced with steel bars called?
113.x: Building materials – Mortar = cement + sand + water; concrete + gravel; RCC = concrete + steel bars

113.s: What colour is potassium chromate, as against orange-red dichromate?
113.x: Colour – The salt itself is yellow; dichromate is orange-red

113.s: What is the pH of pure water at 100 °C, though it is still neutral?
113.x: Pure water – pH 7 (25 °C); on heating pH falls (~6.1 at 100 °C) though still neutral

113.s: Why is the pH of distilled water exposed to air slightly below 7?
o: It dissolves CO2 forming carbonic acid

113.x: Phenolphthalein – Colourless in acid/neutral, pink in alkali

113.x: Oxides – Non-metal (CO2, SO2) – acidic; metal – basic; ZnO, Al2O3 amphoteric

113.x: CO2 – Acidic oxide, turns lime water milky, not poisonous (CO is)

o: It can act as both acid and base

113.x: Water of crystallisation – Blue vitriol, washing soda, gypsum have it; baking soda NaHCO3 has none

113.x: Carbon – In all organic compounds; cyanides, carbonates, oxides of carbon, carbides treated as inorganic

113.x: Acetylene (ethyne) – Oxy-acetylene welding; raw material for PVC (via vinyl chloride); calcium carbide + water

113.x: Ethanol + sodium – Sodium ethoxide + hydrogen (weak acidity)

113.x: Methylpropane (isobutane), C₄H₁₀ – Chain isomer of n-butane

113.x: Benzene + chlorine – Fe/FeCl3 → chlorobenzene (substitution); UV → benzene hexachloride (addition)

113.x: Organic suffixes – -al aldehyde (propanal), -ol alcohol, -one ketone (propanone), -yne alkyne

113.x: Glycerol → nitroglycerine – Dynamite (Nobel); TNT from toluene

113.x: Fluorine isolation – H. Moissan (1886) – electrolysis of HF + KHF₂ (Nobel 1906)

113.s: Which of these is NOT an essential micronutrient for most plants?
113.x: Essential plant micronutrients – Boron, zinc, copper, iron, manganese, molybdenum, chlorine, nickel – sodium is not essential for most plants

113.x: Boron deficiency – Internal cork of apple, heart rot; molybdenum – whiptail

113.s: In which part of a plant cell is calcium found as calcium pectate?
o: Middle lamella of the cell wall
113.x: Calcium in plants – Cell wall (calcium pectate of the middle lamella)

113.s: Which nutrient is a part of amino acids, proteins and chlorophyll?
113.x: Nitrogen – Amino acids, proteins, chlorophyll, nucleic acids (NPK); H, C, O come from air and water

113.x: Chlorophyll – Magnesium (Mg) at the centre of its porphyrin ring (haemoglobin – iron; vitamin B12 – cobalt)

113.s: Which of these is NOT a nitrogen fertiliser?
113.x: N fertilisers – Urea, ammonium sulphate, ammonium nitrate, ammonium phosphate, CAN; ammonium sulphide is not a fertiliser

113.s: Which of these is not a fertiliser nutrient?
113.x: Fertilisers – Supply N, P, K (Cl in KCl); hydrogen is not a fertiliser nutrient

113.s: Which oxygen-containing carotenoid pigment differs from carotene?
113.x: Carotene – Hydrocarbon pigment (no oxygen); xanthophyll – oxygen-containing carotenoid

113.s: Of which group of plant compounds are phytochemicals a subset?
113.x: Phytochemicals – Subset of secondary metabolites – give colour, flavour and disease resistance; non-nutritive but often health-promoting

113.s: What is an idioblast?
o: A parenchyma cell storing crystals, tannin or oil
113.x: Idioblast – Parenchyma cell storing ergastic substances (crystals, tannin, oil)

113.s: What do green plants do by photosynthesis?
113.x: Photosynthesis – Green plants make their own food: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2 – light energy → chemical energy (glucose)

113.s: Which colour of light gives the highest rate of photosynthesis?
113.x: Light – Greatest in blue and red light (green reflected); red light gives the highest rate

113.s: What does chlorophyll do in photosynthesis?
113.x: Chlorophyll – Absorbs light energy

113.s: Which tracer showed that photosynthetic O2 comes from water (Ruben and Kamen)?
113.x: O2 – By-product, from splitting water (photolysis) – shown with O-18 tracer (Ruben and Kamen); sugar is the product, CO2 a raw material

113.s: In which cycle does CO2 combine with RuBP to give 3-PGA in C3 plants?
113.x: Calvin cycle – CO2 + RuBP → 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA) – first stable product (C3 plants)

113.s: Which organelle is the site of photosynthesis?
113.x: Chloroplast – Site of photosynthesis (chlorophyll in thylakoids); solar energy → ATP (photophosphorylation)

113.s: What does the mitochondrion carry out?
113.x: Mitochondrion – Aerobic respiration – ATP from food

113.s: Why is sleeping under a tree at night considered harmful?
o: Plants give out CO2 at night
113.x: At night – Plants only respire, giving out CO2 – sleeping under a tree is harmful

113.s: Besides gas exchange, what process do stomata serve?
113.x: Stomata – Leaf pores for gas exchange and transpiration; two kidney (bean)-shaped guard cells

113.s: What does xylem carry upward?
113.x: Xylem – Water and minerals upward + mechanical support; xylem parenchyma – the only living xylem cell; tracheids, vessels, fibres dead

113.s: Which plant tissue transports food?
113.x: Phloem – Food transport

113.s: Which force mainly lifts water up the xylem?
113.x: Transpiration pull – Main force lifting water up the xylem

113.s: What is the loss of water as liquid droplets from leaf tips called?
113.x: Guttation – Excess water lost as liquid droplets from leaf tips (transpiration – vapour)

113.s: Which part of the root absorbs the most water?
113.x: Root hairs – Zone of maturation – absorb the most water; roots – main absorbing organ

113.s: What energy source does active transport of ions use?
113.x: Active transport – Ions against the concentration gradient using ATP from respiration; diffusion and osmosis are passive

113.s: What is absorption of water by solids like seeds and dry wood, making them swell, called?
113.x: Imbibition – Solids like seeds or dry wood absorb water and swell

113.s: Into which two kinds are plant tissues classified by dividing capacity?
113.x: Meristematic cells – Living, thin-walled, actively dividing – plant growth; tissues classified by dividing capacity (meristematic vs permanent)

113.s: Which meristem at root and shoot tips causes growth in length?
113.x: Apical meristem – Root and shoot tips – growth in length (onion root tip – mitosis slides)

113.s: What growth does the lateral meristem (cambium) cause?
113.x: Lateral meristem (cambium) – Growth in girth (secondary growth)

113.s: Which meristem lets grasses regrow after grazing?
113.x: Intercalary meristem – Base of internodes and leaf bases – grasses regrow after grazing

113.s: Which of these are complex tissues?
113.x: Complex tissue – Xylem, phloem – more than one cell type

113.s: Which of these is not a conducting tissue?
113.x: Conducting tissues – Xylem (tracheids, vessels, fibres, parenchyma), phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres); pericycle is not

113.s: What substances thicken the corners of collenchyma cells?
113.x: Collenchyma – Living; corners thickened with cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin – flexible support

113.s: Which plant tissue is dead and lignified?
113.x: Sclerenchyma – Dead, lignified (fibres, sclereids); epidermis, parenchyma, collenchyma living

113.s: Which type of stele is the most primitive?
113.x: Stele – Protostele (solid xylem core) – most primitive (Rhynia); siphono-, dictyo-, atactostele – advanced

113.s: In which trees are annual rings most distinct?
113.x: Annual rings – Distinct in temperate trees – spring (early) wood + autumn (late) wood

113.s: What increase defines growth in plants?
113.x: Measuring plant growth – Growth = increase in protoplasm, hard to measure directly – proxies: fresh/dry weight, length, area, volume, cell number

113.s: Which plant hormone causes phototropism by cell elongation on the shaded side?
113.x: Auxin – Cell elongation on the shaded side → phototropism

113.s: Which plant hormone is the stress hormone that closes stomata?
113.x: Abscisic acid (ABA) – Stress hormone – closes stomata, drought tolerance, seed dormancy

113.s: What movement do the long roots of desert plants show towards deep water?
113.x: Desert plants – Long roots grow towards deep water (hydrotropism)

113.s: Besides photosynthesis and gas exchange, what is a function of the leaf?
113.x: Leaf – Photosynthesis, gas exchange, transpiration; lamina (blade), petiole (stalk), midrib; arrangement = phyllotaxy

113.s: What is a flower, botanically?
113.x: Flower – Modified shoot – floral meristem; parts are modified leaves

113.s: Which parts make up the stamen?
113.x: Stamen – Anther + filament = male; pollen made in the anther

113.s: Where does fertilisation take place in a flower?
113.x: Pistil/carpel – Stigma, style, ovary = female; fertilisation in the ovary; reproductive whorls – stamens and carpels

113.s: In which part of young buds is meiosis in plants studied?
113.x: Meiosis in plants – Studied in anthers (young buds)

113.s: What is dichogamy?
o: Anther and stigma mature at different times
A physical barrier between anther and stigma
113.x: Dichogamy – Anther and stigma mature at different times; herkogamy – physical barrier

113.s: What is pollination by pollen from another flower of the same plant called?
113.x: Pollination – Autogamy – same flower; geitonogamy – another flower of the same plant; xenogamy – another plant

113.s: What kind of pollen do insect-pollinated flowers have?
113.x: Insect-pollinated flowers – Pollen rough and sticky; wind-pollinated – light, smooth, dry

113.s: How many nuclei and cells does the angiosperm embryo sac have?
113.x: Angiosperm embryo sac – 8-nucleate, 7-celled

113.s: To which plants is double fertilisation unique?
113.x: Double fertilisation – Unique to angiosperms

113.s: What comes right after pollination in the plant life sequence?
113.x: Sequence – Pollination → fertilisation → zygote → embryo → seed → seedling

113.s: From which part does a true fruit develop?
113.x: True fruit – Only from the ovary; false fruit also from thalamus (apple)

113.s: With which hormones can parthenocarpy (seedless fruit) be induced?
113.x: Parthenocarpy – Fruit without fertilisation (seedless banana, grapes) – natural or by auxins/gibberellins; parthenogenesis – embryo from unfertilised egg; apomixis – seed without fertilisation

113.s: Which plant has a corymb inflorescence?
113.x: Corymb – Delonix regia (gulmohar), mustard family; mango and teak – panicle

113.s: What conditions does seed germination need?
113.x: Seed germination – Water, air (O2), suitable temperature

113.x: Seed dispersal – Wind, water, animals, explosive fruits

113.s: Which of these are dicot seeds?
113.x: Dicot seeds – Pulses, gram, pea, bean; monocots – rice, wheat, maize

113.s: Which plant's pods develop underground (geocarpy)?
113.x: Modified parts – Potato – stem tuber ('eyes' = nodes with buds); onion scales – leaves; pea tendril – leaflet; carrot – root; peanut develops underground (geocarpy)

113.s: What are plants raised by vegetative propagation genetically?
113.x: Vegetative propagation – Clones, most of the year, but passes viruses on (meristem culture frees them)

113.x: Asexual reproduction – Budding (yeast, Hydra), fragmentation (Spirogyra), gemmules (sponges), spores; syngamy – gamete fusion

113.s: Which cryptogams have no differentiated plant body?
113.x: Cryptogams – No seeds/flowers – thallophytes (no differentiated body), bryophytes (no vascular tissue; Funaria is a moss), pteridophytes (vascular cryptogams)

113.s: What are phanerogams?
113.x: Phanerogams – Seed plants

113.x: Pteridophytes – First vascular plants, no seeds – ferns, Marsilea (aquatic fern, water clover), horsetails, club mosses

113.s: Which of these are fern allies?
113.x: Fern allies – Horsetails (*Equisetum*), club mosses (*Lycopodium*), *Selaginella*

113.s: What kind of seeds do gymnosperms like Cycas and Pinus have?

113.x: Angiosperms – Seeds inside fruits – cashew, coffee, groundnut; banyan (*Ficus benghalensis*, national tree, prop roots)

113.x: Bamboo – Flowers once in its life (~30 years; Mizoram *Melocanna baccifera* ~48 years – 'mautam')

113.s: What kind of stem do trees have?

113.x: Lamarck – Use and disuse (limb loss in snakes, giraffe's neck), inheritance of acquired characters

113.x: Diversity of organisms – Adaptation to varied environments; mutation – source of variation

113.x: Ruminants (cow, goat), elephant – Digest fibre with gut microbes; the pig (monogastric) cannot

113.x: Dubai Camel Hospital (2017) – World's first camel hospital

113.s: Which vegetable is a rich source of vitamin C?

113.s: Which kind of milk is a source of vitamin D?

113.s: Which is the richest source of vitamin E?
113.x: E – Wheat-germ oil

113.s: Which foods are a typical source of vitamin K?
113.x: K – Green leafy vegetables; also nuts, eggs, animal liver

113.s: Which of these nutrients is milk poor in?
113.x: Milk: several B vitamins (riboflavin B2, B12) and calcium, but poor in vitamin A, vitamin C and iron.

113.s: Who coined the word "vitamine" in 1912?
113.x: Casimir Funk – Coined "vitamine" (1912)

113.s: Who called vitamins "accessory food factors"?
113.x: Hopkins – "Accessory food factors"

113.s: Who showed that citrus fruits cure scurvy?
113.x: James Lind – Citrus cures scurvy

113.s: In which year did McCollum identify vitamin D in cod-liver oil?
113.x: McCollum and Davis – Vitamin A (1913); McCollum also identified vitamin D (1922, anti-rickets factor in cod-liver oil)

113.s: Who extracted aberic acid (vitamin B1) from rice bran?
113.x: Umetaro Suzuki – Rice-bran extract (aberic acid, B1)

113.s: What kind of compounds are vitamins?
o: Organic compounds needed in small amounts
113.x: Nature – Vitamins are organic compounds needed in small amounts; they do not kill bacteria

113.x: Synthesis – The body cannot make most vitamins (exceptions: D in skin, K and B12 by gut bacteria, niacin from tryptophan); proteins, enzymes and hormones are made in the body

113.x: Vitamin A and season – Standard RDAs (ICMR-NIN) give no season-specific need; night blindness peaks in the hot pre-harvest season

113.s: Which vitamin A deficiency disorder is the leading cause of preventable child blindness in India?
113.x: Xerophthalmia – Leading cause of preventable child blindness – India's priority deficiency; the National Prophylaxis Programme gives children vitamin A doses

113.s: What causes malaria?
113.x: Malaria – Mosquito bite (*Plasmodium* via female *Anopheles*)

113.s: What causes goitre?
113.x: Goitre – Iodine deficiency

113.s: What causes rickets?
113.x: Rickets – Vitamin D deficiency

113.s: What causes night blindness?
113.x: Night blindness – Vitamin A deficiency

113.s: What happens to the weight of an iron nail when it rusts?
113.x: Rusting – Hydrated iron oxide – a chemical change; the nail's weight increases

113.s: Which compound forms when silver tarnishes?
113.x: Tarnishing of silver – Ag2S – corrosion

113.x: Signs of a chemical reaction – Gas evolved, colour change, heat change

113.s: What kind of reaction is C + O2 → CO2 in terms of heat?
113.x: Reactions – Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen; acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation); C + O2 → CO2 – exothermic

113.x: Limestone – CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 on heating – CO2 puts out a flame; quicklime + water → slaked lime Ca(OH)2 + much heat

113.x: Egg shell + acid (HCl) – CO2 – turns lime water milky

113.x: Propane combustion – C3H8 + 5 O2 → 3 CO2 + 4 H2O

113.s: Which compound does the Haber process make?
113.x: Haber – N2 + 3 H2 ⇌ 2 NH3

113.s: What does combustion need besides fuel and oxygen?
113.x: Combustion – Needs fuel, oxygen and ignition temperature

113.s: Why is magnesium used in crackers?
o: It gives bright light on oxidation to MgO
113.x: Magnesium in crackers – Bright light from oxidation to MgO

113.x: Ignition temperature – A substance burns only once heated to it – at 100 °C, substances igniting at 95 °C and 98 °C burn, those at 105 °C and 108 °C do not

113.s: What type of reaction is an iron nail in copper sulphate solution?
113.x: Displacement – Iron nail in copper sulphate – brown copper coat, solution pale green; iron + dilute HCl → iron chloride + hydrogen

113.s: Why does silver bromide turn grey in sunlight?
113.x: Silver bromide – Turns grey in sunlight (photolysis)

113.s: Where is helium placed in the periodic table?
113.x: Helium – Noble gas, Group 18, period 1 – top right corner; inert – safe in balloons; hydrogen is lighter but inflammable

113.s: Which force holds the nucleons together in an atom's nucleus?
113.x: Atom – Electrons held by the electrostatic (Coulomb) force; nucleons by the strong nuclear force

113.s: What are the atomic number and mass number of protium?
113.x: Protium (¹H) – Atomic number = mass number = 1

113.x: Periodic table – Metals on the left, metalloids on the zigzag, non-metals on the right

113.x: Group IA = alkali metals – Li, Na, K…; potassium can be cut with a knife

o: An electron jumping to a higher orbit

113.x: Spectral (emission) line – Electron jumps from a higher to a lower orbit, emitting a photon

113.s: Which element must an organic compound contain?
113.x: Organic compound – Must contain carbon; ammonia = N + H (NH3)

113.s: About how many elements occur naturally?
113.x: Elements – ~94 occur naturally (118 known – "about 100"); hydrogen – most common in the Universe

113.s: Which block of elements typically forms coloured compounds due to d–d transitions?
113.x: Transition (d-block) metals – Coloured compounds (d–d transitions)

113.x: Cations – Positively charged ions – atom loses electrons, typically metals (Na⁺, Ca²⁺); anions – negative, gain electrons, non-metals (Cl⁻)

113.s: What kind of metals are the actinides like uranium and thorium?
113.x: Actinides – Radioactive metals – uranium, thorium, plutonium – nuclear energy and weapons

113.s: What are alcohols oxidised into when they act as reducing agents?
113.x: Alcohols as reducing agents – Themselves oxidised to aldehydes or ketones

113.x: Hydrogenation – Unsaturated oils + nickel catalyst (vanaspati)

113.x: Wurtz reaction – Alkyl halides + sodium in dry ether → higher alkanes

113.x: Vulcanisation – Rubber with sulphur (Goodyear, 1839)

113.x: Perspex (PMMA) – Monomer methyl methacrylate, made with methyl alcohol

113.s: Which compound is the tear gas CN?

113.x: Etard – Aromatic methyl → aldehyde (chromyl chloride)

113.x: Stephen – Nitrile → aldehyde (SnCl2/HCl); Gattermann–Koch – formylation (CO + HCl)

113.x: Functional groups – Alcohols –OH (hydroxyl); esters – fruity smell; smallest ketone – acetone (3 C); C2H6O – ethanol

113.x: Ethanol reactions – Conc. H2SO4 at 170 °C → alkene; alkaline KMnO4 → acid; acid + ethanol → ester

113.s: Which alkaloid is obtained from Rauwolfia?
113.x: Alkaloids – Nicotine – tobacco; morphine – opium poppy; reserpine – Rauwolfia

113.x: Benzene – In crude oil, petrol – carcinogen causing leukaemia

113.s: Which metal is the most malleable and ductile?
113.x: Gold – Most malleable and ductile (silver next)

113.s: Which metal is the most used in nearly pure form, in foil, cans and conductors?
113.x: Aluminium – Most used metal in nearly pure form (foil, cans, conductors)

113.s: What is the thermite mixture, used to weld rails?
113.x: Thermite – Iron oxide + aluminium – welds rails

113.s: What coating is applied in galvanisation?
113.x: Galvanisation – Zinc coating

113.s: Which metal is the best electrical conductor?
113.x: Silver – Best electrical conductor

113.s: Which toxic metal is used in car batteries?
113.x: Lead – Toxic metal of car batteries

113.s: Where does pure copper deposit in electrolytic refining of copper?
113.x: Electrolytic refining of copper – Impure anode dissolves; pure copper deposits at the cathode

113.x: Excess metal colour – Lithium in LiCl → pink (F-centres); K in KCl – violet; Na in NaCl – yellow

113.s: What is smelting?
o: Extraction by reduction at high temperature
113.x: Smelting – Extraction by reduction at high temperature

113.x: Blast furnace – Coke → CO; limestone → CaO + CO2; CO reduces Fe2O3

113.s: What does seasoning with oil do to cast iron?
113.x: Seasoning – Oil coating stops cast iron rusting

113.x: Extraction methods – Pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy and electrometallurgy

113.s: What does pyrometallurgy involve?
o: Extraction by reduction at high temperature
113.x: Pyrometallurgy – Last step refining (e.g. electrolytic refining of copper)

113.s: What process is used in hydrometallurgy, as with gold and cyanide?
113.x: Hydrometallurgy – Aqueous solutions – leaching (acid, base or water; gold leached with cyanide), then solvent extraction

113.x: Anodising – Thick oxide layer on aluminium – article as anode, electrolysed in dilute sulphuric acid

113.x: Saponification – Fat/oil + strong base (NaOH) → soap + glycerol; hydrocarbon tail grips oily dirt, ionic head faces water (micelles)

113.x: Alum – Purifies water by coagulation of suspended mud (Al³⁺ neutralises the charge)

113.s: Which natural water is the purest?
113.x: Rain water – Purest natural water (natural distillation)

113.s: What is on the striking strip of a safety match?
113.x: Safety match – Red phosphorus on the striking strip; head – potassium chlorate + antimony trisulphide

113.s: What is melamine used to make?
113.x: Melamine – Unbreakable crockery

113.s: What is tincture of iodine used as?
113.x: Tincture of iodine – Antiseptic

113.s: What are enzymes?
113.x: Enzymes – Biocatalysts

113.s: What is DNA fingerprinting used for?
113.x: DNA fingerprinting – Identifying criminals

113.s: What does borax do in making water-based varnish?
113.x: Borax – Dissolves shellac for water-based varnish

113.s: Which compound is washing soda, also used in making glass?
113.x: Sodium carbonate – Washing soda, glass

113.s: What is sodium benzoate used as?

113.x: Calcium carbonate – Flux in metal extraction; chalk = CaCO3

113.s: What is calcium phosphate used as?
113.x: Calcium phosphate – Fertiliser

113.s: For which poison is sodium thiosulphate an antidote?
113.x: Sodium thiosulphate – Antidote for cyanide

113.s: What is normal saline?

113.s: What is gunpowder made of?
113.x: Gunpowder – Sulphur + charcoal + potassium nitrate

113.s: What is potash alum chemically?
113.x: Alum – Potassium aluminium sulphate dodecahydrate

113.s: What is the chemical name of aspirin?
113.x: Aspirin – Acetylsalicylic acid

113.x: Barium nitrate – Oxidiser giving a green flame in fireworks (strontium red, copper blue)

113.x: All acids contain hydrogen – H⁺ in water; pH = "potential of hydrogen"

113.x: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O – Neutralisation – a double displacement

113.x: Acids – Conduct in water, sour, change indicators, react with active metals (H2)

113.x: Litmus – Purple in neutral; blue → red in acid; ammonia (weak base) turns red litmus blue

113.x: Turmeric – Natural acid–base indicator (red-brown in base)

113.x: Dry litmus + dry HCl gas – No change – no ionisation without water

113.x: Graphite – Inorganic solid lubricant (lanolin, mineral oil, PTFE are organic)

113.s: Which element is a common fungicide?
113.x: Sulphur – Common fungicide

113.x: Bromine – Only non-metal liquid at room temperature (mercury – a metal)

113.x: Titration – Burette; pipette transfers a fixed volume

113.x: Burn first aid – Cool in cold running water; do not pull off stuck cloth or apply butter

113.x: Heat stroke – Body cooling fails, core temperature rises quickly (> 40 °C); give lemon water or buttermilk

113.x: Wounds – Abscess – cavity with pus; hematoma – collected blood; contusion (bruise) – classic closed wound

113.x: Root canal therapy – Saves an abscessed tooth

113.s: What are capsule shells made of?

113.s: What does Dettol contain?
113.x: Dettol – Chloroxylenol + α-terpineol

113.s: What is a KOH mount used for?

113.x: KOH mount – Clears skin scrapings for fungi/mites; sulphur ointment controls mange

113.s: What do antipyretics like paracetamol do?
113.x: Antipyretics (paracetamol) – Lower fever; analgesics relieve pain

113.s: What does bronchoscopy examine?
113.x: Bronchoscopy – Examines airways; nervous-system tests – EEG, myelography

113.s: What kind of disorders are anorexia nervosa and bulimia?
113.x: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia – Eating disorders

113.s: What does the digestive system do?
o: Breaks food down and absorbs nutrients
113.x: Digestive system – Breaks food down and absorbs nutrients

113.x: Alimentary canal – Mouth → anus; oesophagus links pharynx to stomach

113.x: Stomach – Cardiac, fundic, body, pyloric parts (serosa is a wall layer); HCl from gastric glands

113.x: Pancreas – Digestive enzymes and insulin

113.x: Bile – Made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder; emulsifies fat

113.x: Saliva – pH ~6.7; salivary amylase (ptyalin) digests starch

113.s: Which enzyme digests fat?
113.x: Enzymes – Lipase – fat; amylase – starch; trypsin – protein; lactase – lactose

113.x: Fat digestion – Completed by lipase in the small intestine; digested fats enter lacteals, carried by lymph

113.s: What is the normal resting heart rate range of an adult?
113.x: Resting heart rate – Adult 60–100 beats/min (~72)

113.s: What does a sphygmomanometer measure?
113.x: Sphygmomanometer – Measures blood pressure

113.s: How many valves does the human heart have?
113.x: Heart valves – 4 – tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic

113.s: What is blood like in terms of pH?
113.x: Blood pH – 7.35–7.45 (slightly alkaline)

113.s: What is hypernatraemia?
113.x: Hypernatraemia – Excess sodium

113.s: What share of blood volume do WBCs and platelets (buffy coat) make up?
113.x: WBCs (with platelets) – ~1% of blood volume (buffy coat)

113.s: Where are red blood cells made?
113.x: Blood cells – Erythrocytes = RBC (from red bone marrow); leucocytes = WBC (colourless, no haemoglobin); thrombocytes = platelets

113.s: Which white blood cells are the rarest?
113.x: Basophils – Rarest WBC; inflammation, allergy – histamine, serotonin, heparin; neutrophils – most abundant

113.s: Which disease is marked by thrombocytopenia (fewer platelets)?
113.x: Thrombocytopenia – Fewer platelets → bleeding tendency; a feature of dengue

113.s: Which are the narrowest blood vessels, one cell thick?
113.x: Capillaries – Narrowest (5–10 µm, one cell thick)

113.s: Which is the largest artery?
113.x: Aorta – Largest artery; arteries carry blood from the heart to the body

113.s: What does the pulmonary artery carry to the lungs?
113.x: Pulmonary artery – CO2-rich blood to the lungs

113.s: Which blood vessels supply the liver?
113.x: Named vessels – Renal – kidney; hepatic – liver; coronary – heart

113.s: How much does an adult human brain weigh?
113.x: Adult brain – ≈ 1.3–1.4 kg (~3 pounds)

113.s: Which abilities does the right cerebral hemisphere control?
113.x: Right cerebral hemisphere – Spatial abilities, face recognition; left – language

113.s: Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions like BP and salivation?
113.x: Medulla oblongata – Involuntary actions – BP, salivation, vomiting, breathing

113.s: Which part of a neuron carries impulses away from the cell body?
113.x: Neurons – Send and receive information; axon – long fibre carrying impulses away from the cell body; dendrites – short, branched

113.s: Where are Nissl's granules found?
113.x: Nissl's granules – In the neuron cell body

113.s: What is a synapse?
113.x: Synapse – Junction between two neurons

113.s: Which is the largest cranial nerve?
113.x: Trigeminal (V) – Largest cranial nerve – sensory + motor

113.s: Which bones make up the axial skeleton?
113.x: Axial skeleton – Skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum

113.s: Which is the longest and strongest bone of the human body?
113.x: Femur – Longest and strongest bone (tibia – lower leg)

113.s: What is ossification?
o: Deposition of calcium on cartilage forming bone
113.x: Ossification – Calcium and minerals deposited on cartilage → bone

113.s: Which is the hardest substance in the human body?
113.x: Tooth enamel – Hardest substance in the body – calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite); calcium + phosphorus give bones strength

113.s: At what age do milk teeth start falling?
113.x: Milk teeth – Fall from 6–8 years (strictly ~6 to 12)

113.s: How many molars does an adult have?
113.x: Adult dentition (32) – 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, 12 molars

113.s: What kind of muscle is skeletal (striated) muscle?
113.x: Skeletal (striated) muscle – Voluntary; smooth and cardiac – involuntary

113.s: What visual acuity counts as legally blind?
113.x: Eye – Visual acuity 20/200 = legally blind; ciliary muscles change lens curvature (accommodation); one eye only → two-dimensional world (no depth)

113.s: Which cells give the iris its colour?
113.x: Iris – Eye colour – pigment from melanocyte cells

113.s: What do the kidneys do?
113.x: Kidneys – Filter waste and excess water

113.s: Which structure is part of the nephron?
113.x: Nephron – Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, Henle's loop; ureters carry urine; alveoli – lungs; Schwann cells – nerve myelin

113.s: What is the normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
113.x: Reabsorption – Of ~180 litres filtrate a day (GFR ~125 ml/min) only ~1.5 litres leaves as urine – tubules reabsorb about 99%

113.s: What does cuboidal epithelium line?
113.x: Cuboidal epithelium – Cube-shaped cells lining kidney tubules and salivary gland ducts; stratified squamous – skin

113.s: What is the total capacity of human lungs?
113.x: Lungs – Gas exchange in the alveoli; total capacity ≈ 6 L (vital capacity ~4.5–4.8 L)

113.s: About how large is the spread-out surface of the alveoli?
113.x: Alveoli – Spread out ≈ a tennis court (~70 m²)

113.s: Of which system is sneezing a reflex?
113.x: Sneezing – Reflex of the respiratory system

113.s: Which element makes up about 65% of the human body by mass?
113.x: Human body by mass – Oxygen ~65% > carbon > hydrogen > nitrogen > calcium

113.s: What does physiology study?
113.x: Anatomy – Structure of body parts; physiology – how they function

113.s: Which element is treated as a trace element though its essentiality in humans is unproven?
113.x: Arsenic – Treated as a trace element with a functional requirement (essentiality in humans unproven)

113.s: Which of these is part of innate (first-line) immunity?

113.s: Which bacterium causes pneumonia?

113.s: Which is the male sperm duct?

113.s: What is goitre?

113.s: What do sebaceous glands secrete?
113.x: Sebaceous glands – Sebum – protective oily layer; eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons, waxes

113.s: What is rubbed on a nettle sting to neutralise its formic acid?

113.s: Which fruit is the main source of citric acid?

113.s: Which acid is found in vinegar?

113.s: Which acid is found in tamarind and grapes?
113.x: Tartaric acid – Tamarind, grapes; baking powder (with baking soda)

113.s: What is the pH of fresh milk?

113.s: Which acid is the main acid of apples and ripe banana?
113.x: Malic acid – Apples, ripe banana (main acid)

113.x: Oxalic acid – Tomato, spinach, wood sorrel; removes ink stains; photography (ferrous oxalate developer)

113.s: Which vitamin is ascorbic acid?

113.s: Which acid is found in cola soft drinks?
113.x: Phosphoric acid – Cola soft drinks (with caffeine)

113.s: Which acid makes soda water acidic?

113.s: Where is hydrochloric acid found in the body?
113.x: HCl – Stomach (gastric juice)

113.s: What is concentrated sulphuric acid also called?

113.s: Which acid gives rancid butter its smell?

113.s: Where is stearic acid found?
113.x: Stearic – Fats

113.s: Which fat is rich in oleic acid?

113.s: Why is formic acid stronger than acetic acid?
o: The CH3 group in acetic acid pushes electrons and weakens it

113.s: Which of these are carboxylic acids?
