113.s: What effect does caffeine in tea and coffee have on urine output?
113.x: Caffeine (tea, coffee, colas) – Diuretic

113.s: Which of these food acids is also a vitamin?
113.x: Citric vs ascorbic – Only ascorbic acid is a vitamin

113.s: What is the formula of blue vitriol?
113.x: Blue vitriol – CuSO4

113.s: At what temperature does pure (glacial) acetic acid melt, so it freezes in winter?
113.x: Glacial acetic acid – Pure ethanoic acid melts at 290 K (16.6 °C) – fairly high – so it freezes in winter

113.s: Which enzyme released on cutting onions starts the reaction that causes tears?
113.x: Onion tears – Cutting releases alliinase – amino-acid sulfoxides → sulfenic acid → syn-propanethial-S-oxide

113.s: In which device does orange potassium dichromate turn green on oxidising alcohol?
113.x: Potassium dichromate – Breath analyser – orange dichromate turns green when it oxidises alcohol

113.s: Which deadly poison is prussic acid (HCN)?
113.x: Prussic acid (hydrocyanic acid, HCN) – The deadly poison "cyanide"

113.s: What was mustard gas used for?
113.x: Mustard gas (sulphur mustard) – Blister agent of chemical warfare, World War I; unrelated to mustard oil

113.s: What can aqua regia do that no single acid can?
113.x: Aqua regia (3 HCl : 1 HNO3) – Only common reagent that dissolves gold – no single acid or sulphuric–nitric mixture does

113.s: In which products is bisphenol A (BPA) used?
113.x: Bisphenol A (BPA) – Polycarbonate plastics and food-can linings (food packaging)

113.s: What stains does sodium hypochlorite bleach remove from white cloth?
113.x: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) – Oxidising bleach – removes coffee and tea stains from white cloth

113.s: What is merthiolate (thiomersal) used to preserve?
113.x: Merthiolate (thiomersal) – Preservative for serum and vaccines; heparin and oxalates are anticoagulants

113.s: Which acid formed in chlorination of water disinfects it?
113.x: Chlorination – Chlorine + water → hypochlorous acid (HOCl) + HCl – HOCl disinfects

113.s: Which metal is the most reactive in the reactivity series?
113.x: Reactivity series – K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au – potassium most reactive

113.s: Which order shows the electron-releasing tendency of zinc, copper and silver?
113.x: Tin (Sn) and lead – Just above hydrogen; Cu, Hg, Ag, Au below; electron-releasing tendency Zn > Cu > Ag

113.s: Why are food cans tin-plated rather than zinc-coated?
o: Zinc is more reactive and forms toxic salts with food acids
113.x: Food cans are tin-plated, not zinc-coated – Zinc is more reactive – would form toxic salts with food acids

113.s: With which metal are brass and copper vessels coated in tinning (kalai)?
113.x: Tinning (kalai) – Brass/copper vessels coated with tin against copper contamination

113.s: How is the hydrogen from zinc and dilute HCl identified?
113.x: Metal + dilute acid → hydrogen – Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2; burns with a pop

113.s: What is the approximate pH of gastric juice?
113.x: pH ladder – Gastric juice ~1.5 < lemon ~2 < vinegar ~3 < pure water 7 < blood 7.4 < baking soda ~8.5 < milk of magnesia ~10 < NaOH ~14

113.s: What does an acid do to blue litmus?
113.x: Litmus – A base turns red litmus blue; an acid turns blue litmus red; neutral salt changes neither

113.s: What does it mean if red litmus stays red in a solution?
113.x: Litmus test logic – Red stays red → not a base (acid or neutral); blue stays blue → not an acid

113.s: Which flower petals are used as a natural indicator?
113.x: Natural indicators – Turmeric, litmus, Hibiscus / China rose (Gudhal) petals; litmus – most commonly used

113.s: What is the botanical name of ashwagandha?
113.x: Ashwagandha – *Withania somnifera* (Solanaceae); *W. coagulans* = paneer dodi

113.s: What is the botanical name of black nightshade?
113.x: Black nightshade – *Solanum nigrum*

113.s: Which of these is a pseudocereal?
113.x: Pseudocereals – Seeds used like grain, not grasses: buckwheat (kuttu, Polygonaceae), amaranth, quinoa

113.s: Which plant is Zingiber officinale?
113.x: Botanical names – Fennel *Foeniculum vulgare*; ginger *Zingiber officinale*; garlic *Allium sativum*; touch-me-not *Mimosa pudica*

113.s: Which plant is Mimosa pudica?
113.x: Botanical names – Fennel *Foeniculum vulgare*; ginger *Zingiber officinale*; garlic *Allium sativum*; touch-me-not *Mimosa pudica*

113.s: Which drug for hypertension comes from sarpagandha (Rauvolfia serpentina)?
113.x: Sarpagandha (*Rauvolfia serpentina*) – Nervous disorders, hypertension (reserpine); traditional snake-bite antidote; the Rauwolfia drug comes from its root

113.s: What is isabgol used for?
113.x: Isabgol – Chronic constipation

113.s: Which organ does Arjuna bark help?
113.x: Arjuna – Heart

113.s: Which plant is used as a diuretic and refrigerant?
113.x: Sandal – Diuretic, refrigerant

113.s: What is Cissus quadrangularis (hadjod) used for?
113.x: Cissus quadrangularis (hadjod, "bone-setter") – Herb for bone healing

113.s: Whose seeds help diabetics?
113.x: Fenugreek – Seeds help diabetics

113.s: What kind of plant is the pitcher plant?
113.x: Pitcher plant – Insectivorous (eats mosquitoes)

113.s: Which is India's national tree?
113.x: National tree – Banyan, *Ficus benghalensis*

113.s: What are plants that complete their life cycle in one season called?
113.x: Annuals (seasonal plants) – Complete their life cycle in one season; biennials in two; perennials live many years

113.s: What kind of seeds do pine and cycas have?
113.x: Gymnosperms – Naked-seeded (pine, cycas)

113.s: Which plants bear flowers and have seeds enclosed in an ovary?
113.x: Angiosperms – Bear flowers; seeds enclosed in an ovary; usually have vessels

113.s: What is agrostology?
113.x: Agrostology – Study of grasses

113.s: Which of these is not part of the plant kingdom?
113.x: Plant kingdom – Algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms (annelids are animals)

113.s: Which of these is an alga with no roots, stem or leaves?
113.x: Algae (Thallophyta) – Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Cladophora, Chara – no roots, stem or leaves

113.s: Which class of algae are the green algae?
113.x: Algae – three classes – Chlorophyceae (green algae; pyrenoids store protein and starch), Phaeophyceae, Rhodophyceae

113.s: From which algae is agar obtained?
113.x: Agar – From Gelidium and Gracilaria

113.s: Which alga is a protein-rich food supplement for space travellers?
113.x: Chlorella – Protein-rich food supplement for space travellers

113.s: What is the endodermis of a dicot stem also called?
113.x: Endodermis of dicot stem – Starch sheath

113.s: Who classified plant tissues into dermal, vascular and fundamental systems?
113.x: Sachs – Three tissue systems – dermal, vascular, fundamental

113.s: What is the banana plant, botanically?
o: A giant herb with a pseudostem
113.x: Banana – A giant herb (pseudostem), not a tree

113.s: What part of the plant is a potato?
113.x: Potato – Modified stem (tuber); its "eyes" = axillary buds

113.s: What part of the plant is a carrot?
113.x: Carrot – Modified root

113.s: What part of the plant is eaten in garlic?
113.x: Garlic – Edible bulb (cloves)

113.s: From which part of the flower does the fleshy part of an apple develop?
113.x: Apple – Fleshy, swollen thalamus (not the mesocarp); a pome (enlarged receptacle)

113.s: What part of the plant is a cabbage?
113.x: Cabbage – Vegetative bud

113.s: What is a sorosis, as in pineapple and jackfruit?
113.x: Sorosis – Inflorescence-derived fruit of mulberry, pineapple and jackfruit

113.s: What is entomophily?
113.x: Entomophily – Pollination by insects – bright, scented, nectar-rich flowers

113.s: What is anemophily?
113.x: Anemophily – Wind

113.s: In which plant is pollination by water seen, with the male flower floating to the female?
113.x: Hydrophily – Water – in Vallisneria the whole male flower floats to the female flower

113.s: What is ornithophily?
113.x: Ornithophily – Birds

113.s: What does the ovary become after fertilisation?
113.x: After fertilisation – The ovary → fruit; the ovules → seeds

113.s: Which substance of the pollen exine is the most resistant organic material?
113.x: Sporopollenin (pollen exine) – Most resistant organic material: withstands high temperature, strong acids and alkalis; no enzyme degrades it – so pollen fossilises well

113.s: What does repeated self-pollination lead to?
113.x: Repeated self-pollination – Inbreeding depression, weak seeds; cross-pollination gives vigour

113.s: Which plant has winged seeds dispersed by wind?
113.x: Seed dispersal – Winged seeds (wind) – drumstick, maple; hooks – Xanthium, Urena; explosive – castor, balsam

113.s: Which type of placentation is seen in Hibiscus?
113.x: Placentation – Axile – Hibiscus (Malvaceae); marginal – legumes

113.s: What is phyllotaxy?
o: Arrangement of leaves on the stem
113.x: Phyllotaxy – Arrangement of leaves on the stem

113.s: Which plants produce "dust seeds"?
113.x: Orchids – "Dust seeds"

113.s: Which ions move in and out of guard cells to open and close stomata?
113.x: Stomata – Pores for gas exchange and transpiration; opened and closed by guard cells through potassium ions moving in and out

113.s: What do chloroplasts hold?
113.x: Chloroplasts – Hold chlorophyll

113.s: What are enzymes called because they speed up reactions in living cells?
113.x: Enzymes – Biocatalysts

113.s: What do green plants make by photosynthesis?
113.x: Photosynthesis – Green plants make their own food (glucose) from CO2 and water with sunlight and chlorophyll

113.s: Which of these is a product, not an input, of photosynthesis?
113.x: Inputs – Chlorophyll, light, CO2, water; O2 and glucose are products

113.s: What happens to CO2 during photosynthesis?
113.x: Chemistry – Light absorbed by chlorophyll; CO2 reduced; the O2 released comes from water (photolysis)

113.s: Which C4 plant uses the NADP-ME pathway?
113.x: C4 types – Panicum – PEP-CK; maize, sugarcane – NADP-ME; Amaranthus – NAD-ME

113.s: What colour is chlorophyll a?
113.x: Chlorophyll a – Blue-green; chlorophyll b – yellow-green

113.s: In which season is root pressure lowest?
113.x: Root pressure – Lowest in summer (heavy transpiration); highest in the rainy season

113.s: What does xylem carry?
113.x: Xylem – Carries water and minerals upward from roots to leaves; vessel end walls and pit pores stop cavitation spreading

113.s: What is the transport of food through phloem called?
113.x: Phloem – Carries food (translocation); a vascular bundle holds both xylem and phloem

113.s: Where does transpiration occur?
113.x: Transpiration – Evaporation at the leaf–air surface; its tension pulls water up

113.s: What is growth in response to gravity called?
113.x: Geotropism – Growth in response to gravity – shoots grow up, roots grow down

113.s: What is the response of tendrils of climbing plants to touch called?
113.x: Other tropisms – Phototropism (light), hydrotropism (water), chemotropism (chemicals), thigmotropism (touch – climbing plants, tendrils)

113.s: What is the taproot a direct prolongation of?
113.x: Taproot – Direct prolongation of the radicle

113.s: What are the outgrowths linking a tree's stem base with lateral roots called?
113.x: Adventitious roots – Arise from parts other than the radicle; in trees buttresses (outgrowths linking the stem base with lateral roots) and stilt roots (from the butt of the tree above ground)

113.s: How much energy does one gram of protein give?
113.x: Proteins – Body-building nutrients (growth and repair) – most important for growing children and athletes building muscle; ~4 kcal/g

113.s: How many common amino acids build proteins?
113.x: Amino acids – Building blocks of proteins; 20 common, ~9–10 essential; not stored

113.s: What kind of polymers are proteins, made of 20 kinds of amino acids?
113.x: Structure – Proteins are linear chains of amino acids and heteropolymers (20 kinds); nucleotides build nucleic acids

113.s: Which of these is an essential amino acid?
113.x: Essential amino acids (from food) – Histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine

113.s: Which of these is a non-essential amino acid?
113.x: Non-essential – Tyrosine, alanine, aspartic acid, cysteine, glycine, proline

113.s: Why is egg protein said to have the highest biological value?
o: It has all essential amino acids in the right proportion
113.x: Egg – Highest biological value – contains all essential amino acids in the right proportion

113.s: What is lactoderm?
o: The protein film (skin) on heated milk
113.x: Lactoderm – The sticky protein film (skin) on heated milk

113.s: Which protein makes up about 80% of milk protein?
113.x: Casein (~80% of milk protein) – Milk; whey proteins make up the rest

113.s: Which grain contains gluten?
113.x: Gluten – Wheat

113.s: Which grain contains the protein zein?
113.x: Zein – Maize

113.s: Which keratin is found in skin, hair, nails and horns?
113.x: Keratin – Hair, nails, horn; alpha-keratin – skin (epidermis), hair, nails, horns, wool; beta-keratin – feathers, scales

113.s: Where is the protein myosin found with actin?
113.x: Myosin (with actin) – Muscle

113.s: Where is the protein albumin found?
113.x: Albumin – Egg white, blood

113.s: In which material is the protein fibroin found?
113.x: Collagen / fibroin – Connective tissue / silk

113.s: Which of these are proteins?
113.x: Keratin and myosin are proteins; fructose, maltose and sucrose are sugars.

113.s: What causes kwashiorkor?
o: Lack of both protein and calories
113.x: Kwashiorkor – Protein deficiency (calories adequate), children over 1 – Oedema, swollen belly, skin and hair changes

113.s: Which signs are typical of kwashiorkor?
113.x: Kwashiorkor – Protein deficiency (calories adequate), children over 1 – Oedema, swollen belly, skin and hair changes

113.s: What causes marasmus?
o: Severe lack of both protein and calories
113.x: Marasmus – Severe lack of both protein and calories, infants – Extreme wasting, no oedema

113.s: Which sign is typical of marasmus?
113.x: Marasmus – Severe lack of both protein and calories, infants – Extreme wasting, no oedema

113.s: What causes marasmic kwashiorkor?
o: Deficiency of both proteins and calories
113.x: Marasmic kwashiorkor – Deficiency of both proteins and calories – Wasting + oedema

113.s: Which signs does marasmic kwashiorkor show?
113.x: Marasmic kwashiorkor – Deficiency of both proteins and calories – Wasting + oedema

113.s: Which disease is caused by vitamin C deficiency?
113.x: Other deficiency and disease causes: scurvy (vitamin C), goitre (iodine), mumps (virus), achondroplasia (genetic dwarfism), rickets (vitamin D).

113.s: Which grain has the highest protein content (~40 g per 100 g)?
113.x: Protein per 100 g (increasing): egg white (~11 g) < fish (~20 g) < Bengal gram dal (~21 g) < groundnut (~25 g) < skimmed milk powder (~35 g); soybean is the highest-protein grain (~40 g).

113.s: How much protein does a nursing mother need a day?
113.x: Nursing mother – Needs 65 g protein a day

113.s: How much protein per kg do older adults need (PROT-AGE)?
113.x: Older adults – Need more protein per kg (1.0–1.2 g/kg, PROT-AGE) than young adults (0.8 g/kg) to prevent muscle loss

113.s: What does pepsin break proteins into in the stomach?
113.x: Pepsin (stomach) – Breaks proteins into peptides; trypsin works later in the small intestine

113.s: What are most enzymes made of?
113.x: Enzymes – Biological catalysts, mostly proteins (e.g. pepsin, trypsin, amylase); a few are RNA enzymes – ribozymes

113.s: What kind of hormone is oxytocin (9 amino acids)?
113.x: Oxytocin – Peptide hormone (9 amino acids) from the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary – not counted as a protein

113.s: Which of these are structural proteins?
113.x: Structural proteins – Keratin, fibroin, collagen

113.s: Which bonds in hair keratin are broken and re-formed in perming?
113.x: Hair keratin – Has sulphur (disulphide) bonds; hair setting and perming break and re-form them

113.s: How does henna (lawsone) stain skin and hair?
o: By binding to their proteins and amino acids
113.x: Henna (lawsone) – Stains by binding to proteins and amino acids of skin and hair

113.s: Which of these is not a base of DNA?
113.x: DNA – Bases adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine (+ sugar, phosphate); tyrosine is an amino acid

113.s: What is the prosthetic group of glycoproteins like mucins?
113.x: Glycoproteins – Carbohydrate (mucins in mucus)

113.s: What is the prosthetic group of lipoproteins like HDL?
113.x: Lipoproteins – Lipid (HDL in blood)

113.s: Of which conjugated proteins, carrying metal ions as prosthetic groups, is haemoglobin an example?
113.x: Metalloproteins – Metal ions (haemoglobin)

113.s: What is the main role of carbohydrates in food?
113.x: Carbohydrate – Main energy-giving food – Rice has the highest carbohydrate share – its major nutrient

113.s: What is the major nutrient of rice?
113.x: Carbohydrate – Main energy-giving food – Rice has the highest carbohydrate share – its major nutrient

113.s: What is the main role of fat in the body?
113.x: Fat – Stored energy – ~9.3 kcal/g (most per gram); built from fatty acids + glycerol

113.s: How much energy does one gram of fat give?
113.x: Fat – Stored energy – ~9.3 kcal/g (most per gram); built from fatty acids + glycerol

113.s: What is the main role of protein in the body?
113.x: Protein – Body-building – ~4 kcal/g

113.s: What role do vitamins and minerals play in food?
113.x: Vitamins, minerals – Regulatory, micronutrients – Protein, carbohydrate and fat = macronutrients (also for livestock)

113.s: Which nutrients are macronutrients, as against micronutrient vitamins and minerals?
113.x: Vitamins, minerals – Regulatory, micronutrients – Protein, carbohydrate and fat = macronutrients (also for livestock)

113.s: To which food group do vitamins and minerals belong?
113.x: Food groups – Energy-giving (carbohydrates, fats); body-building (proteins); protective / regulatory (vitamins and minerals – yellow and orange fruits, vegetables)

113.s: What is a balanced diet?
o: An optimal mix of nutrients with water and roughage
113.x: Balanced (healthy) diet – An optimal mix of carbohydrate, protein and fat with adequate water and roughage (fibre), plus vitamins and minerals

113.s: Which part of food gives no energy but adds bulk and prevents constipation?
113.x: Roughage (dietary fibre) – Gives no energy but adds bulk and helps expel undigested food (prevents constipation)

113.s: Which of these is not a food made by plants?
113.x: Foods made by plants – Carbohydrates, fats and proteins; nucleic acids are genetic material, not a food

113.s: What share of soybean is protein?
113.x: Soybean – Rich in all three – protein (~40%), fat (~20%) and carbohydrate

113.s: What kind of product is oatmeal?
113.x: Oatmeal – A cereal-grain product; sago and arrowroot are starches from stems or roots; soya flour is from a legume

113.s: Why do we need more fat-rich food in winter?
113.x: Winter – Needs more fat-rich (energy-dense) food to keep the body warm

113.s: In which kind of exercise does fat supply ~50% or more of the fuel?
113.x: Exercise fuel – Carbohydrate (muscle glycogen, blood glucose) fuels hard and endurance exercise; in prolonged low-moderate exercise fat supplies ~50% or more

113.s: What is ATP called in the cell?
113.x: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) – Energy currency of the cell; glucose is the fuel, pyruvic acid the product of glycolysis

113.s: Why do salted chips make you thirsty?
o: Extra sodium raises the salt concentration of body fluids
113.x: Salted chips – Make you thirsty – the extra sodium raises the salt concentration of body fluids

113.s: Which of these has the most caffeine by dry weight?
113.x: Caffeine (equal dry weight) – Tea leaves (~3–4%) > coffee beans (~1–2%)

113.s: What is the H : O ratio in carbohydrates, Cx(H2O)y?
113.x: Carbohydrates – Cx(H2O)y (H : O = 2 : 1); contain C, H and O

113.s: Which class of carbohydrates do ribose, glucose and fructose belong to?
113.x: Classes – Monosaccharides (ribose, glucose, fructose), oligosaccharides / disaccharides (maltose, lactose, sucrose), polysaccharides (cellulose, starch)

113.s: What is the formula of sucrose?
113.x: Formulae – Glucose and fructose C6H12O6; sucrose C12H22O11; starch (C6H10O5)n

113.s: What kind of carbohydrate is starch?
113.x: Starch – A polysaccharide (glucose polymer); the iodine test turns it blue-black

113.s: Which plant glucose polymer gives no colour with iodine?
113.x: Cellulose – Gives no colour with iodine; like starch, a plant glucose polymer

113.s: Which enzyme makes starchy food taste sweet on chewing?
113.x: Taste of starch – Almost tasteless; on chewing, salivary amylase turns it into maltose, so starchy food tastes sweet

113.s: Which is the sweetest natural sugar?
113.x: Fructose – Fruit sugar, the sweetest natural sugar; gives fruits their sweet taste

113.s: Which sugar combines with glucose to form sucrose?
113.x: Sucrose – Glucose + fructose (disaccharide); sugarcane juice is mainly sucrose (cane sugar)

113.s: Which sugar is the main sugar of honey?
113.x: Honey – Mainly fructose (~38%) > glucose (~31%); sucrose and maltose minor; not a colloid

113.s: Which order of sweetness is correct?
113.x: Relative sweetness – Fructose > sucrose > glucose > maltose (> lactose)

113.s: What is the mixture of glucose and fructose made by hydrolysis of sucrose called?
113.x: Invert sugar – Glucose + fructose made by hydrolysis of sucrose; sweeter than sucrose because of its free fructose

113.s: Which was the first popular artificial sweetener?
113.x: Saccharin (ortho-sulphobenzimide) – First popular artificial sweetener (~550× sucrose)

113.s: Which artificial sweetener is a dipeptide about 100 times as sweet as cane sugar?
113.x: Aspartame – Most widely used; dipeptide, about 100 times as sweet as cane sugar

113.s: Which sweetener is about 2,000 times as sweet as sucrose?
113.x: Alitame – High-potency sweetener (~2000×)

113.s: Which sweetener is a trichloro derivative of sucrose?
113.x: Sucralose – Modified sugar – trichloro derivative of sucrose (~600×)

113.s: What kind of sweetener is stevia?
113.x: Stevia – Natural sweetener

113.s: Why are unsaturated fats more reactive?
113.x: Unsaturated fats – Have C=C double bonds, so they are more reactive (oxidise, go rancid, can be hydrogenated); saturated fats have only single bonds

113.s: Which oilseed has the most α-linolenic acid (omega-3)?
113.x: Linseed (flaxseed) oil – Most α-linolenic acid (omega-3) among oilseeds

113.s: What does a "no trans-fats" label mean?
113.x: "No trans-fats" – No partially hydrogenated oils – better for heart health (animal fats may still be used)

113.s: From which fatty acids are eicosanoids made?
113.x: Eicosanoids – Signalling molecules from 20-carbon fatty acids (arachidonic acid)

113.s: What do prostaglandins mediate?
113.x: Prostaglandins – Inflammation, pain, fever

113.s: What do thromboxanes do?
113.x: Thromboxanes – Blood clotting

113.s: What do leukotrienes mediate?
113.x: Leukotrienes – Allergic and inflammatory responses

113.s: What units are terpenes built from?
113.x: Terpenes – Hydrocarbons built from isoprene units; terpenoids include plant growth hormones (gibberellins) and pigments

113.s: Which of these liquids has the lowest boiling point?
113.x: Boiling points – Mercury ~357 °C > water 100 °C > benzene 80 °C > ethanol 78 °C

113.s: Why does iron from the fridge feel colder than wood at the same temperature?
o: It is a good conductor that draws heat faster
113.x: Conduction – Iron from the fridge feels colder than wood at the same temperature – a good conductor draws heat from the hand faster

113.s: Which mode of heat transfer do air-conditioners and heaters use to circulate air?
113.x: Convection – Air-conditioners and heaters circulate air (cool air sinks, warm air rises)

113.s: By which process do mothballs (naphthalene) work?
113.x: Sublimation – Solid → gas; mothballs (naphthalene) work by it

113.s: What is deposition?
113.x: Deposition – Gas → solid

113.s: What is the specific heat of kerosene?
113.x: Specific heat – Heat to raise 1 g by 1 °C; water has a high value (1) – a watermelon stays cool longer than an apple; kerosene ≈ 0.5 cal/g °C

113.s: How many joules is one calorie?
113.x: Calorie – 1 calorie ≈ 4.2 J (4.186)

113.s: What happens to a corked glass bottle full of water in the freezer?
113.x: Freezing water – Expands ~9% – a corked glass bottle full of water breaks in the freezer

113.s: To what temperature does water contract when heated from 0 °C?
113.x: Anomalous expansion – Water contracts from 0 °C to 4 °C (maximum density) and expands above it

113.s: What is cooling a liquid below its freezing point without it solidifying called?
113.x: Supercooling – Cooling a liquid below its freezing point without it solidifying

113.s: What does dissolved salt do to the boiling point of water?
113.x: Dissolved salt – Raises the boiling point and lowers the freezing point (colligative); salt in boiling water stops the boil until the new, higher boiling point; rock salt melts ice on roads

113.s: What does pressure do to the melting point of ice?
113.x: Pressure on ice – Lowers its melting point (regelation) – ice skating

113.s: Why does the temperature of melting ice stay at 0 °C?
113.x: Melting ice – Stays at 0 °C (latent heat of fusion)

113.s: What is the triple point of water?
113.x: Triple point of water – 0.01 °C (273.16 K, ~611.657 Pa)

113.s: Which materials are used for sound-proofing?
113.x: Sound-proofing – Rockwool, wood, laminated glass

113.s: Which kitchen practice saves LPG?
113.x: Kitchen – Copper-bottomed pans – copper conducts heat better than steel; a small LPG burner saves gas

113.s: How do a brick and a feather fall without air resistance?
113.x: Free fall – Without air resistance all bodies fall with the same g – brick and feather land together (Galileo; Apollo 15)

113.s: What is change of position with time called?
113.x: Motion – Change of position with time (strictly, change of position = displacement)

113.s: What is the shortest path between initial and final position called?
113.x: Displacement – Shortest path between initial and final position (distance = actual path)

113.s: What is the velocity of a body thrown up at its maximum height?
113.x: Body thrown up – At maximum height its velocity is 0

113.s: Which laws cover inertia, F = ma and action–reaction?
113.x: Newton's laws – 1st – inertia: rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts; 2nd – F = ma; 3rd – action–reaction

113.s: In which of these activities does friction help?
113.x: Friction – Slows a moving object; acts in brakes, striking a match, walking and writing with a pencil

113.s: Which force causes the tides?
113.x: Gravity – Planets' revolution (in near-vacuum), rolling rock, tides

113.s: How does the value of g change as one goes down a deep mine?
113.x: g – Decreases with depth below the surface (and with height) – weight decreases slightly in a deep mine

113.s: What will a ball released from an orbiting satellite do?
113.x: Ball released from an orbiting satellite – Keeps its orbital speed and revolves in the same orbit

113.s: How many classes of levers are there?
113.x: Levers – 3 classes – fulcrum, load or effort in the middle

113.s: Which law explains a man on frictionless ice moving by whistling?
113.x: Conservation of momentum – With no external force, momentum cannot change – a man on frictionless ice can move by whistling

113.s: Which gas law explains an air bubble growing as it rises in a lake?
113.x: Boyle's law – V ∝ 1/P at constant T – an air bubble grows as it rises in a lake

113.s: Which gas law explains a balloon swelling in hot water?
113.x: Charles's law – V ∝ T at constant P – a balloon in hot water swells

113.s: What happens to two sheets of paper when air is blown fast between them?
113.x: Bernoulli – Fast air blown between two sheets lowers the pressure there → the papers come closer

113.s: Which property lets water striders walk on water?
113.x: Surface tension – Lets insects (water striders) walk on water

113.s: What happens to the lake level when stones in a boat are thrown into the lake?
113.x: Floating – Stones in a boat displace their weight of water; thrown in, only their volume – the lake level falls

113.s: What is the density of water?
113.x: Density of water – ≈ 1 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³), highest at 4 °C

113.s: What did Otto von Guericke's hemispheres experiment demonstrate?
113.x: Otto von Guericke (17th century) – Pumped the air out of two hollow metal hemispheres – they could not be pulled apart, showing the force of atmospheric pressure

113.s: What does aerobic respiration need?
113.x: Aerobic respiration – Needs oxygen → CO2 + water + energy

113.s: What does anaerobic respiration produce in muscle?
113.x: Anaerobic respiration – In muscle → lactic acid; in yeast → ethanol + CO2 (yeast fermentation)

113.s: Which of these processes is endothermic?
113.x: Nature – Continuous (day and night) and exothermic; composting is exothermic; sweating (evaporation) is endothermic

113.s: Which stage of glucose oxidation produces pyruvic acid?
113.x: Glycolysis – First stage of glucose oxidation → pyruvic acid

113.s: What is ATP synthesis via the electron transport chain called?
113.x: Oxidative phosphorylation – ATP made via the electron transport chain (photophosphorylation in photosynthesis)

113.s: How many chromosomes does a human body cell have?
113.x: Humans – 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs: 22 autosome pairs (44 autosomes) + 1 sex pair

113.s: Which sex chromosome pair do birds have?
113.x: Sex chromosomes – XY male, XX female; ZW in birds; genes pass through both sperm and egg

113.s: Which codon is the start codon (methionine)?
113.x: Genetic code – Triplet codon, nearly universal; AUG = start (methionine); stop = UAA, UAG, UGA

113.s: What is variation?
o: Differences among individuals of a species
113.x: Variation – Differences among individuals of a species

113.s: What fixes the limit of growth of an organism?
113.x: Limit of growth – Fixed by internal (genetic, hormonal) factors

113.s: What is the DNA content of a cell in G2 and prophase?
113.x: DNA content – G1, telophase = 2C; G2, prophase = 4C

113.s: What is the ratio of chromosomes in somatic cells to gametes?
113.x: Chromosome ratio – Somatic : gamete = 2 : 1 (2n : n)

113.s: What is egg shell mostly made of?
113.x: Egg shell – ~95% calcium carbonate; dissolved in acid, it leaves a semi-permeable membrane – the egg shrinks in salt water (hypertonic), swells in plain water

113.s: Which part of the cell is its control centre?
113.x: Nucleus – Control centre; nucleolus makes ribosomes

113.s: Which organelle is the powerhouse of the cell?
113.x: Mitochondria – Powerhouse (ATP) – removing them stops energy metabolism

113.s: What do chloroplasts do?
113.x: Chloroplasts – Make food

113.s: What do ribosomes do?
113.x: Ribosomes – Protein synthesis

113.s: What does the cell membrane do?
113.x: Cell membrane – Regulates passage

113.s: Which structure is found only in plant cells?
113.x: Plant cells only – Cellulose cell wall (both cell types have vacuoles, membrane, Golgi)

113.s: What does the cytoskeleton regulate?
113.x: Cytoskeleton – Regulates cell shape, moves chromosomes, drives cytoplasmic streaming (plant and animal cells)

113.s: Which pigments give chromoplasts their yellow, orange and red colour?
113.x: Chromoplasts – Carotenoid pigments (carotene, xanthophyll) → yellow, orange, red; chloroplasts hold chlorophyll

113.s: What colour are leucoplasts, which store nutrients?
113.x: Leucoplasts – Colourless, store nutrients – amyloplasts (starch, e.g. potato), elaioplasts (oils, fats), aleuroplasts (proteins)

113.s: What happens in prophase of mitosis?
o: Chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope dissolves
113.x: Prophase – Chromosomes condense, nuclear envelope dissolves, spindle forms

113.s: Where do chromosomes align during metaphase?
113.x: Metaphase – Chromosomes align on the equatorial plane; spindle fibres attach to centromeres

113.s: What separates and moves to opposite poles in anaphase?
113.x: Anaphase – Sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles, becoming individual chromosomes

113.s: What happens to chromosomes in telophase?
113.x: Telophase – Chromosomes unwind into chromatin

113.s: What share of a cell's mass are proteins?
113.x: Cell composition (% of mass) – Water 70–90; proteins 10–15; nucleic acids 5–7; carbohydrates 3; lipids 2

113.s: About how much energy is released when one mole of ATP is hydrolysed to ADP?
113.x: ATP = adenosine triphosphate – The cell's energy molecule (energy currency); ATP → ADP releases ~30.5 kJ/mol (7.3 kcal)

113.s: What kind of polymer of beta-glucose is cellulose, the main carbohydrate of plant cell walls?
113.x: Cellulose – Structural carbohydrate of plant cell walls; homopolymer of β-glucose; most abundant organic compound on Earth

113.s: Which metal ion lies at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule?
113.x: Chlorophyll – Central ion = magnesium

113.s: Besides glycerol and two fatty acids, which group does a phospholipid such as lecithin contain?
113.x: Phospholipids – Glycerol + two fatty acids + a phosphate group – major component of cell membranes (e.g. lecithin)

113.s: With which biomolecules are fatty acids combined in glycolipids?
113.x: Glycolipids – Fatty acids + carbohydrates

113.s: Which organism commonly reproduces by binary fission?
113.x: Binary fission – Amoeba

113.s: Which pair of organisms reproduces asexually by budding?
113.x: Budding – Yeast, Hydra

113.s: Which flatworm is the classic example of reproduction by regeneration?
113.x: Regeneration – Planaria

113.s: Which bread mould reproduces by forming spores?
113.x: Spores – Rhizopus

113.s: By which process does Paramecium reproduce sexually?
113.x: Unicellular organisms – Also reproduce sexually: Paramecium (conjugation), Chlamydomonas, yeast

113.s: What is the term for one species evolving into many forms suited to different niches?
113.x: Adaptive radiation – One species → many forms for different niches

113.s: Which structures came before the first primitive cells in the sequence of biogeny?
113.x: Biogeny sequence – Coacervates → first cells (mycoplasma-like) → heterotrophs → aerobes

113.s: At what standard setting does a hot-air oven sterilise glassware?
113.x: Hot-air oven – Sterilises glassware at 160 °C for 60 min (170 °C/30 min, 180 °C/20 min)

113.s: Which preservative, coded E211, is used in soft drinks, pickles and sauces?
113.x: Sodium benzoate / benzoic acid (E211) – Soft drinks, pickles, sauces (acidic foods)

113.s: Which preservative is most commonly used against moulds and yeasts in cheese and cooked foods?
113.x: Sorbic acid / potassium sorbate – Most common against moulds, yeasts, fungi and bacteria – cheese, pickles, cooked foods

113.s: In which foods is sodium metabisulphite commonly used as a preservative?
113.x: Sodium metabisulphite – Jams, sauces

113.s: Which preservative gas is used for dried fruits and in winemaking?
113.x: SO2 – Dried fruits, winemaking

113.s: Which preservatives are used mainly for stored grains and cheese?
113.x: Propionates – Stored grains, cheese

113.s: Which acid is vinegar, used to preserve pickles?
113.x: Vinegar (acetic acid) – Pickles; made by fermenting sugarcane juice

113.s: Which preservative is old and no longer used because it is toxic?
113.x: Boric acid – Old, no longer used (toxic)

113.s: Which bread improver was removed from permitted additives by FSSAI in 2016 as a possible carcinogen?
113.x: Potassium bromate (bread improver) – Removed from permitted additives by FSSAI (2016) – possible carcinogen

113.s: What are substances added intentionally to food, like preservatives, colours and emulsifiers, called?
113.x: Food additives – Added intentionally to improve food (preservatives, colours, emulsifiers, sweeteners, flavour enhancers)

113.s: What is the term for adding inferior or harmful substances to food?
113.x: Adulteration – Adding inferior/harmful substances; causes poisoning, allergies, nutritional deficiency

113.s: For what is MSG (Ajinomoto) used in food?
113.x: MSG (Ajinomoto) – Flavour enhancer, umami

113.s: Which of these is an artificial or low-calorie sweetener and not a natural sugar?
113.x: Sweeteners – Aspartame and stevia; fructose is a natural sugar

113.s: What kind of food additives are tartrazine and sunset yellow?
113.x: Artificial food colours – Tartrazine, sunset yellow – mostly coal-tar dyes

113.s: What is adding iodine to salt or iron, folic acid and B12 to rice called?
113.x: Fortification – Iodised salt; rice with iron, folic acid, B12; oil/milk with A and D; FSSAI logo "+F"

113.s: How long can gamma irradiation keep potato and onion fresh without cold storage?
113.x: Irradiation – Ionising (gamma) radiation kills organisms without much nutrient loss; potato/onion shelf life 8 months without cold storage; DAE: 25 irradiators in PPP mode

113.s: How many irradiation units were approved under the Cold Chain scheme of PM Kisan Sampada Yojana (Aug 2025)?
113.x: PM Kisan Sampada Yojana (MoFPI) – Cold Chain scheme: 16 irradiation units approved, 9 operational (Aug 2025)

113.s: Which dual certification does the "One Nation, One Regulator" food reform of July 2026 end?
113.x: Jul 2026 reforms – Food Safety on Wheels, blockchain batch tracing, "One Nation, One Regulator" ends dual BIS/AGMARK certification

113.s: How does cold storage keep fruits fresh longer?
o: It lowers their rate of respiration
113.x: Cold storage – Low temperature lowers the rate of respiration of fruits

113.s: At what temperature or below should frozen meat such as pork be stored?
113.x: Frozen storage – Meat such as pork at −18 °C or below; 3–5 °C is only chilling

113.s: What does IQF stand for in frozen food processing?
113.x: IQF – Individually Quick Frozen – each piece frozen separately and fast

113.s: How does drying preserve food?
o: It adds salt to the food
It removes the moisture microbes need
113.x: Drying (sun drying, dehydration) – Removes the moisture microbes need

113.s: Which substance is the common desiccant packed in moisture-absorbing packets?
113.x: Silica gel – Common desiccant (absorbs moisture in packets)

113.s: What causes food spoilage that refrigeration, drying and canning prevent?
o: Exposure to air, moisture and microbes
113.x: Spoilage – Exposure to air, moisture, microbes causes it; prevented by refrigeration, drying, salting, canning, preservatives

113.s: Which process causes rancidity of fats and oils?
113.x: Rancidity – Oxidation of fats and oils (check the manufacture date of fried foods); nitrogen-flushed chip packets prevent it

113.s: What is the recrystallisation of starch, the main cause of stale bread, called?
113.x: Retrogradation of starch – Recrystallisation – main cause of staleness of bread

113.s: Which enzyme makes a cut apple turn brown?
113.x: Cut apple turns brown – Polyphenol oxidase oxidises phenols in air (enzymatic browning)

113.s: What causes blackheart of potato in storage?
113.x: Blackheart of potato – Oxygen deficiency in storage (an abiotic disorder)

113.s: Which gaseous plant hormone causes fruit ripening?
113.x: Ethylene – Gaseous plant hormone for fruit ripening (and the gas used for artificial ripening)

113.s: Which gas released by calcium carbide is used illegally to ripen mangoes?
113.x: Calcium carbide – Releases acetylene, which acts like ethylene – (illegally) used to ripen mangoes

113.s: Which disease is caused by adulteration of mustard oil with argemone oil?
113.x: Mustard oil – Argemone oil/seeds – epidemic dropsy

113.s: Which adulterants are commonly found in turmeric?
113.x: Turmeric – Metanil yellow, lead chromate

113.s: Of which food are urea and starch typical adulterants?
113.x: Milk / chilli – Water, urea, starch / brick powder, Sudan dyes

113.s: Which food was Rhodamine B, banned in Tamil Nadu in 2024, illegally used to colour?
113.x: Rhodamine B – Textile dye illegally used to colour cotton candy; carcinogenic; sale banned in Tamil Nadu (Feb 2024)

113.s: In which products is aristolochic acid found?
113.x: Aristolochic acid – Aristolochia plants in some herbal medicines

113.s: Which chemical is found in polycarbonate plastics, food-can linings and thermal receipts?
113.x: BPA – Polycarbonate plastics, food-can linings, thermal receipts

113.s: Which antibacterial chemical is found in soaps, toothpaste and deodorants?
113.x: Triclosan – Antibacterial soaps, toothpaste, deodorants

113.s: Which toxic metal comes from old paints, pipes and chromate-adulterated spices?
113.x: Lead – Old paints, pipes, cosmetics, lead-chromate spices (not an MRI contrast agent)

113.s: Which chemicals are used as PVC plasticisers in toys and cosmetics?
113.x: Phthalates – PVC plasticisers, toys, cosmetics

113.s: Which organisms produce aflatoxins on badly stored grain?
113.x: Aflatoxins – Made by moulds (*Aspergillus flavus*, *A. parasiticus*) on badly stored grain and oilseeds; not destroyed by cooking

113.s: What are chemicals like BPA and phthalates that mimic or block hormones called?
113.x: Endocrine disruptors – Man-made chemicals (BPA, phthalates, some pesticides) that mimic or block hormones

113.s: Which sterol is found in vegetable fats, in place of cholesterol in animal fats?
113.x: Oils and fats – Lubricant mineral oil = petroleum; vegetable fats = phytosterol; animal fats = cholesterol

113.s: What is the severe fall in blood pressure seen in serious food allergy called?
113.x: Food allergy signs – Flushing/hives, swelling of lips and throat (difficulty swallowing, speaking), fall in blood pressure (anaphylaxis)

113.s: Which animal phylum has ostia, osculum and choanocytes and a cellular level of organisation?
113.x: Porifera – Ostia, osculum, choanocytes; cellular level

113.s: Which phylum has polyp and medusa body forms and a tissue level of organisation?
113.x: Cnidaria – Polyp and medusa; tissue level

113.s: Which phylum has comb plates and shows bioluminescence?
113.x: Ctenophora – Comb plates, bioluminescence

113.s: Which phylum is organ-level and acoelomate?
113.x: Platyhelminthes – Organ level; acoelomates

113.s: Why are Aschelminthes called roundworms?
o: Their body is circular in cross-section
113.x: Aschelminthes (roundworms) – Body circular in cross-section (hence the name); organ-system level; pseudocoelomates

113.s: Which phylum is named for its jointed appendages?
113.x: Arthropoda – Jointed appendages

113.s: Which phylum has a water vascular system?
113.x: Echinodermata – Water vascular system

113.s: Which group of animals has a true mesoderm-lined body cavity?
113.x: Coelomates (mesoderm-lined cavity) – Annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates, chordates

113.s: What type of body symmetry do all chordates show?
113.x: Symmetry – All chordates are bilateral; many non-chordates are radial

113.s: Which animal is a marsupial that carries its young in a pouch?
113.x: Marsupial – Koala (pouch)

113.s: To which group of animals does Clarias belong?
113.x: Clarias – Catfish (Pisces); Bufo, Rana, Hyla are amphibians

113.s: Which bird lacks a crop?
113.x: Emu – Has no crop

113.s: Into which structures is the first pair of legs of a centipede modified?
113.x: Centipedes – First legs → poison claws (forcipules)

113.s: Which two vertebrate groups have a dicondylic skull?
113.x: Skull – Mammals and amphibians dicondylic; reptiles and birds monocondylic

113.s: What kind of beak do insect-eating birds have?
113.x: Beaks – Insect-eaters long and sharp; seed-eaters short and strong

113.s: Through which structures do grasshoppers and cockroaches breathe?
113.x: Grasshopper, cockroach (insects) – Breathe through tracheae (spiracles); cockroach has open circulation

113.s: Which pair of animals shows cutaneous respiration (breathing through the skin)?
113.x: Cutaneous respiration – Frog and earthworm

113.s: How does Amoeba take in its food?
113.x: Protozoa (Amoeba) – Take food by phagocytosis; digest it with enzymes in food vacuoles

113.s: Which feature of birds' bones helps them fly?
113.x: Birds – Pneumatic (air-filled) bones

113.s: From which country does the Chihuahua dog breed come?
113.x: Chihuahua – Dog breed from Mexico

113.s: What kind of venom do the krait and cobra have?
113.x: Krait (and cobra) venom – Neurotoxic – neuroparalysis

113.s: What kind of venom do Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper have?
113.x: Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper venom – Haemotoxic – disrupts blood clotting; pythons are non-venomous

113.s: What is an animal called that harms you by biting or stinging you?
113.x: Poisonous vs venomous – Poisonous – harms if you bite or eat it; venomous – it bites or stings you

113.s: Of which organ is the sting of a wasp a modified form?
113.x: Wasp sting (modified ovipositor) – To defend self and colony; solitary wasps paralyse prey

113.s: Which reptile is popularly known for changing colour to protect itself?
113.x: Chameleon – Changes colour to protect itself (strictly, for signalling and temperature)

113.s: What are the sterile female honeybees that collect nectar and make honey called?
113.x: Worker bees (sterile females) – Collect nectar and pollen, make honey and wax; the queen lays eggs

113.s: Which serum enzyme rises in a downer cow?
113.x: Downer cow – Serum creatine phosphokinase rises

113.s: How many lobes does the left lung of a cow have?
113.x: Left lung of cow – 3 lobes

113.s: With which substances is rumen lactic acidosis in cattle treated?
113.x: Rumen lactic acidosis – Treated with alkalis; vinegar is used for urea poisoning

113.s: In which artery is a dog's pulse usually felt?
113.x: Dog pulse – Femoral artery

113.s: Which is the preferred post-mortem sample in veterinary diagnosis of abortion?
113.x: Post-mortem sample – Aborted fetus

113.s: What is a veterinary drug paste made with honey or jaggery called?
113.x: Electuary – Drug paste with honey or jaggery

113.s: What is saurology the study of?
113.x: Saurology – Lizards

113.s: What is mycology the study of?
113.x: Mycology – Fungi

113.s: What is palynology the study of?
113.x: Palynology – Pollen

113.s: What is oncology the study of?
113.x: Oncology – Tumours

113.s: What is palaeontology the study of?
113.x: Palaeontology – Fossils

113.s: What is entomology the study of?
113.x: Entomology – Insects

113.s: What is limnology the study of?
113.x: Limnology – Fresh waters

113.s: About how many nanometres is the shortest wavelength of red light, the longest band of the visible spectrum?
113.x: Visible spectrum (VIBGYOR) – Wavelength rises from violet to red (orange > yellow > indigo > violet); red is the longest (~620–750 nm)

113.s: Why does grass look green?
113.x: Colour of objects – An opaque object shows the colour it reflects – grass looks green because it reflects green

113.s: What are the three primary colours of light?
113.x: Primary colours of light – Red, green, blue

113.s: What kind of light source does a TV remote use?
113.x: TV remote – Infrared LED

113.s: How does a water tank look from above because of refraction?
113.x: Refraction – Change of direction (bending) of light passing into another medium – a tank looks shallower

113.s: What causes the twinkling of stars?
113.x: Atmospheric refraction – Twinkling of stars; Sun seen ~2 min before sunrise and after sunset

113.s: What is the splitting of white light into seven colours by a prism called?
113.x: Dispersion – Splitting of white light into seven colours by a prism (each colour refracted differently); the rainbow

113.s: Which optical phenomenon makes the sky blue and the Sun red at sunrise and sunset?
113.x: Scattering – Blue sky, red Sun at sunrise and sunset

113.s: What limits how small the aperture of a pinhole camera can usefully be?
113.x: Pinhole camera – Smallest aperture limited by diffraction

113.s: What principle of light does Fermat's principle state?
113.x: Fermat's principle – Principle of least time (light)

113.s: Which device converts AC into DC?
113.x: Rectifier – AC → DC (inverter: DC → AC)

113.s: What happens to a 110 V heater connected to the Indian 230 V supply?
o: It draws about 4 times its power and burns out
It draws twice the current but stays safe
113.x: Indian supply – 230 V, 50 Hz – a 110 V heater draws ~4× its power and burns out within seconds or minutes

113.s: On which factor does the resistivity of a conductor NOT depend?
113.x: Resistivity – Depends on material and temperature, not on shape (resistance does)

113.s: What is the resistance of an insulator practically equal to?
113.x: Insulators – Practically infinite resistance

113.s: What happens to the resistance of a semiconductor when it is heated?
113.x: Semiconductor – Resistance decreases on heating (a metal's increases)

113.s: What is the condition called when resistance falls to nearly zero and current rises heavily, melting a fuse?
113.x: Short circuit – Resistance ≈ 0 → current increases heavily; a fuse melts on heavy current

113.s: Which instrument detects current and its direction and serves as the null detector in bridges?
113.x: Galvanometer – Detects current and its direction; null detector in bridges; more sensitive (not more accurate) than an ammeter

113.s: On which principle does a transformer work?
113.x: Transformer – Works on mutual induction

113.s: What type of wave is sound in air?
113.x: Sound – Longitudinal mechanical wave; cannot travel in vacuum (ultrasound too)

113.s: About how much does the speed of sound in air rise per 1 °C rise in temperature?
113.x: Speed – Rises with temperature (~0.6 m/s per °C in air)

113.s: In which medium can both longitudinal and transverse mechanical waves travel?
113.x: Solids – Carry both longitudinal and transverse waves

113.s: On which property of a sound wave does its loudness depend?
113.x: Loudness – Depends on amplitude; pitch on frequency

113.s: On which factor alone does the frequency of a sound wave depend?
113.x: Frequency – Depends only on the source (same in every medium); speed and wavelength change with the medium

113.s: At what minimum distance must a reflector be to hear a distinct echo (sound at 344 m/s)?
113.x: Echo – Reflected sound must arrive ≥ 0.1 s later → reflector at least 17.2 m away (344 m/s)

113.s: Why do women's voices usually have a higher pitch than men's?
113.x: Women's voices – Higher pitch (shorter, thinner vocal cords)

113.s: How is an instrument protected from external magnetic fields (magnetic shielding)?
o: By placing it in a plastic box
By placing it inside soft iron of high permeability
113.x: Magnetic shielding – Put the instrument inside soft iron of high permeability

113.s: What is the expulsion of a magnetic field by a superconductor called?
113.x: Superconductors – Perfect diamagnetism – the Meissner effect (they expel a magnetic field); superconductivity is destroyed above a critical magnetic field

113.s: In which kind of magnetism do adjacent spins align in opposite directions and cancel out?
113.x: Antiferromagnetism – Adjacent magnetic moments (spins) align in opposite directions and cancel – no net magnetic moment

113.s: Which group of metals are ferromagnetic and keep their magnetisation?
113.x: Ferromagnets – Iron, nickel, cobalt – keep magnetisation

113.s: Which plant part is turmeric?
113.x: Turmeric – Rhizome (underground stem)

113.s: Which modified plant part is ginger?
113.x: Ginger – Rhizome

113.s: Which part of the chicory plant is roasted and mixed with coffee?
113.x: Chicory (mixed with coffee) – Roasted root

113.s: Of which plant is hing (asafoetida) the dried gum-resin?
113.x: Hing (asafoetida) – Dried gum-resin from the roots/rhizome of *Ferula*

113.s: Which plant part is clove?
113.x: Clove – Dried unopened flower bud (*Syzygium aromaticum*)

113.s: Of which tree is chilgoza the edible seed?
113.x: Chilgoza – Edible seed of the pine *Pinus gerardiana*

113.s: Which plant part is the potato?
113.x: Potato – Underground stem (tuber) with eyes/buds

113.s: Which plant part is the sweet potato?
113.x: Sweet potato – Modified (tuberous) root

113.s: Of which plant part are the corms arbi and jimikand a modified form?
113.x: Arbi, jimikand – Corms – stems (ginger and sugarcane also store food in stems)

113.s: Which plant part are carrot and turnip?
113.x: Carrot, turnip – Roots

113.s: Which plant part of groundnut do we eat (as the pod)?
113.x: Groundnut – Fruit

113.s: How are cultivated (seedless) bananas propagated?
113.x: Banana – Propagated vegetatively by suckers (cultivated bananas are seedless)

113.s: To which plant family do tomato, potato, brinjal and chilli belong?
113.x: Tomato – Family Solanaceae (with potato, brinjal, chilli)

113.s: In what are papaya, mango, peaches and apricots especially rich?
113.x: Papaya, mango, peaches, apricots – Rich in antioxidants, carbohydrates and soluble fibre

113.s: Which carotenoid pigment gives tomato and watermelon their red colour?
113.x: Lycopene – Red of tomato (a carotenoid; also watermelon)

113.s: Which pigment gives carrots their orange colour?
113.x: Carotene – Orange (carrot)

113.s: Which yellow xanthophyll pigment is found in marigold, egg yolk and the eye's macula?
113.x: Lutein – Yellow xanthophyll (marigold, egg yolk, eye macula)

113.s: Which pigment: Red, pink, blue, purple flowers (in cell sap); yellow/orange flowers = carotenoids?
113.x: Anthocyanins – Red, pink, blue, purple flowers (in cell sap); yellow/orange flowers = carotenoids

113.s: Which compound gives chilli its pungency (heat)?
113.x: Capsaicin – Pungency (heat) of chilli – not a colour

113.s: What is the main protein of milk?
113.x: Milk – An emulsion (fat in water); casein is its main protein

113.s: What is the protein skin that forms on boiled milk called?
113.x: Lactoderm – Protein skin on boiled milk

113.s: Which pigment in the milk fat makes cow's milk slightly yellow?
113.x: Cow's milk is slightly yellow – Carotene (beta-carotene) in the milk fat; riboflavin only gives whey a greenish-yellow tint

113.s: How much fat does double toned milk contain?
